passages.text: Epigenetic modulation to overcome immune suppression in pancreatic cancer

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, primarily due to its highly fibrotic and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), which limits both drug delivery and immune cell infiltration. Epigenetic dysregulation plays a pivotal role in shaping these barriers by controlling transcriptional programs that govern tumor-immune interactions, stromal remodeling, and immune evasion.

This review synthesizes current insights into the contribution of aberrant epigenetic mechanisms to PDAC progression and immune resistance. We outline how epigenetic alterations suppress antigen presentation, sustain immunosuppressive cell populations, such as regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and tumor-associated macrophages, and upregulate immune checkpoint molecules across cancer and stromal compartments. Emerging evidence shows that epigenetic therapies targeting DNA methyltransferases, histone deacetylases, histone methyltransferases, or bromodomain proteins can restore tumor immunogenicity, reprogram cancer-associated fibroblasts, and promote cytotoxic T cell infiltration. Furthermore, combining epigenetic modulators with immune checkpoint blockade or targeted therapies has demonstrated the capacity to remodel the PDAC TME and convert immunologically 'cold' tumors into more responsive ones. Therefore, we also summarize key completed and ongoing clinical trials in PDAC and solid tumors, emphasizing outcomes and biomarker discoveries that support the translation of epigenetic-immunotherapy combinations into clinical practice. Finally, we discuss persistent challenges that impede progress, including poor drug penetration through the desmoplastic stroma, off-target effects and toxicity of epigenetic agents, tumor hypoxia, adaptive resistance, and the scarcity of physiologically relevant immuno-oncology models.

passages.text: Findings from preclinical and early clinical studies indicate that epigenetic reprogramming represents a promising avenue to overcome PDAC immunoresistance by reactivating antigen presentation, disrupting immunosuppressive cellular networks, and enhancing antitumor immunity. However, realizing this potential will require rationally designed combination regimens, predictive biomarkers for patient stratification, and a deeper understanding of cell type-specific and context-dependent epigenetic regulation. Only through these advances can the integration of epigenetic modulation with immunotherapy and stroma-targeting approaches ultimately redefine therapeutic strategies for patients with PDAC.
Introduction

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the most common and aggressive form of pancreatic cancer, accounting for more than 90% of all pancreatic malignancies. It arises from the epithelial tissue of the exocrine pancreas, originating from either ductal or acinar cells. PDAC is characterized by late clinical presentation, rapid disease progression, and poor prognosis, making it one of the deadliest cancers worldwide. Due to its largely asymptomatic course in the early stages, most patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage with distant metastases, resulting in a dismal 5-year survival rate of approximately 3%.

PDAC exhibits marked molecular heterogeneity influenced by its regional and cellular origin within the pancreas. The majority of PDAC cases arise sporadically, with only about 10% attributable to inherited mutations. The most frequent germline alterations occur in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, followed by PALB2, ATM, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, and CDKN2A. Other hereditary cancer syndromes associated with an elevated PDAC risk include familial adenomatous polyposis (APC), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, hereditary pancreatitis, and cystic fibrosis.

Sporadic PDAC, in contrast, is driven predominantly by somatic mutations, most notably in the KRAS gene, which occur in approximately 90% of cases and result in constitutive activation of Ras-GTPase signaling. Additional commonly altered genes include TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4, RNF43, ARID1A, TGFBR2, GNAS, RREB1, and PBRM1. In KRAS wild-type tumors, other components of the Ras pathway, such as GNAS, BRAF, and CTNNB1, are frequently mutated.

Despite advances in molecular understanding and therapeutic development, PDAC remains largely refractory to current treatments, including immunotherapy. Its aggressiveness is strongly influenced by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), dense desmoplastic stroma, and profound therapeutic resistance. The TME not only supports tumor growth and invasion but also actively facilitates escape from immune effector mechanisms.

PDAC is characterized by a low tumor mutational burden, leading to limited neoantigen generation and weak immunogenicity. Furthermore, oncogenic pathways, particularly KRAS and Wnt signaling, contribute to immune escape by downregulating antigen presentation, upregulating immune checkpoints such as PD-L1, and reshaping cytokine signaling to favor an immunosuppressive milieu. Consequently, PDAC is considered an immunologically 'cold' tumor, with poor infiltration of effector T cells and dominance of immunosuppressive cell populations such as regulatory T cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).

Given these challenges, therapeutic approaches that can remodel the TME and enhance immune responsiveness are urgently needed. Emerging evidence indicates that epigenetic regulation is a key contributor to PDAC pathogenesis and immune evasion. Aberrant DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and RNA-based regulatory mechanisms can silence tumor suppressor genes, disrupt antigen presentation, and attenuate interferon (IFN) signaling, further reinforcing immune tolerance. Conversely, pharmacologic modulation of the epigenome offers a promising strategy to promote immune recognition, enhance tumor immunogenicity, and sensitize PDAC to immunotherapy.

This review summarizes current knowledge on the epigenetic mechanisms underlying PDAC progression and immune resistance and discusses how epigenetic therapies, alone or in combination with immunotherapy, may help overcome the profound immune unresponsiveness characteristic of this malignancy.
The immunosuppressive landscape of PDAC

PDAC represents a complex ecosystem comprising not only malignant cells but also distinct subpopulations of non-cancerous cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix (ECM) components, collectively forming TME. Notably, the tumor stroma can constitute up to 90% of the tumor volume, significantly influencing tumor progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance.
Desmoplastic stroma

Epigenetic alterations associated with immunosuppressive and immune-activated tumor microenvironment (TME) states in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). A) Schematic representation of epigenetic dysregulation linked to the establishment of an immunosuppressive TME in PDAC. Aberrant activity of chromatin regulators, including EZH2, histone demethylases (KDM family members, LSD1), histone deacetylases (e.g., HDAC6), and DNA methyltransferases (DNMT1/3A/3B), drives transcriptional programs that promote stromal activation, desmoplasia, and immune exclusion. These alterations correlate with accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), enrichment of M2-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs), impaired dendritic cell (DC) maturation and antigen presentation, T cell dysfunction/exhaustion, upregulation of immune checkpoint pathways, as well as increased levels of immunosuppressive mediators, including TGF-beta, IL-6, and CXCL12. B) Conceptual model of therapy-associated epigenetic reprogramming leading to a more immune-permissive TME. Epigenetic modulation contributes to stromal reprogramming, reduction of immunosuppressive cell populations, enhanced DC activation, increased cytotoxic T cell and natural killer (NK) cell infiltration and function, elevated IFN-gamma and IL-12 production, together with decreased immune checkpoint expression, consistent with a shift toward an immune-activated ('hot') tumor phenotype.

Recent advancements in single-cell technologies have enabled detailed characterization of the heterogeneous PDAC TME, providing valuable insights into the diverse cellular interactions and functional states contributing to the malignancy and its response to treatment. PDAC TME is distinctly immunosuppressive and comprises a variety of infiltrating cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), MDSCs, TAMs, and Tregs (Fig. 1). It is characterized by either low infiltration or a dysfunctional state of effector cells such as T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), and natural killer (NK) cells.

A hallmark of PDAC is its extensive desmoplastic reaction, characterized by a dense, fibrotic stroma composed primarily of ECM proteins such as collagens, fibronectin, and proteoglycans, which are actively remodeled by CAFs. In response to tumor- and immune cell-derived signals, CAFs secrete large amounts of ECM components and matrix metalloproteinases, reinforcing a supportive scaffold for tumor expansion while simultaneously creating a physical barrier that hinders the penetration of therapeutic agents.

Beyond their structural contributions, CAFs play a central role in establishing an immunosuppressive environment. By releasing cytokines and chemokines, including transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta), interleukin (IL)-6, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), CAFs recruit suppressive immune cells, such as MDSCs and Tregs. This immune modulation further enables tumor cells to evade immune surveillance. Moreover, as PDAC tumors rapidly expand, they often outgrow their blood supply, resulting in hypoxic regions. CAFs respond to hypoxia by secreting additional pro-fibrotic and pro-angiogenic factors, thereby perpetuating a cycle of ECM remodeling, increased desmoplasia, and further hypoxia. The rigidity of the ECM, in turn, not only facilitates tumor cell migration and invasion but also alters cell signaling pathways that contribute to a more aggressive tumor phenotype.

Given the multifaceted contribution of CAFs and the TME in PDAC progression and treatment resistance, targeting these components has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. Approaches aimed at disrupting CAF activation, modulating ECM deposition, or inhibiting key cytokine pathways (such as TGF-beta signaling) may improve drug delivery, restore immune function, and ultimately enhance clinical outcomes. However, the widespread depletion of CAFs or the disruption of specific signaling pathways involved in CAF activation has been shown to accelerate PDAC progression. These findings highlight the complex role of CAFs in PDAC, suggesting that rather than complete depletion, targeted modulation of their activity may be a more effective therapeutic strategy.

In addition to CAFs, the PDAC TME contains several other cellular components. Cancer-associated mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) have been identified in PDAC and shown to promote malignant progression through paracrine signaling, including granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor-dependent mesenchymal-epithelial crosstalk that enhances invasion and metastatic potential. MSCs can further promote PDAC growth by skewing macrophages toward an alternatively activated (M2-like) phenotype, supporting a functional link between MSC-like stromal cells and immunosuppressive myeloid programming within the TME.

Endothelial cells in the PDAC TME contribute to the characteristic immune-excluded phenotype. Integrated proteogenomic analyses demonstrate that endothelial cell remodeling is associated with reduced infiltration of antitumor immune cells in immune-cold PDACs, highlighting a vascular component of immune suppression in this disease. Aberrant vascular pericyte dynamics also contribute to dysfunctional tumor vasculature and hypoxia. Strategies that increase pericyte coverage improve vascular normalization and perfusion, underscoring the role of mural cells in shaping the TME and potentially regulating immune cell access to the tumor.

Another major stromal population comprises pancreatic stellate cells (PSCs), which contribute to fibrosis and immunosuppression via cytokine and chemokine secretion as well as ECM remodeling. Finally, neural and Schwann cell components are increasingly recognized as active players in PDAC progression, including perineural invasion and dynamic crosstalk with CAFs and immune cells. Recent studies demonstrate that Schwann cells can reshape PDAC stromal states, including inflammatory CAF programs, and promote malignant progression, while Schwann-macrophage paracrine loops contribute to perineural invasion.

Although direct epigenetic interrogation of these stromal TME components in PDAC remains limited, they represent an important non-immune axis through which epigenetic therapies could indirectly sensitize tumors to immunotherapy. Accordingly, integrating strategies that target both malignant cells and their supportive stroma holds promise for improving therapeutic efficacy. Nevertheless, careful consideration of the complex TME is essential to avoid unintended consequences.
Tumor immune microenvironment

Besides desmoplastic stroma, PDAC is characterized by an immunosuppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), which severely limits the effectiveness of antitumor immune responses. A defining feature of PDAC is its classification as a 'cold' tumor, meaning it lacks a robust immune infiltrate capable of mounting an effective antitumor response. Within this 'cold' tumor landscape, PDAC can exhibit two distinct immune phenotypes: immune desert and immune exclusion.

Immune desert tumors are defined by a profound lack of immune cell infiltration, particularly cytotoxic T cells, within both the tumor parenchyma and surrounding stroma. This immune evasion can result from several factors, including low tumor immunogenicity, inadequate antigen presentation, and elevated concentrations of immunosuppressive cytokines such as TGF-beta, IL-10, and IL-35. In this setting, the immune system fails to recognize the tumor, leading to minimal antitumor activity. Immune exclusion tumors, on the other hand, contain immune cells, including CD8+ T cells, but these cells are restricted to the peritumoral stroma and fail to infiltrate the tumor core. This exclusion is often mediated by physical barriers, such as desmoplastic stroma, as well as by molecular signals, including TGF-beta, VEGF, and activation of the beta-catenin pathway. In addition, hypoxia, through the activity of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), promotes angiogenesis and metabolic reprogramming, thereby further impairing immune cell function and restricting their access to the tumor. Within this immunosuppressive context, T cells often exist in an exhausted and dysfunctional state, characterized by sustained expression of inhibitory immune checkpoints such as PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3. This exhaustion severely limits their cytotoxic capacity, reducing their ability to recognize and eliminate tumor cells. Tregs, which include both thymus-derived Tregs (tTregs) and peripherally induced Tregs (pTregs), further exacerbate this dysfunction by suppressing the proliferation of effector T cells through multiple mechanisms. They secrete immunosuppressive cytokines, deplete IL-2, thereby depriving cytotoxic T cells of an essential growth factor, and prevent antigen-presenting cells from effectively priming cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs).

A key mechanism of immune evasion in PDAC is the overexpression of immune checkpoint molecules by both cancer and stromal cells. In particular, the upregulation of PD-L1 on these cells enables tumors to escape immune surveillance by binding to the PD-1 receptor on exhausted T cells, thereby further suppressing their cytotoxic activity. NK cells are also present at low frequency within PDAC lesions and exhibit impaired cytotoxicity, mainly due to exposure to inhibitory cytokines and insufficient activation within the TME. Similarly, DCs, which are essential for effective antigen presentation, are reduced in both number and functionality, often remaining in a semimature state characterized by elevated expression of PD-L1 and CD276 (also known as B7-H3), resulting in suboptimal T cell priming. As PDAC progresses, macrophages undergo a phenotypic transition from pro-inflammatory M1-like to tumor-promoting M2-like states, establishing an immunosuppressive milieu. In addition, MDSCs contribute to immune evasion by expressing PD-L1 and immunoregulatory markers such as F4/80 and CD124, thereby inhibiting effector T cell activation. Their suppressive function is mediated through the production of arginase and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, which deplete L-arginine, a key amino acid for T cell proliferation, and impair T cell receptor (TCR) signaling via nitration of the TCR/CD8 complex. The combined actions of MDSCs, M2-polarized TAMs, and dysfunctional DCs culminate in a profoundly suppressive TME, which is further reinforced by metabolic reprogramming. The Warburg effect, in which tumor cells predominantly utilize glycolysis for energy production despite the availability of oxygen, leads to the accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites, such as lactate. Lactate and other metabolic byproducts can inhibit T cell activation and promote the differentiation of immunosuppressive cells such as pTregs and MDSCs.

Overall, a profoundly immunosuppressive TME, characterized by immune exclusion and desertification, T cell exhaustion, suppressive myeloid and stromal populations, immune checkpoint activation, and metabolic reprogramming, renders PDAC highly resistant to immunotherapy. Gaining insight into the epigenetic regulation of these mechanisms is essential for identifying rational combination strategies that may improve patient outcomes.
Tumor-intrinsic epigenetic dysregulation in PDAC

Epigenetic modifications are heritable and reversible changes that influence gene expression without altering the underlying DNA sequence. These modifications are essential for normal physiological processes and can be influenced by external factors such as lifestyle, nutrition, and environmental exposures. When dysregulated, they contribute to the development of various diseases, including cancer. In PDAC, epigenetic dysregulation is closely linked to tumor initiation, progression, and therapy resistance. The main epigenetic mechanisms include DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and RNA-dependent regulatory mechanisms, including non-coding RNAs and epitranscriptomic alterations.
DNA methylation shaping transcriptional identity in PDAC subtypes

DNA methylation, one of the most extensively studied epigenetic modifications, refers to the covalent addition of a methyl group to the 5th carbon of the cytosine ring within CpG dinucleotides. Although this modification occurs throughout the genome, methylation within promoter-associated CpG islands is particularly linked to transcriptional repression. This process, catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), regulates gene expression by hindering transcription factor binding and recruiting chromatin-remodeling complexes. Integrated epigenomic analysis has shown that coordinated reprogramming of chromatin and DNA methylation landscapes defines the transcriptional identities of the classical and basal-like PDAC subtypes. The classical subtype retains an epithelial, metabolically active phenotype supported by hypomethylation and sustained GATA6 expression, which promotes differentiation-related transcription programs. In contrast, the basal-like subtype exhibits epigenetic suppression of GATA6, accompanied by widespread chromatin and DNA methylation remodeling that activates oncogenic pathways such as MYC (c-MYC), TGF-beta, and ErbB/EGFR, resulting in a more aggressive, undifferentiated phenotype. Among the GATA6 epigenetic regulators is TET3, a member of the ten-eleven translocation (TET) family of dioxygenases involved in DNA demethylation. Aberrant DNA methylation in PDAC is further reinforced by the overexpression of DNMT1, which maintains promoter hypermethylation and propagates transcriptional silencing across cell divisions. Notably, locus-specific methylation alterations have been associated with patient survival and prognosis, underscoring the clinical relevance of epigenetic dysregulation in PDAC.
Histone modifications impacting oncogenic signalling

Histone modifications, including acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, deamination, ubiquitination, sumoylation, and others, regulate gene expression by modulating chromatin structure and thereby influencing the accessibility of DNA to transcription factors. Beyond global chromatin regulation, histone modifications shape oncogenic signaling programs, including those driven by RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways. In this context, histone acetylation and methylation establish landscapes that sustain MYC expression and activity. In parallel, a histone methylation-MAPK signaling axis has been described in which hypoxia-induced chromatin reprogramming enhances MAPK-dependent transcriptional activation and promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).

Histone acetylation, mediated by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) such as CREB-binding protein (CBP, also known as CREBBP), E1A-associated protein (p300, also known as EP300), and P300/CBP-associated factor (PCAF, also known as KAT2B), promotes transcriptional activation by loosening chromatin structure. In contrast, histone deacetylation by histone deacetylases (HDACs) results in chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression. HDACs are frequently overexpressed in PDAC and contribute to oncogenesis by repressing tumor suppressor genes. HDAC inhibitors (HDACi) are currently being explored as potential therapeutic agents. Acetylated histones are recognized by bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) proteins, which act as transcriptional co-activators. The BET family of proteins (BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT) contains bromodomains BD1 and BD2, which recognize and bind acetylated lysine residues on histones. BET proteins are crucial in mediating chemoresistance in PDAC. BRD4 drives the expression of mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGCS2), an enzyme involved in cholesterol biosynthesis, which is upregulated in chemoresistant PDAC cell lines. Inhibition of BRD4 sensitizes these cells to gemcitabine.

Histone methylation, catalyzed by histone methyltransferases (HMTs), involves the covalent addition of methyl groups to lysine or arginine residues on histone tails. This process can either activate or repress gene transcription depending on the specific residue and chromatin context. Among these enzymes, enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) plays a pivotal role in PDAC by silencing genes through the H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) mark. This epigenetic repression, in addition to DNA methylation described above, targets differentiation-associated factors, such as GATA6, leading to the loss of epithelial-like tumor phenotype and promoting a transition toward a mesenchymal-like state. Conversely, histone demethylases (HDMs) remove methyl groups from histones, reversing the effects of HMTs and regulating chromatin accessibility. Recent evidence highlights the tumor-suppressive role of lysine-specific demethylase KDM6A in PDAC. Loss of KDM6A is associated with increased metastasis and a more aggressive, undifferentiated tumor phenotype. Beyond classical histone modifications, several emerging histone modifications have been implicated in PDAC biology. These include histone phosphorylation, with elevated gamma-H2AX levels associated with poor survival and the basal-like PDAC subtype, as well as histone ubiquitination, lactylation, and serotonylation, which have been linked to tumor cell metabolism, protein homeostasis, and malignant progression.
Chromatin remodeling orchestrating transcriptional plasticity

Chromatin remodeling refers to ATP-dependent modifications of nucleosome positioning and structure that regulate DNA accessibility and gene transcription. Remodeling complexes can reposition, eject, or restructure nucleosomes, thereby shaping transcriptional programs and cell identity. Dysregulation of these processes alters gene expression landscapes and contributes to PDAC tumorigenesis. Multiple multiprotein chromatin remodeling complexes, including SWItch/sucrose non-fermentable (SWI/SNF), imitation SWI (ISWI), chromodomain-helicase DNA-binding protein (CHD), and INOsitol-requiring mutant 80 (INO80), participate in this regulation. The SWI/SNF complex is an ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling assembly that modulates nucleosome positioning to regulate gene expression, DNA replication, and repair. Loss-of-function mutations in SWI/SNF subunits such as ARID1A, PBRM1, and SMARCA4 have been reported in a subset of PDAC patients. Overall, chromatin remodeling acts as an instructive interface linking oncogenic KRAS signaling, enhancer reprogramming, and transcriptional plasticity in PDAC.
Non-coding RNAs regulating proliferation, EMT, metabolism

Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), particularly microRNAs (miRNAs) and long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), represent an important layer of post-transcriptional gene regulation with broad relevance to tumor biology. miRNAs, typically 18-24 nucleotides in length, suppress gene expression by either degrading target mRNA or inhibiting its translation. In PDAC, aberrant miRNA expression has been linked to ECM remodeling, EMT, metabolic reprogramming, and immunosuppression. Beyond miRNAs, other ncRNA classes, including lncRNAs and circular RNAs (circRNAs), further contribute to malignant transformation by functioning as oncogenes or tumor suppressors. For instance, lncRNAs such as MALAT1 and HOTAIR, as well as circRNAs such as circ-PDE8A, promote tumor invasiveness by activating EMT-associated transcriptional programs, whereas tumor-suppressive miRNAs, such as the miR-200 family, counteract EMT and maintain epithelial identity. Collectively, ncRNA-mediated regulatory networks influence multiple facets of PDAC progression and represent potential targets for therapeutic interventions.
RNA modifications promoting tumor growth

RNA modifications, also known as the epitranscriptome, constitute an additional epigenetic layer of post-transcriptional regulation. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and 5-methylcytosine (m5C) are emerging as a new category of gene expression regulators, implicated in tumor cell proliferation, metabolic reprogramming, EMT, therapy resistance, and modulation of the TME. These modifications influence RNA stability, splicing, and translation efficiency. In PDAC, m6A dysregulation has been linked to the altered expression of oncogenes (KRAS, MYC) and tumor suppressors, thereby contributing to tumor growth and metastasis. However, comprehensive characterization of RNA modifications beyond m6A, along with their associated writers, readers, and erasers, remains limited by methodological challenges and remains an active area of investigation.

Collectively, these findings underscore that epigenetic dysregulation is a defining feature of PDAC, shaping its molecular heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance, and highlight the need for a deeper understanding of how these mechanisms influence tumor biology. Given that tumor-intrinsic epigenetic mechanisms have been extensively reviewed elsewhere and constitute a broad field beyond the scope of the present article, we provide only a brief overview to introduce their relevance to the PDAC TME.
Epigenetic regulation of the tumor immune ecosystem

Epigenetic mechanisms also play a crucial role in shaping tumor-immune interactions, allowing cancer cells to evade immune surveillance and maintain an immunosuppressive TME. DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin remodeling have a critical influence on PDAC immunopathology by modulating antigen presentation, cytokine signaling, and immune cell infiltration (Table 1). Cancer cells can epigenetically silence key components of the antigen-presenting machinery, as well as the expression of cytokines, and chemokines, thereby impairing immune recognition and facilitating immune escape. Consequently, PDAC tumors exploit these mechanisms to attenuate antigen presentation and reinforce an immunosuppressive TME, which hinders effective antitumor immunity.

DNMT1-associated suppression of MHC-I and IFN responses

Overexpression of DNMT1, observed in approximately 80% of PDAC tumors, has been shown to suppress antigen presentation. Its inhibition restores tumor immunogenicity by upregulating surface major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) expression and promoting IFN-gamma secretion from tumor-specific CD8+ T cells. In a stromal-rich PDAC mouse model, DAC reduced aberrant DNA methylation in both tumor cells and CAFs, slowing progression and prolonging survival. Mechanistic analyses revealed that DAC impaired proliferation across both compartments and activated STAT1-dependent pathways, thereby sensitizing PDAC cells to IFN-gamma. These findings support further exploration of DNA-demethylating agents in combination with cytokine-based or other immunomodulatory strategies in PDAC. Inhibition of DNMTs also leads to transcriptional reactivation of normally silenced repetitive elements, resulting in double-stranded RNA accumulation and induction of type I IFN signaling through a viral mimicry response. Genome-wide transcriptome and methylome profiling of purified epithelial cells from human PDAC revealed two distinct subtypes defined by differential methylation of repetitive elements. Tumors with low methylation levels exhibited increased endogenous retroviral expression and activation of intrinsic IFN signaling, which correlated with worse patient outcomes, whereas highly methylated tumors lacked this inflammatory signature. These findings indicate that PDAC heterogeneity reflects both epigenetic state and cell of origin, and suggest that the aggressive methylation-low/IFN-high subtype may be susceptible to therapies targeting the IFN pathway.
DNA methylation-mediated immune cell exclusion and macrophage polarization

DNA methylation also regulates immune cell infiltration and functional balance within the TME. Methylation-dependent regulation of PUM1 expression alters immune composition by reducing the infiltration of NK cells, B cells, and helper T cells, while promoting the recruitment of Tregs. Hypomethylation of GBP4, a gene with prognostic significance in PDAC, is associated with T cell exhaustion and poor patient outcomes. Epigenetic control through DNA methylation also critically shapes macrophage fate in PDAC. Specifically, tumor cell-macrophage interactions involving GARP1 and integrin alphaV/beta8 trigger methylation-dependent transcriptional reprogramming that promotes polarization toward an immunosuppressive M2-like phenotype at the expense of pro-inflammatory M1-polarized macrophages, facilitating tumor progression. Tumor-derived CCL5 is also crucial for efficient T cell infiltration, and its loss in human tumors is associated with DNA hypermethylation. DNA methylation is directly involved in CAF activation and the establishment of a pro-tumorigenic stromal niche. During MSC differentiation toward a CAF phenotype, widespread DNA methylation loss leads to upregulation of CXCL4, thereby promoting cancer cell invasion. This process is driven by tumor-derived lactate, which increases alpha-ketoglutarate levels in CAFs and activates TET enzymes, resulting in DNA demethylation.
HDAC-dependent PD-L1 regulation and CAF activation

By altering chromatin accessibility, histone modifications control the expression of genes involved in antigen presentation, cytokine signaling, and immune checkpoint regulation. HDACs act as key regulators of immune checkpoint expression and stromal activation. In PDAC, HDAC3 has been shown to enhance PD-L1 expression and promote desmoplastic remodeling, likely through context-dependent modulation of chromatin accessibility at the PD-L1 promoter, thereby facilitating immune evasion. Class I HDACs also contribute to TME remodeling by regulating the activation of stromal fibroblasts and their associated gene expression programs. In the stroma, HDACs maintain a pro-tumorigenic, desmoplastic phenotype by promoting the expression of genes involved in fibrosis, inflammation, and ECM remodeling, including ACTA2, COL1A1, TGFB1, and TNF-alpha-responsive genes.
BET proteins regulating CD276 and SHH-fibroblast signaling axis

BET proteins also influence immune regulation in PDAC. The immune checkpoint molecule CD276, overexpressed in PDAC, is transcriptionally regulated by BRD4. CD276, in turn, promotes the expression of toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), a receptor involved in inflammatory responses, thereby amplifying inflammatory signaling and contributing to tumor progression. BET proteins further promote PDAC growth and shape the TME by driving sonic hedgehog (SHH) expression, which activates GLI-dependent signaling in stromal fibroblasts. Inhibiting BET proteins disrupts this SHH-GLI axis, reducing CAF activation and desmoplasia.
Epigenetic control of immune balance by EZH2 and histone demethylases

HMTs and HDMs further modulate immune balance in PDAC. EZH2 represses the transcription of immune and inflammatory genes. In PDAC, MYC-dependent CXCL1 production, regulated by EZH2-mediated H3K27 methylation, disrupts the balance between T cells and MDSCs. Beyond tumor cells, EZH2 also sustains Treg differentiation and suppressive identity, while its inhibition in Tregs induces a pro-inflammatory gene signature that enhances the recruitment of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. However, EZH2 inhibition with GSK126 increased MDSC accumulation and reduced CD4 and IFN-gamma+ CD8+ T cells in the TME, suggesting a context-dependent role in MDSC generation. KDM3A regulates immune infiltration and immunotherapy responsiveness in PDAC through epigenetic control of EGFR expression, as demonstrated by in vivo functional genetic screens. Elevated expression of KDM5A/B/C correlates with increased immune cell infiltration in PDAC. In contrast, loss of KDM6A, common in metastatic and poorly differentiated PDAC, induces extensive chromatin remodeling and gene activation, promoting transition toward the squamous subtype.
SWI/SNF alterations and immunotherapy responsiveness

Evidence linking chromatin remodeling complexes to immune regulation in PDAC remains limited. However, genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens in human and murine tumor models have identified subunits of the cBAF and INO80 complexes as regulators of T cell exhaustion. Depletion of these chromatin remodeling factors, particularly ARID1A, significantly enhanced antitumor immune responses. Consistent with these findings, Botta et al. observed clinical responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in a subset of PDAC patients harboring SWI/SNF mutations, suggesting these alterations may confer increased immunotherapy sensitivity, though validation in larger cohorts is necessary. In addition, single-cell ATAC-seq analysis has identified multiple myeloid cell subpopulations with distinct chromatin accessibility profiles, highlighting epigenetically defined myeloid states that may represent novel therapeutic targets in PDAC.
LncRNAs and p300-driven immune suppression

LncRNAs are key regulators of metabolic signaling and immune interactions within the PDAC TME. Sun et al. identified a lactate-related lncRNA signature associated with elevated ICI expression, implicating lactate-linked lncRNAs in the establishment of an immune-evasive TME. Moreover, the lncRNA PACERR interacts with the transcription factor CTCF to recruit the HAT p300 to the promoters of PACERR and PTGS2, which encodes cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2). This targeted recruitment enhances histone acetylation, activates PTGS2 transcription, and promotes M2 polarization of TAMs, thereby contributing to immunosuppressive TME.
m6A RNA methylation regulating immune infiltration and viral mimicry

Besides its tumor-intrinsic functions, m6A methylation regulates immune infiltration and PD-L1 expression. In addition, RNA modifications modulate antitumor immunity by activating viral mimicry pathways. METTL3, a key m6A methyltransferase, promotes the accumulation of endogenous double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), derived from transcription of normally silent repetitive elements, including endogenous retroviruses (ERVs), LINEs, and Alu sequences. Accumulated dsRNA is detected by innate immune sensors such as MDA5, RIG-I, PKR, and TLR3, triggering type I IFN and antiviral-like signaling programs that enhance antitumor immune responses. Extending the concept of RNA modification-driven immune activation through viral mimicry, Wang et al. demonstrated that targeting the ac4C RNA writer NAT10 enhances PDAC immunotherapy by simultaneously promoting CD8+ T cell activity and reducing tumor-intrinsic immune evasion.

This connection between epigenetic modulation and immune escape sparked growing interest in epigenetic-targeted therapies aimed at enhancing immune responses. Preclinical and clinical evidence indicate that pharmacological inhibition of epigenetic regulators can restore tumor immunogenicity and reprogram immunosuppressive cells, such as TAMs, MDSCs, and Tregs, thereby creating a more permissive microenvironment that supports cytotoxic T cell activation and effector functions.
Therapeutic strategies in PDAC

Clinical management of PDAC depends on disease stage and resectability. Surgery remains the only potentially curative option, yet recurrence is frequent, and long-term survival remains below 20%. Adjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine-based regimens improves outcomes but is limited by toxicity. For locally advanced unresectable tumors, induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy can enable secondary resection in a subset of patients, whereas metastatic PDAC is managed palliatively using FOLFIRINOX, NALIRIFOX, or gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel. Growing understanding of PDAC biology has prompted the development of targeted therapies. Tumors with germline BRCA1/2 or PALB2 mutations respond to platinum-based chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, whereas KRAS mutations, present in over 90% of cases, remain a significant therapeutic challenge, despite the emergence of KRAS inhibitors. Other actionable alterations include ERBB2 amplification and EGFR overexpression, which are currently being explored in clinical trials using HER2- and EGFR-targeted agents.

passages.text: Poor response of PDAC to immunotherapy

Immunotherapy represents an innovative approach to cancer treatment by harnessing the immune system to recognize and eliminate malignant cells. Key immunotherapy modalities include ICIs, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), cancer vaccines, adoptive cell transfer (ACT), including chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy, cytokine therapies, innate immune agonists, and oncolytic viruses. These represent only a subset of the numerous immunotherapeutic strategies currently under investigation, which have been comprehensively reviewed elsewhere. Despite their mechanistic diversity, clinical outcomes across these immunotherapy platforms have been largely disappointing in PDAC. ICIs, antibodies targeting PD-1, PD-L1, or CTLA-4, which have transformed the treatment of several tumors, have failed to demonstrate meaningful clinical benefit as monotherapy in PDAC. Similarly, bispecific antibodies and therapeutic cancer vaccines have shown immunogenicity in early-phase trials but have not yet translated into durable clinical responses. Adoptive cell transfer strategies, including CAR-T cell therapies, remain limited by poor persistence and efficacy in solid tumors. Several additional immunotherapeutic strategies, including cytokine-based therapies, innate immune agonists, and oncolytic viruses, have demonstrated immune activation in preclinical models and early-phase clinical studies. However, their therapeutic potential in PDAC has thus far been constrained by limited tumor selectivity, systemic toxicity, and modest clinical activity.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: The poor efficacy of immunotherapy in PDAC reflects common biological barriers rather than shortcomings of individual therapeutic platforms. PDAC typically exhibits a low tumor mutational burden, resulting in restricted neoantigen availability and weak immunogenicity. Defective antigen presentation, driven in part by DC dysfunction, further compromises effective T cell priming. In parallel, the dense desmoplastic stroma and immune exclusion further limit the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Therefore, stimulating the immune system alone is insufficient to produce lasting responses in PDAC. Ultimately, meaningful clinical progress will require coordinated enhancement of immune activation and targeted reshaping of the TME to render PDAC vulnerable to sustained immune control. The integration of molecular profiling into clinical practice and clinical trials that incorporate targeted, epigenetic, and immune-based therapies holds promise for overcoming intrinsic resistance and improving survival in this highly aggressive malignancy.
Immunomodulatory potential of epigenetic drugs

Building on this need for microenvironmental reprogramming, epigenetic-targeted therapies hold considerable promise for improving PDAC outcomes. Although their integration with immunotherapy in PDAC is still in the early stages, accumulating evidence supports their ability to modulate TME. Unlike traditional cytotoxic treatments, epigenetic drugs act on both tumor cells and the TIME, reshaping immune dynamics and restoring antitumor immunity. By reactivating silenced immune genes, they can transform immunologically 'cold' tumors, thereby improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and other immunotherapies.

The immunomodulatory effects of epigenetic therapies operate through several complementary mechanisms, including (i) restoration of immune recognition through re-expression of MHC molecules and antigen-processing machinery, (ii) modulation of immune checkpoints and cytokine signaling, (iii) reprogramming of immunosuppressive cell populations such as Tregs, MDSCs and TAMs and (iv) enhancement of the effector T cell infiltration, activation and persistence. One example of this reprogramming is pharmacological inhibition of EZH2, which restores the expression of antigen-presenting genes, thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity and facilitating recognition by cytotoxic T cells. Inhibition of DNMTs, HDACs, or EZH2 reduces the abundance and suppressive activity of Tregs, MDSCs, and M2-like macrophages, shifting the balance toward an immune-permissive milieu that supports T cell effector function. Furthermore, epigenetic modulation can improve T cell trafficking and prevent functional exhaustion, suggesting that these drugs not only act on tumor and stromal cells but also directly enhance T cell memory and persistence. Preclinical studies combining epigenetic inhibitors with ICB have demonstrated synergistic effects, supporting further exploration of this therapeutic strategy in PDAC (Table 2). Based on their mechanisms of action, epigenetic inhibitors can be classified into several major categories, which are discussed below.

passages.text: Targeting aberrant DNA methylation

DNA methylation plays a central role in enforcing immune exclusion and suppressing antigen presentation in PDAC, providing a strong rationale for targeting DNMT activity to restore antitumor immune responses. DNMT inhibitors (DNMTi) counteract these epigenetic abnormalities by blocking DNMT activity and thereby reactivating silenced tumor suppressor and immune-related genes. In addition, DNMT inhibition can induce a 'viral mimicry' response, in which the reactivation of endogenous retroviral elements (ERVs) triggers IFN signaling, enhancing immune recognition and promoting antitumor immunity. Several recent works have reviewed the ability of epigenetic therapies to induce a viral-mimicry state by reactivating ERVs or other transposable elements, thereby triggering dsRNA sensing and type I/III IFN responses in the TME. A range of DNMTi, such as 5-azacitidine (5-Aza), hydralazine, decitabine (DAC, 5-Aza-2'-deoxycytidine), and guadecitabine (GuaDAC), have been evaluated for anticancer efficacy. Among these, 5-Aza and DAC are the best-characterized nucleoside analogs, both approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for hematological malignancies, but not yet for solid tumors. Nevertheless, extensive preclinical research highlights their potential in PDAC, and both agents have been evaluated in several clinical trials (Table 3).

In PDAC, 5-Aza treatment enhanced tumor immunogenicity by upregulating antigen presentation and T cell-attracting chemokines in tumor cells and increasing immune cell infiltration in vivo, resulting in tumor regression. Combination strategies have further amplified these effects. Li et al. reported that combining 5-Aza or an EZH2 inhibitor 3-Deazaneplanocin A (DZNep) with anti-PD-1 therapy led to approximately 50% tumor regression, increased CD4+IL-17+ and CD8+ T cells, and enhanced apoptosis within the TME. Clinically, 5-Aza has been tested in combination with ICIs. The Phase II trial NCT03264404 (5-Aza + pembrolizumab) demonstrated a favorable safety profile in metastatic PDAC but did not significantly improve progression-free survival. Another early-phase study, NCT02959437, explored similar combinations in solid tumors but was terminated prematurely. Despite these limitations, 5-Aza remains a promising agent for immuno-epigenetic combination strategies, warranting further investigation. DAC, another nucleoside DNMTi, incorporates into DNA to promote demethylation and reactivate silenced genes. Preclinical studies have shown that DAC slows tumor growth, prolongs survival, and enhances tumor immunogenicity, particularly when combined with ICB. DAC combined with anti-PD-1 therapy increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cell infiltration and induced tumor regression. Two active clinical trials are currently investigating DAC-based combinations in PDAC. NCT02650986 assesses the safety of adoptive TGFbetaDNRII-transduced TIL transfer with or without DAC, and NCT06454448, a Phase IB/II study, tests DAC plus adebrelimab, gemcitabine, and nab-paclitaxel. More clinical trials focused on combination therapy of DAC and immunotherapy in PDAC or solid tumors are listed in Table 2. However, DAC's application in solid tumors remains limited by rapid degradation, suboptimal tumor delivery, and narrow dosing ranges. Ongoing research focuses on formulation improvements, nanoparticle delivery, and rational drug combinations to overcome these barriers. GuaDAC is a next-generation, more stable analog of DAC, formed by linking DAC to deoxyguanosine, which confers resistance to cytidine deaminase and prolongs plasma half-life. GuaDAC has demonstrated enhanced stability and bioavailability, making it suitable for combination regimens. Current clinical trials, including NCT03257761 (GuaDAC+durvalumab) and NCT02998567 (GuaDAC+pembrolizumab), are investigating the combination of DNMT inhibition with ICB in solid tumors. These studies aim to optimize dosing and evaluate synergistic antitumor effects. In addition to nucleoside analogs, non-nucleoside DNMTi offer an alternative approach by directly blocking the DNMT catalytic site, thereby preventing DNA incorporation. Agents such as RG108 and SGI-1027 selectively inhibit DNMT1 and DNMT3A, reversing aberrant methylation and reactivating silenced genes in preclinical cancer models. Although these compounds have not yet reached clinical evaluation, their favorable pharmacological profiles and lower cytotoxicity make them attractive candidates for combination therapies. Overall, DNMTi hold strong potential to restore immune visibility, enhance responsiveness to immunotherapy, and reverse epigenetic silencing characteristic of PDAC. Continued optimization of delivery methods, dosing schedules, and combination strategies will be essential for translating these findings into durable clinical benefit.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Normalizing histone modification landscape

Given the central role of histone modifications in establishing an immunosuppressive landscape, inhibition of these epigenetic regulators represents a potential strategy to rebalance the TIME in PDAC. Epigenetic inhibitors targeting histone-modifying enzymes, such as HDACi, HAT (HATi), HDM (HDMi), lysine-specific demethylases (KDM1Ai, KDM5i), and HMTs (HMTi, EZH2i, DOTLi, PRMTi), modulate chromatin structure and transcriptional activity to restore gene expression homeostasis. HDACi are among the most extensively studied classes, inducing differentiation, cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and profound effects on the TIME. HDAC inhibition can reprogram TAMs from an M2-like to an M1-like state, enhancing IL-12 production, antigen presentation, and the recruitment of CTLs. Concurrently, HDACi can reduce the suppressive function of Treg cells by interfering with Foxp3 acetylation, thereby diminishing Treg stability and activity. Some HDACi, such as entinostat and vorinostat, selectively impair Tregs while enhancing effector T cell responses, thereby creating a more immunogenic TME that can synergize with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Several HDACi are under investigation for the treatment of solid tumors, including vorinostat, entinostat, panobinostat, belinostat, romidepsin, ivalitinostat, and trichostatin A. Vorinostat, a pan-HDAC inhibitor approved by the FDA for cutaneous T cell lymphoma, targets class I and II HDACs and exerts pleiotropic effects, including the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of angiogenesis through the suppression of HIF-1 and VEGF, and downregulation of IL-10, an immunosuppresive cytokine.

In PDAC models, vorinostat has demonstrated potential immunomodulatory synergy. Booth et al. reported that prior exposure to vorinostat, combined with sorafenib, enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy in syngeneic PDAC models. This combination reduced the expression of beta-catenin, Beclin1, ERBB1, BCL-XL, and MCL-1 in PDAC cell lines. In vivo, it led to smaller tumors, increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, NK cells and M1 polarization of macrophages. Entinostat, a class I selective HDAC inhibitor, suppresses MDSC function and enhances antigen presentation, while simultaneously reducing Treg-mediated immunosuppression. It has demonstrated synergy with ICB in several solid tumor models, and early-phase clinical trials are investigating its combination with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. Panobinostat, a potent pan-HDAC inhibitor, enhanced the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy in PDAC by promoting tumor cell apoptosis and driving differentiation of CAR-T cells toward a central memory phenotype, leading to effective tumor eradication in preclinical models. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, HDACi have shown limited efficacy as monotherapies in PDAC due to poor tumor penetration and complex resistance mechanisms. Current research focuses on combination strategies, particularly pairing HDACi with ICIs, chemotherapy, or targeted agents. Vorinostat and other HDACi are not yet approved for PDAC, and no active clinical trials currently evaluate their use in combination with immunotherapy specifically for this cancer type. However, their ability to reprogram immune and stromal compartments remains a key factor in making them candidates for combination therapy in PDAC.
Chromatin readers, transcriptional co-regulators

The BET family of proteins plays a central role in PDAC pathobiology by regulating transcriptional programs that sustain oncogenic signaling and immune evasion, as described earlier. BET inhibitors (BETi) disrupt the interaction between BET bromodomains and acetylated histones, thereby suppressing transcription of oncogenes and inflammatory mediators. Although none have yet received FDA or EMA approval, several compounds, including JQ-1, XP-524, apabetalone, BMS-986158, and ABBV-181, are under preclinical or early clinical investigation. One of the BETi is XP-524, a dual inhibitor targeting BRD4 and HAT p300EP300/CBP, both of which are implicated in PDAC tumorigenesis. In a study by Principe et al., XP-524 demonstrated potent tumoricidal activity, inhibition of KRAS/MAPK signaling, and enhanced T cell infiltration into the TME. The inhibitor was tested in vitro, ex vivo in human organotypic slice cultures, and in vivo. In mouse models, XP-524 significantly reprogrammed the TME and sensitized tumors to pembrolizumab, thereby significantly prolonging survival. Given its novel mechanism of action, XP-524 might represent a promising avenue in epigenetic cancer therapy, particularly for PDAC. However, subsequent independent or clinical validation studies are still lacking, and further research is required to confirm its therapeutic potential. Another extensively characterized BETi, JQ-1, selectively targets BRD4 and has been widely used in preclinical research. In PDAC, JQ-1 downregulates MYC and other transcriptional programs associated with the aggressive squamous subtype, thereby promoting a shift toward a more differentiated classical phenotype. Despite its efficacy in preclinical models, JQ-1's short half-life limits its clinical applicability, underscoring the need for optimized analogs or combination regimens. Combination approaches have shown superior therapeutic potential. BET inhibition with JQ-1 synergizes with the HDAC inhibitor vorinostat, producing enhanced antitumor effects in PDAC xenografts. In addition, combining JQ-1 with anti-PD-L1 significantly reduced tumor growth and increased apoptosis in PDAC xenograft models, highlighting the potential of BET inhibition to sensitize tumors to immunotherapy. The dense desmoplastic reaction in PDAC is primarily driven by activated PSCs, which produce collagen I and contribute to fibrosis. BET proteins are expressed in primary PSCs, and pan-BET inhibition with JQ-1 and I-BET151, primarily through BRD4 blockade, suppresses collagen I expression, induces PSC quiescence, and reduces fibrosis in vivo. Nanomedicine further expands therapeutic options. CD44-targeted supramolecular nanoplatforms such as hyaluronic acid-based carriers, co-delivering the photosensitizer PPa and the BETi JQ-1, have demonstrated the ability to induce phototherapy-mediated immunogenic cell death while suppressing Myc/PD-L1-driven immune evasion.

Overall, BETi interfere with the transcriptional networks sustaining PDAC growth, stromal activation, and immune escape. While their activity as monotherapy remains limited, preclinical studies demonstrate a strong rationale for incorporating BETi into combination regimens with immunotherapy or other epigenetic agents. Ongoing efforts focus on improving pharmacokinetics, minimizing toxicity, and identifying predictive biomarkers to enable clinical translation.

passages.text: Histone methylation, chromatin repression

Aberrant EZH2 activity drives tumor progression and immune evasion in PDAC, making it an important therapeutic target. However, compensatory activity of EZH1 can mitigate the effects of EZH2 inhibition, indicating that simultaneous blockade of both EZH1 and EZH2 may offer a more effective therapeutic strategy. Tazemetostat is the most clinically advanced EZH2i, and is currently approved by the FDA and EMA for the treatment of follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma. It selectively inhibits mutant EZH2 while displaying partial activity against EZH1. In PDAC models, pharmacologic EZH2 inhibition has been shown to derepress GATA6, promoting a phenotypic shift from the basal-like to the classical subtype. Clinically, the ongoing Phase II trial NCT04705818 is assessing tazemetostat in combination with the PD-L1 inhibitor durvalumab, following preliminary results from NCT02875548, a Phase I/II study of tazemetostat as monotherapy and in combination regimens for advanced solid tumors. Another selective EZH2i, lirametostat, prevents H3K27 trimethylation and exhibits potent activity across several preclinical models. It has been tested in multiple clinical trials, including NCT03525795, which evaluated its combination with the CTLA-4 inhibitor ipilimumab in patients with advanced solid tumors. With tazemetostat already approved for selected cancers and next-generation EZH2i advancing clinically, upcoming studies should determine whether EZH2 blockade can also normalize the aberrant TME in PDAC. Consistent with its transcriptional activity, the CD274 locus encoding PD-L1 is marked by high levels of H3K4me3, a modification deposited by the histone methyltransferase MLL1. Inhibiting MLL1 with HMTi verticillin A has been shown to attenuate PD-L1 upregulation, thereby limiting tumor immune evasion.
Therapeutic targeting of MiRNAs and RNA modifications

In addition to targeting canonical epigenetic mechanisms, a range of emerging molecular and technology-driven approaches are under investigation to recondition the stromal and immune landscape of PDAC. For instance, the miR-29 family plays a critical role in restraining stromal activation. While loss of miR-29 in PSCs increases ECM deposition, its restoration attenuates desmoplasia and improves chemotherapy responsiveness. This highlights the potential of miRNA-based strategies to simultaneously target tumor cells, CAFs, and the broader TME, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy and drug delivery. Dysregulated miRNAs may be modulated using miRNA mimics to restore tumor-suppressive miRNA function or antagomiRs/locked nucleic acid (LNA) inhibitors to silence oncogenic miRNAs. Advances in nanoparticle- and lipid-based delivery systems have improved the stability and tumor-specific delivery of miRNA therapeutics, enabling modulation of tumor-immune interactions within the PDAC TME. Targeting RNA modifications, particularly m6A and m5C, primarily relies on small-molecule inhibitors or genetic modulation of epitranscriptomic enzymes, including m6A writers (e.g., METTL3), erasers (e.g., FTO, ALKBH5), and readers. Altering m6A levels can modulate immune-cell infiltration and sensitivity to ICB, influence the activation and function of CTLs and suppressive myeloid populations. Several studies also highlight that m6A-dependent stabilization of PD-L1 mRNA contributes to immune escape, suggesting opportunities for combination therapies that target RNA-modifying enzymes to enhance ICB efficacy. In PDAC models, this strategy significantly reduced tumor burden and metastatic spread, and improved immune cell infiltration. Although these approaches remain primarily preclinical, they collectively underscore the importance of leveraging non-canonical epigenetic mechanisms to remodel the TME and improve treatment responses.
Challenges and future perspectives

By reversing transcriptional silencing of antigen-processing and IFN-response genes, epigenetic drugs can enhance PDAC immunogenicity and reprogram TME toward an immune-permissive state. However, their therapeutic efficacy in PDAC remains limited by pharmacologic and structural barriers (Table 4).

First, the dense desmoplastic stroma and poor vascularization impede efficient intratumoral delivery, while many epigenetic compounds exhibit suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties. Nucleoside analogues, such as DAC and 5-Aza, undergo rapid degradation, and most HDACi and BETi have low solubility and high systemic clearance, resulting in insufficient drug concentrations within the TME. These limitations underscore the need for improved formulations, such as liposomal or nanoparticle-based carriers and stroma-penetrating delivery systems, to improve pharmacological stability and tissue accumulation. Without resolving these constraints, even the most potent epigenetic agents are unlikely to achieve sustained therapeutic benefit in PDAC. Furthermore, early approaches aimed at stromal depletion demonstrated that targeting CAFs or fibrosis can accelerate disease progression and exacerbate immunosuppression, revealing a protective role of specific stromal compartments in PDAC biology.

Systemic toxicity and off-target effects represent another critical challenge. As epigenetic drugs modulate chromatin regulators expressed in both malignant and normal tissues, they frequently cause hematologic suppression, gastrointestinal toxicity, and hepatic dysfunction, which limit dose intensity and combination strategies. The development of isoform-selective or reversible inhibitors, together with intermittent 'epigenetic priming' schedules, has emerged as a promising strategy to widen the therapeutic window, while preserving immunomodulatory efficacy. Achieving effective epigenetic reprogramming with acceptable tolerability remains a key translational objective.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Although DNA methyltransferase inhibitors induce viral mimicry and IFN signaling, these responses often remain transient and insufficient to achieve durable tumor control in the absence of effective immune effector engagement. Therapeutic resistance reflects the intrinsic plasticity of PDAC cells. Redundant enzymatic activity, such as EZH1 compensation after EZH2 inhibition, and broad transcriptional rewiring can rapidly restore oncogenic and immune-evasive signaling. Resistance may also arise from altered drug metabolism, efflux mechanisms, or TME-driven adaptive signaling. Rationally designed dual-target or sequential regimens, combined with real-time molecular monitoring, will be required to track and counteract these adaptive processes. Given the transient nature of chromatin remodeling, optimizing the timing and scheduling of epigenetic therapy in conjunction with immunotherapy or chemotherapy is likely critical to maintain favorable transcriptional states and achieve durable responses.

Tumor heterogeneity further limits treatment efficacy. PDAC comprises diverse epigenetic, metabolic, and stromal subpopulations shaped by hypoxia, nutrient gradients, and spatial variation in stromal and immune cell composition. These microenvironmental factors directly influence the activity of oxygen- and metabolite-dependent dioxygenases such as TET enzymes and JmjC-domain KDMs, thereby creating regional variability in DNA and histone methylation landscapes. Capturing this complexity requires spatially resolved, single-cell, and multi-omic approaches capable of linking epigenetic states to therapeutic responses across distinct tumor niches.

A persistent obstacle to clinical translation is the absence of validated predictive biomarkers. Expression of DNMT1, EZH2, or BRD4, as well as promoter methylation of immune-related genes, IFN-response signatures, and induction of chemokines such as CXCL9/10, have emerged as promising pharmacodynamic or response markers but remain unvalidated in clinical settings. Integrating epigenomic, transcriptomic, and immune spatial profiling into trial design may enable biomarker-driven stratification and dynamic response monitoring. In parallel, circulating tumor DNA methylation patterns and peripheral immune transcriptional readouts offer noninvasive tools for adaptive dosing and treatment optimization.

Preclinical models remain another limiting factor for translational fidelity. Conventional PDAC cell lines fail to reproduce the desmoplastic and immunosuppressive features of human disease. Although genetically engineered mouse models, patient-derived organoids, and organotypic slice cultures offer a more faithful recapitulation of tumor-stroma-immune interactions, they are not yet standardized or scalable. Developing harmonized, immune-competent, and spatially preserved model platforms will be essential for evaluating combination regimens and validating biomarkers prior to clinical application.

Current evidence indicates that epigenetic therapies are the most effective as sensitizing agents rather than as monotherapy. Dual-function inhibitors such as the BET/EP300 modulator XP-524 and the DNMT1/G9a inhibitor CM-272 exemplify this strategy by simultaneously targeting complementary epigenetic circuits that sustain oncogenic transcription, stromal activation, and immune evasion. While such combination approaches can enhance antitumor efficacy and immunotherapy responsiveness, they also increase pharmacologic complexity and cumulative toxicity, underscoring the need for rigorous preclinical validation and carefully designed clinical evaluation.

passages.text: Conclusions

The therapeutic potential of epigenetic modulation in PDAC lies in its ability to reprogram the tumor ecosystem's response to treatment. Rather than targeting individual genes, epigenetic interventions can reshape the regulatory interface between cancer cells, stroma, and immune components. Recent advances in functional epigenomics indicate that epigenetic vulnerabilities in PDAC are highly context-dependent and dynamically rewired at the level of enhancers rather than promoters. Single-cell and spatial profiling demonstrate pronounced enhancer plasticity across malignant, stromal, and immune compartments, enabling rapid transcriptional adaptation following inhibition. Consistently, CRISPR-based functional screens show that epigenetic dependencies governing immune evasion or stromal activation are often restricted to specific cell states or microenvironmental niches, explaining why bulk epigenetic modulation frequently fails to translate into consistent immune infiltration or clinical benefit. Future research should focus on capturing these dynamics in real time through spatial multi-omics, imaging, and immune profiling to identify actionable states of chromatin plasticity. In this setting, epigenetic agents should be viewed as sensitizers that reshape the TME, restore immune recognition, improve drug delivery, and responsiveness to established therapies. The translation of these insights into biomarker-guided, adaptive clinical trials represents the most direct route to transforming epigenetic therapy from an experimental concept into a clinically relevant strategy for one of the most treatment-refractory human cancers.

passages.text: Distinct cMET inhibitors uncover pharmacological heterogeneity in SHH medulloblastoma cell lines

The c-MET kinase signalling pathway is crucial in cerebellum development and has emerged as a potential therapeutic target for medulloblastoma treatment. Our study confirms that c-MET and its ligand HGF are highly expressed in the SHH medulloblastoma subgroup, with SHH-alpha and SHH-beta subtypes showing the highest expression levels of both genes, respectively. HGF treatments and siRNA-mediated c-MET knockdown demonstrated the proliferative dependence of SHH MB cells on c-MET signalling. However, time-lapse microscopy revealed heterogeneous behaviours of SHH cell lines following alterations in c-MET levels. Pharmacological inhibition of c-MET signalling showed that tivantinib outperforms other c-MET inhibitors, including crizotinib and foretinib, in killing SHH medulloblastoma cells. Tivantinib induces a prolonged mitotic block followed by apoptotic death in both 2D and 3D cell culture models. Additionally, tivantinib enhances the anti-proliferative activity of vincristine, the standard of care for MB patients, specifically in DAOY cells, where the combination of vincristine and tivantinib synergistically increases the level of PARP cleavage. Moreover, we demonstrated that foretinib and crizotinib induce mitotic slippage in SHH MB cells. The use of navitoclax, a pan-BCL2 inhibitor, initiates the apoptotic program after cells fail mitosis. Taken together, these data suggest that tivantinib is a superior clinical option for SHH MB patients, whereas foretinib or crizotinib should be considered only in combination with BCL2 inhibitors.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12672-026-04717-7.
Introduction

Medulloblastoma (MB) is one of the most common paediatric brain tumours, originating in the posterior fossa of the cerebellum and often spreading to other parts of the Central Nervous System (CNS). According to the 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of CNS tumours, MB includes four genetically distinct subgroups: Wingless (WNT), Sonic Hedgehog (SHH, with TP53-wildtype and TP53-mutant subtypes), Group 3 (G3), and Group 4 (G4). Each subgroup has unique molecular characteristics and clinical outcomes. Recent analyses have further divided MB into multiple subtypes within each subgroup, indicating significant intra- and inter-tumour heterogeneity with potential clinical implications. Despite this heterogeneity, most MB patients receive a uniform treatment regimen consisting of surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy, which often leads to severe long-term side effects. Additionally, 40% of newly diagnosed MB patients develop resistance to therapies and experience recurrence, with TP53-mutant SHH and G3 patients having the poorest survival outcomes and highest relapse rates. Therefore, there is an urgent need for novel treatments that address the heterogeneity of MB and reduce therapy-related morbidities.

Aberrant activation or expression of tyrosine receptor kinases (RTKs) and their ligands is a well-known cause of cancer. Several RTKs, including hepatocyte growth factor receptor (c-MET), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR), and ERBB receptors, along with their ligands (HGF, PDGF, VEGF, FGF, and EGF), are implicated in MB pathogenesis. These factors initiate signalling cascades, such as MAPK/ERK and PI3K/AKT, that promote the proliferation and survival of MB cells. Recent proteomic studies have demonstrated the aberrant enrichment of multiple RTKs and their downstream intermediaries in MB subgroups. Specifically, Forget and colleagues observed an overall specific activation of ERBB4 and its ligand NRG2 in G4 MB, while Archer and colleagues demonstrated that PRKDC activity is essential for G3 survival after DNA damage. These studies reinforced the idea that aberrant enrichment in the expression of RTK receptors and their ligands is a crucial step in the neoplastic transformation and progression of MB cells, and their inhibition may represent a potential subgroup or subtype-specific therapeutic strategy.

Among the RTKs, c-MET and its ligand HGF play a crucial role in cerebellar development and enhance various malignancy parameters in MB, including mitogenicity, motility, and morphogenesis. HGF and c-MET are expressed in both foetal and adult cerebellum. Activation of the HGF/c-MET signalling pathway stimulates the proliferation of cerebellar granule cell precursors (GCPs) and protects them from apoptosis. Reduced activity of this pathway in mice results in cerebellar abnormalities and reduced GCP proliferation. Conversely, aberrant activation of the c-MET pathway promotes MB cell proliferation, anchorage-independent growth, and cell cycle progression via CDK2/p27. HGF treatment also protects MB cells from chemotherapy-induced apoptosis by decreasing levels of cleaved PARP and caspase-3. The oncogenic role of the HGF/c-MET pathway in MB is not typically due to single gene mutations but rather to epigenetic alterations or copy number variations. For example, no activating mutations have been found in the c-MET gene, but HGF and c-MET gene loci on chromosome 7 often show copy number gains in primary MB specimens. Additionally, the SPINT2 gene, an inhibitor of the HGF/c-MET pathway, is frequently silenced by promoter methylation or deletion in primary MB samples. Re-expression of SPINT2 in MB cell lines with active HGF/c-MET signalling impairs cell proliferation and migration and enhances survival in xenograft models. The therapeutic potential of targeting the HGF/c-MET pathway is supported by in vivo studies showing that HGF gene transfer increases MB formation in cerebellar neuronal progenitors in cooperation with SHH signalling. Systemic administration of a monoclonal antibody against HGF has prolonged the survival of xenograft mice, indicating the viability of HGF/c-MET-targeted approaches for treating HGF/c-MET-expressing MB tumours. Small molecule inhibitors against c-MET kinase, which cross the blood-brain barrier more efficiently than antibodies, have also shown promise. Pre-clinical studies of inhibitors like crizotinib, SGX523, foretinib, and PHA665752 have demonstrated efficacy in reducing the proliferation and motility of MB cells, though their effects vary across different cell lines.

In this study, we evaluated c-MET expression and activity in SHH MB cell lines with varying TP53 statuses and investigated the effects of multiple c-MET inhibitors. Our findings indicate that c-MET inhibitors utilise different mechanisms to halt the cell cycle and reduce cell proliferation in SHH MB cells. Notably, tivantinib exhibited the highest anti-proliferative activity and induced apoptosis in a subset of SHH-MB cells, suggesting it as a promising therapeutic candidate for SHH MB patients.

The c-MET/HGF axis has been proposed as a potential target for treating SHH MB. To confirm its activity in SHH MB cells, we assessed the expression of c-MET kinase and the other 56 RTK gene family members in a discovery cohort of 500 MB tumour samples and 9 normal adult cerebella using the publicly available R2 databases (https://r2.amc.nl). Only 29 RTK genes were significantly modulated in MB tumours compared to normal cerebella (Fig. S1, Supplemental Table S1). Of these, only 7 genes (c-MET, RYK, EPHA3, EPHB2, PTK7, ROR1 and 2) including c-MET, were significantly overexpressed in MB tumours, with only c-MET being druggable with multiple, highly selective, and potent inhibitors (Fig. 1A and Fig. S1). We extended this finding by analysing c-MET kinase expression in MB subgroups and subtypes in an independent validation cohort of 763 primary tumour specimens with clinical data. c-MET expression was highest in SHH MB (Fig. 1B). Among the SHH subtypes, SHH-alpha, affecting non-infant children (> 3 years old) with germline and somatic TP53 mutations, MYCN or GLI2 amplification, and ELP1 alterations, showed robust c-MET expression (Fig. 1C). Other SHH subtypes (Shh-beta, Shh-gamma, Shh-delta) also expressed higher c-MET levels compared to the remaining MB samples (Fig. 1C).

Since c-MET lacks activating mutations in MB, the presence of its ligand HGF is required for activating c-MET signalling and has been implicated in promoting MB cell dissemination and invasion. We therefore evaluated HGF expression across MB samples, subgroups, and subtypes. HGF expression was reduced in MB specimens compared with normal cerebella (Fig. S2A), consistent with its predominant production by highly differentiated granule and Purkinje cells that are lost in MB tumours. HGF was preferentially expressed in SHH MB tumours and subtypes (Fig. S2B, C). However, no positive correlation between c-MET and GF expression was observed in SHH MB tumours or in WNT subgroup specimens. Instead, only a weak positive association between c-MET and HGF expression was detenced in a limited subset of MB specimens (< 30%), more frequently among G3 and G4 patients (Fig. S2D).

Additionally, we examined c-MET expression in a publicly available single cell RNA sequencing dataset comprising 6,775 cells from 25 MB patients (Fig. S3A). Only 12.5% of the cells expressed c-MET (Fig. S3B, C). High levels of c-MET expression were observed in cells from all three SHH-subgroup patients, including one sample identified as a metastatic lesion. In contrast, only one G3 patient exhibited relatively high levels of c-MET, and this was confined to a restricted population of cells. No expression of c-MET was detected in fibroblasts (Fig. S3B). Interestingly, HGF expression was either absent or relatively low across the dataset, and only 0.15% of cells co-expressed both c-MET and HGF (Fig. S3C). This further supports the notion that HGF-driven c-MET signalling in MB primarily originates from the normal cerebellar parenchyma.

Finally, we examined the correlation between overall survival and c-MET expression in MB patients. Survival differences were not significant across the full cohort, subgroups or subtypes (Fig. 1D). No significant correlation or positive trend to survival was observed between HGF expression and patient survival (Fig. S12A, B). Overall, these results confirm that c-MET kinase is overexpressed in MB compared to the normal cerebellum, primarily in SHH MB specimens, providing a rationale for targeting c-MET kinase in SHH-MB.
