passages.text: Integration of T-cell functional markers (Supplementary Fig. 7A) confirmed that DLX2-high tumors displayed high expression of exhaustion-associated genes:including PDCD1, TIGIT, LAYN, CTLA4, HAVCR2, and IKZF4:and reduced expression of cytotoxic mediators such as GZMA, GZMK, PRF1, and IFNG. Conversely, Treg markers including FOXP3, IL2RA, and CCR7 were markedly elevated. Population-level quantification further demonstrated that DLX2-high tumors are dominated by Tregs and Tex cells, whereas DLX2-low tumors retain higher proportions of naive and effector T cells (Supplementary Fig. 7B). These patterns position DLX2+ DCs as potential upstream regulators of both T-cell exhaustion and regulatory T-cell expansion.

Macrophage analysis revealed a parallel shift in myeloid polarization: DLX2-high tumors exhibited a significant enrichment of M2 macrophages and depletion of M1 macrophages (Fig. 5C-D). This myeloid remodeling closely aligned with DLX2+ DC prevalence, as correlation matrices placed DLX2+ DCs together with Tregs, Tex cells, and M2 macrophages, whereas DLX2- DCs clustered with effector T-cell states (Fig. 5E-F).

To uncover the mechanisms driving these shifts, we performed ligand-receptor modeling across DCs, T cells, and macrophages. DLX2+ DCs showed dominant engagement of inhibitory pathways with T cells, including robust CTLA4-CD80/CD86, PDCD1LG2-PDCD1, ICOSLG-ICOS, BTLA-TNFRSF14, LGALS9-HAVCR2, and multiple TNFSF-TNFRSF pairs (Fig. 5G). Notably, DLX2+ DCs exhibited increased TGF-beta ligand expression and active TGF-beta receptor interactions:consistent with their ability to induce Tregs and attenuate cytotoxic differentiation.

Interactions with macrophages revealed a complementary set of immunosuppressive communications: DLX2+ DCs engaged TGF-beta/integrin complexes, LGALS9-HAVCR2, NECTIN-PVR networks, and CD40/CD40LG modules, collectively promoting anti-inflammatory M2 polarization (Fig. 5F). Broad ligand-receptor mapping demonstrated that DLX2+ DCs deploy a far more extensive inhibitory and co-regulatory communication repertoire than DLX2- DCs, spanning TNF superfamily, integrin complexes, ICAM family, and TGF-beta-related axes (Fig. 5H).

Together, these findings identify DLX2+ DCs as central architects of a multilayered immunosuppressive network in LUAD. By simultaneously promoting Treg expansion, driving CD8+ T-cell exhaustion, and fostering M2 macrophage polarization through extensive inhibitory ligand-receptor signaling, DLX2+ DCs actively sculpt a tumor microenvironment optimized for immune evasion and tumor progression.

Spatial transcriptomics reveals that DLX2+ dendritic cells localize within immunosuppressive niches enriched for Tregs, exhausted T cells, and M2-like macrophages, forming coordinated spatial hubs of immune tolerance

To determine whether the immunosuppressive programs associated with DLX2+ DCs translate into spatially organized niches within LUAD tissues, we integrated Visium spatial transcriptomics across multiple tumor sections (Fig. 6A). Spatial deconvolution revealed highly structured immune architectures: Tregs, Tex cells, macrophages, and DLX2+ DCs exhibited overlapping, compact regions of high abundance, whereas naive and effector T cells were largely excluded from these areas (Fig. 6B). These findings indicate that DLX2+ DCs do not distribute randomly but instead accumulate in microenvironments already enriched for immunosuppressive lymphoid and myeloid lineages.

Spatial transcriptomics reveals co-localized immunosuppressive niches centered on DLX2+ dendritic cells. A UMAP of spatial transcriptomics libraries and cell clusters (29185 spots). B Spatial enrichment of Tregs, Tex, naive T cells, effector T cells, macrophages, DLX2- DCs, and DLX2+ DCs. C Pathway-to-cell influence matrix identifying TGF-beta signaling as a major determinant of DLX2+ DC spatial localization. D Cell-cell spatial influence matrix showing DLX2+ DCs as predictors of Treg and Tex accumulation

To further interrogate the determinants of this spatial co-localization, we performed spatial-priority modeling to quantify the regulatory influence of signaling pathways and cell populations on one another. TGF-beta signaling emerged as the strongest predictor of DLX2+ DC localization (Fig. 6C), consistent with its known role in driving tolerogenic DC differentiation and Treg stability. Reciprocal modeling identified DLX2+ DCs themselves as key predictors of Treg and Tex spatial enrichment, supporting a feed-forward circuit in which DLX2+ DCs both arise within and reinforce immunosuppressive niches (Fig. 6D). Importantly, macrophage spatial dynamics mirrored this pattern: M2-associated macrophages strongly co-occurred with DLX2+ DC-Treg-Tex regions, whereas M1-like inflammatory macrophages were depleted, mirroring the shifts observed in scRNA-seq analyses (Fig. 6B and D).

Taken together, these spatial data reveal that DLX2+ DCs are not only transcriptionally distinct but also geographically positioned to function as organizational hubs of immune suppression. Their co-localization with Tregs, exhausted T cells, and M2-polarized macrophages defines a structurally coherent immunosuppressive ecosystem, indicating that DLX2+ DCs shape LUAD progression by orchestrating both the molecular and spatial architecture of tumor-immune dysfunction.
Materials and methods
Data sources and preprocessing

Bulk RNA-seq data for lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-LUAD) and corresponding normal lung tissues from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project. To compare transcriptomic profiles between lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and normal tissues, gene expression data from the TCGA and GTEx cohorts were obtained from the UCSC Xena portal in a re-computed and harmonized format via the TOIL pipeline. This standardization process significantly minimizes batch effects arising from different sequencing platforms and processing pipelines between the two databases. For all downstream differential expression and functional enrichment analyses, we utilized log2-transformed transcripts per million (TPM) values, which provide a more comparable metric across samples than raw counts. Gene expression matrices were downloaded as TPM values and log2-transformed after adding a pseudocount. Clinical information, including overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), disease-free survival (DFS), and disease-specific survival (DSS), was retrieved from UCSC Xena. Pan-cancer RNA-seq datasets spanning 33 tumor types were accessed through TCGA and uniformly processed for cross-cohort analyses. Neuroactive ligand-receptor genes were obtained from the published gene set by Dong et al. (Supplementary Table S1).
Differential expression and pathway enrichment analyses

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between LUAD tumors and normal tissues were identified using DESeq2 with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted with the clusterProfiler package using KEGG, GO, and Hallmark gene sets. Enrichment significance was defined as false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05. Pathway networks and functional clusters were visualized using enrichplot and igraph.
Prognostic modeling and random-forest ranking

To identify neuroactive-associated prognostic genes, we intersected: (1) neuroactive ligand-receptor genes, (2) LUAD tumor-upregulated genes, and (3) LUAD risk genes identified by univariate Cox regression. Candidate genes were ranked by random-forest models using survival randomForestSRC. Hazard ratios (HRs) were computed across TCGA pan-cancer cohorts using both Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier survival estimates. Candidate prognostic genes were prioritized using a Random Forest (RF) algorithm. To ensure the reproducibility of our model, the analysis was performed with a fixed seed of 1234, and the key hyperparameters were set as ntree = 1000 and mtry = 5. Prior to model training, genes were pre-filtered based on differential expression analysis (llog2FCl > 1 and FDR < 0.05) and univariate Cox regression (P < 0.05).
Immune microenvironment estimation

Immune and stromal scores were calculated using ESTIMATE. Inferred immune cell fractions were obtained from CIBERSORT, xCell, EPIC, MCP-counter, TIMER, and TIDE. Immune dysfunction, T-cell exhaustion, Treg infiltration, and myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) signatures were scored from established gene sets. Correlation analyses used Spearman coefficients with FDR correction.
Single-cell RNA-seq analysis

scRNA-seq datasets covering the LUAD progression spectrum (AIS-MIA-IAC) were obtained from publicly available GEO datasets. Raw count matrices were processed using Seurat v4. Cells with > 10% mitochondrial content or < 200 detected genes were removed. Furthermore, DoubletFinder was employed to identify and remove potential doublets, ensuring that the downstream analysis was based on high-quality single cells. Normalization was performed by SCTransform with batch correction via Harmony. Clusters were annotated based on canonical markers for epithelial cells, T-cell subsets, B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells (cDC1, cDC2, LAMP3+ DC, moDC), fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and mast cells. To specifically characterize the DLX2-expressing population, DLX2+ DCs were defined as cells with a normalized count of DLX2 > 0 in the expression matrix. This binary classification allowed for a comparative analysis of transcriptional profiles between DLX2+ and DLX2- dendritic cells.
Differential expression and functional profiling of DLX2+ vs. DLX2- dendritic cells

DEGs between DLX2+ and DLX2- DCs were identified using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Bonferroni correction. Pathway enrichment was performed with clusterProfiler for KEGG and GO terms. Stress-response, exhaustion, NF-kappaB, autophagy, unfolded protein response, and cytokine-signaling modules were quantified using AddModuleScore.
Regulon analysis using pySCENIC

Regulatory network inference for DLX2+ and DLX2- DCs was performed using pySCENIC (v0.12.1). GRNBoost2 was used to infer co-expression modules; motif enrichment was conducted using cisTarget databases; and regulon activity was scored using AUCell. Regulons were ranked by specificity index (RSS), and networks were visualized with Cytoscape.
Ligand-receptor interaction analysis

To investigate intercellular communication, we employed CellPhoneDB (v5.0), a publicly available repository of ligands, receptors, and their interactions. For the analysis, we utilized the normalized count data of single-cell clusters. An interaction was considered potentially active only if the corresponding ligand and receptor were expressed in at least 5% of cells in the respective clusters. To evaluate the statistical significance of the interactions, a permutation test (n = 1000) was performed, and interactions with P < 0.05 were prioritized for downstream visualization.

Cell-cell communication among DCs, T cells, and macrophages was inferred using CellPhoneDB. Inhibitory and co-stimulatory pathways:including CTLA4-CD80/CD86, PD-1/PD-L1, LGALS9-HAVCR2, BTLA-TNFRSF14, TGF-beta ligand-receptor pairs, ICOS-ICOSLG, and TNFSF/TNFRSF families:were examined. Communication probability scores were computed from normalized expression of ligand-receptor pairs and significance assessed using permutation tests.
Macrophage polarization scoring

M1 and M2 macrophage states were quantified using validated gene signatures. Scores were computed using Seurat's AddModuleScore and compared between DLX2-low and DLX2-high tumors. Macrophage clusters were annotated by expression of canonical markers (CD68, C1QA/B/C, S100A8/A9, FCN1, IL1B for M1; MRC1, MSR1, CCR2, IL10, and APOE for M2).
Spatial transcriptomics analysis

Visium spatial transcriptomics data were processed and analyzed in Scanpy. Spatial deconvolution of immune and stromal cell populations was performed using cell2location. Co-localization patterns among DLX2+ DCs, Tregs, Tex cells, macrophages, and stromal populations were examined using spatial correlation matrices and Moran's I statistics. Spatial-priority modeling was conducted using MistyR to quantify directional influences of signaling pathways:including TGF-beta, NF-kappaB, JAK-STAT, and TNF signaling:on immune-cell localization.
Statistical analysis

Statistical analyses were performed using R. Two-group comparisons used Wilcoxon tests; multi-group comparisons used Kruskal-Wallis tests. Spearman correlations were used unless otherwise indicated. Multiple testing correction used FDR. To control the FDR in large-scale differential expression and pathway analyses, P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. For specific localized comparisons, the Bonferroni correction was applied where appropriate to maintain a stringent significance threshold. Survival significance was defined as P < 0.05.
Discussion

The present study reveals an unrecognized immunoregulatory axis in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) centered on a transcriptionally distinct dendritic-cell population marked by DLX2. Although dendritic cells (DCs) have long been regarded as pivotal orchestrators of antitumor immunity, accumulating evidence has indicated that tumor-conditioned DCs often acquire dysfunctional or tolerogenic features that suppress T-cell activation rather than promote it. Prior studies have highlighted LAMP3+ DCs, moDCs, and migratory DC subsets as contributors to immune tolerance in solid tumors, yet the regulatory determinants that drive these dysfunctional phenotypes have remained incompletely defined. Our findings position DLX2 as a previously unappreciated molecular switch that marks and potentially drives a state of DC-mediated immune suppression, thereby extending and refining prevailing models of DC dysfunction in cancer.

passages.text: Multiple studies have indicated that developmental transcription factors can be re-engaged by tumor-associated immune cells, leading to lineage plasticity or aberrant differentiation. Existing reports have emphasized TFs such as STAT3, IRF4, and ATF3 in reprogramming DC function within the tumor microenvironment. Our integrative regulon analysis reveals that DLX2+ DCs are governed by an ATF3-FOSL2-FOSB-ZMIZ1 regulatory module enriched for stress-response, inflammatory, and unfolded-protein response programs:distinct from the IRF8-centered regulatory architecture typical of conventional cDC1 or cDC2 lineages. This suggests that DLX2+ DCs represent a transcriptionally rewired DC state rather than a canonical lineage subset. While previous work has linked ATF3 and AP-1 family TFs to tolerogenic or exhausted myeloid states, our study identifies DLX2 as a central node connecting these stress-activated regulons into a cohesive immunosuppressive identity, thereby providing mechanistic insight into how LUAD microenvironments divert DC differentiation.

A notable contribution of this study is the demonstration of spatial organization of DLX2+ DC-mediated immune suppression. Although recent spatial studies have shown that Tregs, exhausted CD8+ T cells, and M2 macrophages tend to co-localize within immunosuppressive niches, the upstream initiators of these microarchitectures have remained unclear. Here, we show that DLX2+ DCs consistently occupy the same spatial hubs as Tregs, Tex cells, and M2 macrophages across LUAD tissue sections. Furthermore, spatial-priority modeling indicates that TGF-beta-rich microenvironments strongly predict the localization of DLX2+ DCs, and reciprocally, that DLX2+ DCs predict the spatial enrichment of Tregs and exhausted T cells. These findings complement prior studies demonstrating that TGF-beta signaling shapes DC tolerogenicity and Treg stability, but they extend the concept by identifying DLX2+ DCs as a structural organizer of immunosuppressive neighborhoods, rather than merely responding to them.

Importantly, our ligand-receptor analyses clarify how DLX2+ DCs actively propagate immune dysfunction. Previous studies have shown that tumor-associated DCs can engage in PD-L1-PD-1 and CTLA4-CD80/CD86 interactions, but the breadth and intensity of inhibitory crosstalk has remained underappreciated. Our results reveal that DLX2+ DCs deploy an expanded spectrum of inhibitory ligands:including TGF-beta, LGALS9, PDCD1LG2, BTLA ligands, and multiple TNFSF/TNFRSF pairs:providing a multi-layered mechanism through which these cells suppress effector T-cell function, promote Treg differentiation, and reinforce M2 macrophage polarization. This suggests that DLX2+ DCs may serve as an upstream "communication hub" that shapes the fate and function of multiple immune lineages simultaneously, filling a conceptual gap in our understanding of how tumor-driven immune suppression becomes systemically coordinated.

Our findings also have implications for immunotherapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) rely on sufficient priming of tumor-specific T cells, a process heavily dependent on functional DCs. Multiple clinical studies have shown that dysfunctional or tolerogenic DC states correlate with diminished ICI responses in lung cancer. Given that DLX2+ DCs are tightly associated with T-cell exhaustion, reduced effector T-cell infiltration, and M2 myeloid skewing, it is plausible that DLX2+ DC abundance may serve as a biomarker of ICI resistance. Moreover, given the extensive inhibitory signaling output of DLX2+ DCs, targeting upstream drivers of this state:such as TGF-beta signaling, ATF3/AP-1 activity, or metabolic stress pathways:may offer opportunities to re-sensitize tumors to immunotherapy. Several therapeutic candidates that modulate DC phenotype, including TGF-beta inhibitors, AP-1 pathway modulators, and metabolic stress regulators, are already under clinical evaluation, suggesting that interventions aimed at the DLX2+ DC program may be clinically actionable.

Despite its strengths, this study has limitations. While our multimodal analyses strongly suggest that DLX2 delineates a tolerogenic DC phenotype, direct lineage-tracing or functional perturbation experiments will be required to determine whether DLX2 is a potential driver or marker of this state. Additionally, although our data indicate that DLX2+ DCs occupy immunosuppressive niches, the molecular cues that initiate DLX2 induction:whether derived from tumor cells, stromal components, or inflammatory stress:require further elucidation. Future experiments employing coculture systems, organoids, or in vivo perturbations will be essential for establishing causality. Finally, given that similar DC states have been observed in other solid tumors, it will be important to investigate whether DLX2 marks a universal tolerogenic DC program or a LUAD-specific adaptation.

In summary, our work uncovers a previously unrecognized DLX2-defined dendritic-cell state that operates as a transcriptional, functional, and spatial organizer of immune suppression in LUAD. By integrating bulk, single-cell, ligand-receptor, and spatial transcriptomics, this study establishes DLX2+ DCs as a central hub linking stress-response transcriptional programs to coordinated T-cell dysfunction and myeloid polarization. These findings fill a critical gap in our understanding of how tumor microenvironments establish immunosuppressive niches and suggest new avenues for therapeutic intervention aimed at reactivating antitumor immunity.

Data availability

Bulk RNA-seq data for lung adenocarcinoma were obtained from the TCGA-LUAD project through the UCSC Xena data portal (https://xenabrowser.net/). Expression matrices and corresponding clinical annotations were downloaded and harmonized for downstream differential, immunogenomic, and survival analyses. To characterize single-cell transcriptional heterogeneity within the LUAD tumor microenvironment, we integrated publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from GSE189357, which provide comprehensive profiling of epithelial, immune, and stromal lineages across LUAD specimens. Spatial transcriptomics validation was performed using the E-MTAB-13530 dataset, from which raw count matrices, spatial spot information, and metadata were retrieved and processed uniformly for cell-type deconvolution, spatial patterning, and microenvironmental interaction analyses. All secondary databases and computational resources used in the study have been explicitly included as follows. KEGG pathway annotations were obtained from the KEGG database (https://rest.kegg.jp/). Gene Ontology annotations were retrieved from the GO database (http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/go.owl). MSigDB Hallmark gene sets were downloaded from MSigDB (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp). The Neuroactive ligand-receptor gene set from Dong et al. was accessed through the supplementary dataset (doi: 10.1093/bib/bbaf082). Immune-cell deconvolution was performed using CIBERSORT (https://cibersortx.stanford.edu/download.php), xCell (https://xcell.ucsf.edu/), EPIC (https://gfellerlab.shinyapps.io/EPIC_1-1/), MCP-counter (https://github.com/ebecht/MCPcounter), TIMER (https://cistrome.shinyapps.io/timer/) and TIDE (http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu/download/). passages.text: Predicting adverse prognostic outcomes in hospitalized breast cancer patients: development and validation of a risk model
Background

Breast cancer prognosis is influenced by diverse clinical factors, necessitating advanced predictive tools for personalized treatment. This study developed machine learning models to predict adverse outcomes in breast cancer patients using comprehensive clinical data.
Methods

We analyzed data from 4,242 patients (3,836 with stable progression and 406 with adverse outcomes) at a single institution. Feature selection via univariate/multivariate analysis and machine learning importance ranking identified 10 key predictors, including metastasis stage, hospitalization duration, total healthcare costs, and laboratory test results. Ten machine learning models were evaluated using 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 undersampling ratios to address class imbalance. Performance was assessed via accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, the area under the curve (AUC), and precision.
Results

The Random Forest (RF) model achieved an optimal balance with 88.69% accuracy, 0.733 sensitivity, and 0.952 specificity (AUC range: 0.881-0.898) across sampling ratios, demonstrating superior class separation.SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed metastasis (SHAP = + 6.0) as the strongest risk factor, while marital status and Luminal A subtype were protective. Logistic Regression(LR) also performed robustly (AUC > 0.88), excelling in specificity (0.950 under 1:3 undersampling).
Conclusion

Machine learning models, particularly RF and LR, effectively predicted prognosis by integrating clinical and laboratory features. RF's stability in imbalanced data and interpretability via SHAP enhanced clinical utility. Future multi-center studies should validate these findings and explore causal mechanisms.

Not applicable.
Introduction

Breast cancer is the most common malignant tumor among women. According to global cancer statistics released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), there were approximately 2.31 million new cases of breast cancer and 665,700 related deaths worldwide in 2022, making it the leading cause of both incidence and mortality among all female malignancies. Women aged 50 and above are considered a high-risk group for breast cancer. However, recent studies have shown an increasing, imposing a significant burden on patients, families, and society. Globally, by 2021, the number of new cases and age-standardized incidence rates of early-onset female breast cancer had increased compared to 1990. In China, new cases rose from 36,700 to 110,400, and the age-standardized incidence rate increased from 6.83 to 13.49 per 100,000, representing a relative increase of 97.51%.

Despite significant advancements in breast cancer treatment in recent years, including the comprehensive application of various methods such as surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, some patients still face adverse prognostic outcomes such as recurrence, metastasis, and death. These outcomes severely impact patients' quality of life and long-term survival rates. Statistical data indicate that approximately 20%-30% of breast cancer patients experience recurrence within five years of treatment, while the five-year survival rate for metastatic breast cancer patients is only about 30%. These adverse outcomes not only impose heavy psychological and economic burdens on patients and their families but also present significant challenges to the healthcare system.

With the rapid development of machine learning and big data technologies, the analysis and modeling of vast amounts of medical data using advanced techniques hold promise for further improving the accuracy and practicality of predictive models. Methods such as decision trees (DT), random forests (RF), neural networks, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), logistic regression (LR), and support vector machines (SVM) have been widely explored. Clift and Dodwell et al. focused primarily on treatment-related factors including medication use, c-erbB-2 status, surgical approach, lymph node involvement, cancer stage and tumor grade, ultimately concluding that traditional Cox and competing risk models may offer greater clinical utility than machine learning approaches. Meanwhile, Sammut and Crispin-Ortuzar employed LR, SVM, and ensemble models to integrate clinical, genomic, and digital pathology data, demonstrating that their integrated model (AUC = 0.87) substantially outperformed clinical-only predictors (AUC = 0.70), thereby highlighting genomic markers as key determinants of treatment response. In another approach, Kalafi et al. applied deep learning techniques to analyze standard demographic and clinical parameters including diagnostic methods, tumor characteristics and nodal status, finding that neural network architectures outperformed conventional machine learning models while confirming established prognostic factors like tumor size, stage and nodal involvement. Despite these advances, current prognostic models remain limited by their predominant focus on diagnostic staging parameters and their general lack of interpretability, while largely overlooking the potential predictive value of routine inpatient laboratory measures.

Machine learning (ML) offers powerful capabilities for analyzing complex clinical data to enhance prognostic accuracy. Techniques including Decision Trees (DT), Random Forests (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and gradient boosting methods (e.g., XGBoost) have been extensively applied in oncology. However, existing models exhibit limitations. Some studies prioritize traditional statistical approaches like Cox models over ML for clinical interpretability, focusing primarily on static diagnostic factors (e.g., tumor stage, grade, nodal status). Others integrate advanced data types (e.g., genomics, digital pathology) to boost performance but often lack immediate clinical deployability in routine inpatient settings. While deep learning shows promise, its "black-box" nature and computational demands hinder interpretability and practical integration into clinical workflows, especially for structured electronic health record (EHR) data. Crucially, most models neglect the potential predictive value of dynamic, routinely collected inpatient laboratory indicators (e.g., serial albumin, potassium levels), which reflect a patient's real-time physiological status and treatment response during hospitalization.

To address these gaps and meet the specific demands of real-time risk stratification in the hospital environment, we developed and validated interpretable ML models leveraging readily available clinical data. This study presents:to our knowledge:one of the first prognostic models to integrate comprehensive inpatient laboratory measures with established predictors such as molecular subtype and metastasis status. Our approach prioritizes clinical utility and interpretability - essential for bedside decision-making. We employed a rigorous methodology: (1) Univariate and multivariate analysis to screen candidate predictors from a broad feature set; (2) Feature importance ranking using diverse ML algorithms (LR, SVM, RF) to identify the most robust predictors; (3) Comprehensive evaluation of multiple classical ML models (including RF, LR, XGBoost) across balanced datasets to ensure generalizability; and critically, (4) SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis to elucidate model logic and feature contributions.We deliberately focused on well-established, efficient, and inherently interpretable ML methods (particularly RF and LR) rather than deep learning or large language models. This choice was driven by key considerations for clinical deployment: the predominance of structured EHR data, moderate dataset size (N = 4,242), the imperative for high model interpretability to gain clinician trust, and the need for computational efficiency within hospital IT infrastructure. RF and LR excel in these aspects, offering transparency alongside strong predictive performance.

By developing this interpretable risk prediction tool, we aim to provide clinicians with actionable insights during a patient's hospitalization, enabling earlier identification of high-risk individuals and facilitating tailored management strategies to ultimately improve outcomes.
Methods
Data source and collection

The EMR data were obtained from breast cancer inpatients at the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University. The data included patients' clinicopathological characteristics, imaging examination results, and sociodemographic information.
Inclusion criteria
Patients must have a confirmed pathological diagnosis of breast cancer, including major subtypes such as invasive ductal carcinoma and invasive lobular carcinoma.
Diagnostic evidence must include histopathological reports, immunohistochemical (IHC) results, and molecular subtype information.
Patients must have received at least one complete breast cancer-related treatment in the hospital, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, or endocrine therapy.
Detailed clinical records during hospitalization must be available, including treatment plans, efficacy evaluations, and adverse reaction monitoring.
Exclusion criteria
Patients lacking key clinical data.
Patients with missing laboratory or imaging examination results.
Patients lost to follow-up or with unavailable follow-up records.
Patients with other primary malignant tumors, to avoid interference with breast cancer-related prognosis analysis.
Patients who received only outpatient care or did not undergo standardized in-hospital treatment.
Patients with severe comorbidities (e.g., end-stage liver disease, renal failure) or who could not tolerate treatment.
Patients who discontinued treatment for non-medical reasons.

Outcome Variable. Adverse outcome was defined as a composite endpoint comprising either disease progression (including local recurrence or distant metastasis) or all-cause mortality during the follow-up period. This composite measure captures clinically significant events reflecting treatment failure and long-term disease burden, and was selected for its relevance to prognosis and clinical decision-making.
Clinical relevance and diagnostic criteria:

Local recurrence: Histologically confirmed recurrence in the ipsilateral breast, chest wall, or regional lymph nodes (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ICD-10]: C50.0-C50.9 with recurrence code Z85.3).
Distant metastasis: Radiologically or pathologically confirmed metastasis to distant organs (ICD-10: C78.0-C79.9 for secondary malignant neoplasms).
All-cause mortality: Death from any cause during follow-up (ICD-10: R96-R99 for ill-defined causes, supplemented by specific cause-of-death codes when available).
This composite endpoint was chosen to provide a comprehensive assessment of treatment failure and long-term disease burden, reflecting both disease-specific progression and overall survival outcomes.
Demographics: Age, gender, marital status, occupation, ethnicity;.
Treatment Process: Length of stay (LOS), total hospitalization costs (THC), ventilator usage duration, resuscitation events;
Comorbidities:Hypertension (HTN), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), heart disease (HD), osteoporosis (Osteo), pulmonary infection (Pulm_Inf), anemia;

Tumor Pathology: Tumor stage (T Stage), nodal stage (N Stage), metastasis stage (M_Stage), metastasis status, HER2 status (positive/overexpression), molecular subtype (Luminal A [LumA], Luminal B [LumB], triple-negative breast cancer[TNBC]), laterality (L/R Breast, L/R Mammary);

Treatment Modalities:Chemotherapy (Chemo), targeted therapy (Target_Tx), hormonal therapy (Horm_Tx);procedures (Mastectomy [Mast], Rad Mastectomy [Rad_Mast], Partial Mastectomy [Part_Mast], Breast Reconstruction [Br_Recon]);

Laboratory Indicators (Admission [Adm_] & Prognostic [Pro_] timepoints): Respiratory rate (BF), heart rate (HR), body temperature (BT), systolic/diastolic blood pressure (SBP/DBP), total cholesterol (TC), triglycerides (TG), glucose ratio (GR), albumin (Alb), total protein (TP), serum globulin (SG), hemoglobin (Hb), potassium (K), albumin-globulin ratio (AGR).

These predictor variables reflect patients' basic characteristics, treatment processes, health status, and disease biology from multiple perspectives, providing rich information for constructing predictive models and analyzing influencing factors.

Data preprocessing

To address missing values in the dataset, we utilized the micepackage in R for multiple imputation. This method generates multiple complete datasets by imputing missing values based on observed data, thereby reducing bias and preserving data variability. After imputation, we first performed univariate analysis to identify potential risk factors associated with the outcomes. Subsequently, multivariate analysis was conducted to adjust for confounding factors and determine independent predictors.
Addressing class imbalance

Given the significant imbalance between the stable progression group (N = 3,836) and the adverse outcome group (N = 406), we employed random undersampling of the majority class to create balanced datasets for model training and evaluation. Three distinct balanced datasets were generated with majority-to-minority ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3. Performance was evaluated across all ratios to assess model robustness to varying degrees of balance. The original imbalanced dataset was also analyzed for comparison.
Data analysis and feature selection

In the Baseline characteristics analysis, normally distributed data were presented as mean and standard deviation (SD), while non-normally distributed data were presented as median and interquartile range (IQR). Categorical variables were described using frequencies and percentages. For between-group comparisons, independent samples t-test was used for normally distributed data, Mann-Whitney U test (for two groups) or Kruskal-Wallis test (for multiple groups) was used for non-normally distributed data, and chi-square test was used for categorical variables.
To rigorously select predictive features, we employed a two-stage approach:

Statistical Filtering: Univariate logistic regression identified variables associated with the outcome (p < 0.05). Significant univariate predictors were then entered into two multivariate logistic regression models:
Model 1 adjusted for all 68 candidate variables.

Model 2 adjusted for core demographic/clinical factors (Ethnicity_Han, Married, LOS, Age, Insur_Cov, Hosp_Freq). Variables achieving statistical significance (p < 0.05) in either multivariate model were retained, yielding 43 candidate predictors (Table 3).

Feature Importance Ranking: To further refine the feature set and enhance generalizability, we calculated feature importance scores using three distinct, interpretable machine learning algorithms applied to the 43 candidate features:
Logistic Regression (LR; L1 regularization)
Support Vector Machine (SVM; linear kernel)
Random Forest (RF)

Features were ranked by their importance score within each algorithm. The top 10 features consistently highlighted across the three rankings from these three diverse methods were selected as the final predictor set for model building (Table 5). This combined approach leverages both statistical rigor and algorithmic robustness to identify the most salient predictors.
Machine learning model development

Based on the specific requirements of clinical deployment - namely, high interpretability, efficiency with structured data, and robustness to moderate sample sizes-we deliberately selected well-established classical machine learning algorithms.We evaluated the following models using their standard implementations:
Logistic Regression (LR)
Random Forest (RF)
XGBoost (XGB)
LightGBM (LGBM)
Support Vector Machine (SVM)
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
Decision Tree (DT)
AdaBoost (AB)
Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)

Notably, deep learning or large language models were not employed, as their "black-box" nature, high computational demands, and data requirements are less suited to the structured EHR data, moderate sample size, and paramount need for interpretability in this clinical risk stratification context. Hyperparameters for each model (e.g., number of trees and depth for RF/XGB/LGBM, regularization strength for LR/SVM, number of neighbors for KNN) were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation on the training set, aiming to maximize the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Model evaluation and validation
Model performance was comprehensively assessed using metrics critical for clinical prognosis:
Accuracy: Overall correct prediction rate.
Sensitivity (Recall): Ability to correctly identify patients with adverse outcomes (minimizing false negatives).
Specificity: Ability to correctly identify patients with stable progression (minimizing false positives).
Precision: Proportion of predicted adverse outcomes that are correct.
Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC): Overall discriminative ability across all classification thresholds.

Validation followed a rigorous two-stage process: (1)Internal Validation & Robustness to Imbalance: Models were trained and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation on four datasets: the original imbalanced data and the three undersampled balanced datasets (1:1, 1:2, 1:3). Performance metrics were averaged across folds. (2) External Validation: To assess generalizability and real-world applicability, we employed a strict temporal split:
Training/Internal Validation Set:Patients admitted between 2005 and 2020;

External Test Set:Patients admitted between 2021 and 2024.Models trained on the 2005-2020 data (using the best-performing sampling ratio identified internally) were evaluated solely on the unseen 2021-2024 data.
Model Interpretability

To enhance clinical utility and trust, we employed SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis using the Python shaplibrary. SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to the prediction for an individual patient, providing intuitive, model-agnostic explanations. This allows clinicians to understand why a patient is predicted to be high-risk, identifying key driving factors.

Baseline characteristics

This study included 4242 patients, divided into the Stable Development Group (3836 cases) and the Adverse Outcome Group (406 cases). As is shown in Table 2, the results showed significant differences between the two groups in demographic characteristics, disease features, laboratory indicators, and clinical outcomes. Patients with adverse outcomes demonstrated significantly older age, rural residence, lower insurance coverage (Insur_Cov), and reduced marriage rates (all p < 0.01), along with higher comorbidity burdens including heart disease (HD), pulmonary infections (Pulm_Inf), and anemia (all p < 0.01). Clinically, this group exhibited more advanced TNM staging (T3/T4, N2/N3, M1), fewer Luminal A (LumA) cases, and lower treatment adherence (chemotherapy [Chemo] and hormone therapy [Horm_Tx], all p < 0.01). Admission laboratory results revealed poorer nutritional status (albumin [Alb], total protein [TP]), abnormal glucose regulation (GR), and potassium (K) levels (all p < 0.05). Post-treatment prognostic markers showed persistent nutritional deficits (Pro_Alb, Pro_TP), dyslipidemia (Pro_TC, Pro_TG), and anemia (Pro_Hb) (all p < 0.01), suggesting sustained metabolic dysregulation contributes to poorer outcomes.

Univariate analysis and Multivariate analysis

Univariate analysis assessed the independent association of each variable with adverse outcomes, while multivariate analysis accounted for interactions among variables and adjusted for potential confounding factors. Through this process, we identified statistically significant variables with potential predictive value. As detailed in Table 4, a total of 43 significant variables from the multivariate analysis were selected as candidate predictors for subsequent model development.

Table 5 presents the model performance metrics trained on the original imbalanced dataset using the 43 candidate predictors. The models showed varying performance characteristics. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.247% and 94.110%, respectively), followed closely by Gradient Boosting (93.836%). However, all models exhibited a characteristic accuracy-sensitivity trade-off, with a maximum sensitivity of only 0.554 (XGBoost) while maintaining robust specificity (> 0.95 for all models). Precision was highest for LightGBM (0.739) and XGBoost (0.735), indicating relatively reliable positive predictions. This pattern:high accuracy and specificity but limited sensitivity:strongly suggests that the models were influenced by the class imbalance, where predictions were dominated by the majority class (stable progression). The consistently high specificity (> 0.95) confirms excellent identification of negative cases, whereas the modest sensitivity reflects the challenge in detecting the smaller adverse-outcome group. These findings underscore the need for imbalance-correction strategies, which we subsequently addressed through systematic undersampling at 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 ratios, as detailed in the following sections.

Feature selection

Three distinct methods were employed to analyze variable feature importance. As illustrated in the figure(Figs. 2, 3 and 4), the relative importance and ranking of variables varied across different models.

The Logistic Regression (LR) model identified the following top five most important features: N_Stage, M_Stage, Pro_Alb, Adm_lb, and Pro_TP; The Linear SVM model yielded: Pro_Alb, M_Stage, N_Stage, Age, and Adm_lb; The Random Forest model selected: M_Stage, LOS, THC, Pro_Alb, and Adm_K.

For subsequent predictive modeling, we selected the top 10 most important features across all methods (ranked by importance score). Predictive performance was evaluated using accuracy_score, achieving values of 0.9219, 0.9192, and 0.9233 respectively. The final selected features were: 'M_Stage', 'LOS', 'THC', 'Pro_Alb', 'Adm_K', 'Pro_TC', 'Pro_TP', 'Adm_TP', 'Adm_lb', and 'Pro_AGR' (Table 6).

Model performance comparison

We performed additional analyses using the ten selected features mentioned above, evaluating four different datasets: the complete original dataset containing 4,242 samples (3,836 patients without adverse outcomes and 406 with adverse outcomes), along with 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 undersampled datasets. The detailed results of these analyses are presented in Table 7; Fig. 5.

Overall, Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy (93.43%) and AUC (0.906), demonstrating robust classification capability, though its sensitivity (0.462) remained suboptimal, indicating limited detection of positive cases. AdaBoost exhibited a balanced performance, with competitive accuracy (93.29%), the highest sensitivity among all models (0.508), and strong specificity (0.974), suggesting its potential as a reliable classifier for imbalanced data. In contrast, Support Vector Machine (SVM) showed poor sensitivity (0.077) despite high specificity (0.994), rendering it unsuitable for scenarios requiring minority class detection. While XGBoost and LightGBM delivered moderate accuracy (92.60-93.15%) and AUC (0.845-0.875), their sensitivity (0.415-0.446) remained inadequate, reflecting a common limitation across models in identifying positive instances. These results highlight the persistent challenge of class imbalance, as evidenced by universally low sensitivity (< 0.55) despite high specificity (> 0.95) and accuracy (> 90%). Future work should prioritize techniques to enhance sensitivity, such as resampling or cost-sensitive learning, particularly for applications where minority class detection is critical.

The 1:1 undersampling analysis revealed significant improvements in model performance compared to the original imbalanced dataset (Table 7). Random Forest emerged as the top-performing model, achieving 86.61% accuracy with balanced sensitivity (0.813) and specificity (0.906), while maintaining high AUC (0.881) and precision (0.867). AdaBoost demonstrated exceptional specificity (0.953) and the highest precision (0.921), albeit with slightly lower sensitivity (0.729), suggesting it may be particularly suitable for applications where false positives carry high costs. XGBoost and LightGBM showed comparable performance, with sensitivity around 0.77-0.79 and AUC > 0.86, indicating robust predictive capability. Notably, Logistic Regression exhibited unexpectedly strong performance (83.93% accuracy, 0.875 precision), challenging the conventional wisdom that linear models underperform on balanced datasets. In contrast, SVM and KNN remained suboptimal, with KNN showing particularly poor specificity (0.516), likely due to their inherent limitations in handling the feature space of this dataset. These results collectively demonstrate that 1:1 undersampling effectively mitigates class imbalance issues, with tree-based ensemble methods (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost) delivering the most balanced performance across all metrics. The strong performance of multiple models suggests that the predictive features in this dataset contain substantial signal for classification when balanced sampling is employed.

The 1:2 undersampling (majority-to-minority ratio) results demonstrate further optimization of model performance compared to both the original imbalanced data and 1:1 balanced approach (Table 7). Gradient Boosting and Random Forest jointly achieved the highest accuracy (88.69% and 88.10%, respectively), with Gradient Boosting showing marginally better sensitivity (0.733 vs. 0.733) and precision (0.936 vs. 0.917). Notably, these models maintained exceptional specificity (> 0.96) and AUC (> 0.89), indicating robust discriminative power while preserving detection capability for the minority class. AdaBoost continued to excel in precision (0.932) and specificity (0.972), though its sensitivity (0.683) slightly trailed the top performers, reinforcing its suitability for precision-critical applications.

The XGBoost and LightGBM models exhibited balanced performance with sensitivity around 0.68-0.70 and AUC > 0.87, though LightGBM showed a small but notable precision drop (0.872 vs. XGBoost's 0.875). Logistic Regression maintained surprisingly strong performance (83.93% accuracy, 0.902 precision) despite its linear nature, though its sensitivity (0.617) remained suboptimal. Strikingly, SVM demonstrated extreme specificity (0.991) and high precision (0.923) but catastrophically low sensitivity (0.200), effectively rendering it useless for minority class detection despite its apparent high accuracy (70.83%). KNN performed poorest overall (67.26% accuracy, 0.350 sensitivity), likely due to the curse of dimensionality in this feature space.

The 1:3 undersampling results reveal several important trends in model performance (Table 7). Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and LightGBM demonstrated identical overall accuracy (88.39%) and sensitivity (0.679), though their underlying characteristics differed. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest AUC (0.875) among these models, suggesting marginally better class separation capability. Notably, all four models maintained excellent specificity (0.952) and comparable precision (0.826), indicating robust performance across evaluation metrics.

The limitations of certain algorithms became particularly apparent in this ratio. SVM showed extreme specificity (0.976) but catastrophic sensitivity (0.196), while KNN performed poorly across all metrics (74.11% accuracy, 0.250 sensitivity), reinforcing their unsuitability for this classification task.

Figure 6 displays the DCA (Decision Curve Analysis) of the model. The DCA results demonstrate that, across the threshold range of 0.0 to 0.5, the predictive model constructed in this study ("Our Model") exhibits greater clinical net benefit than the strategies of "treating all patients" ("All") and "treating no patients" ("None") at the majority of threshold points. Specifically, within the critical decision range of approximately 0.07 to 0.30, the model curve consistently lies above the two reference lines, indicating its clear clinical utility in effectively assisting physicians to balance the risks of overtreatment and undertreatment. Particularly in the threshold range of 0.10-0.20, the model's net benefit reaches a relatively high level, suggesting that it can provide significant benefits for guiding clinical decision-making within this range. In summary, the DCA validates the model's good clinical applicability and potential for decision improvement at reasonable risk thresholds.
Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) Curve

Figure 7 illustrates the calibration performance of the prognostic model.The calibration curve demonstrates that the predicted probabilities of the prognostic model align well with the observed event rates across the probability spectrum, as indicated by the close proximity of the calibration curve (black solid line) to the line of perfect calibration (red dashed line). The bias-corrected curve, derived from 1000 bootstrap repetitions, closely follows the apparent calibration curve, suggesting minimal overfitting. The mean absolute error of 0.01, calculated from 3649 observations, further confirms the model's calibration accuracy. These results collectively indicate that the model provides well-calibrated risk estimates, supporting its reliability for clinical risk stratification.

External validation

As is shown in Table 8; Fig. 8,Our external validation (2021-2024, 1:1 undersampled) demonstrated that Random Forest (RF) achieved the most robust performance among all evaluated models, with an accuracy of 88.39%, sensitivity of 0.679, specificity of 0.952, and an AUC of 0.892, indicating strong discriminative ability. RF not only outperformed other tree-based models (XGBoost: AUC = 0.864; LightGBM: AUC = 0.866) but also maintained a superior balance between sensitivity and specificity compared to logistic regression (AUC = 0.818) and support vector machines (AUC = 0.549). Additionally, RF exhibited high precision (0.826), further confirming its reliability in correctly classifying positive cases. These results highlight RF as the most stable and generalizable model for predicting adverse outcomes in breast cancer patients, particularly when handling imbalanced datasets.

SHAP values (impact on model output)

The SHAP analysis demonstrates the directional influence of clinical features on the model's prediction(Fig. 9). Features are ranked by their impact magnitude, with red bars (rightward arrows) indicating risk-enhancing effects and blue bars (leftward arrows) denoting protective effects.

Key observations reveal Metastasis as the strongest risk predictor (SHAP = + 6.0), followed by Chemo (+ 2.5) and Br_Recon (+ 1.2). Conversely, Married status (-2.8) and Luminal A type(LumA) (-2.1) exhibit marked protective effects. Features like Other_Ca and Pulm_Inf show bidirectional impacts (SHAP range: -1.5 to + 1.0), suggesting context-dependent roles.

Notably, the model prioritizes pathological factors (e.g., metastasis) over demographic variables (e.g., marital status), aligning with clinical intuition. The divergent impact of Br_Recon (post-surgical reconstruction) warrants investigation into potential confounding by indication.

Through the SHAP values(Fig. 10), we can see that the model's average expected value is 0.514, and the prediction value for this particular patient is -1.044. Among them, THC, Adm_K, Adm_TP, Pro_TP, Pro_AGR and Adm_lb have a positive impact on the prediction result, with THC having an impact value of 1.12. On the other hand, M_Stage, LOS, Pro_Alb, Pro_TC have a negative impact on the prediction result.

Discussion

This study included 4242 patients, divided into a stable progression group (3836 cases) and an adverse prognosis group (406 cases). Univariate and multivariate analyses were conducted for indicator screening, followed by the use of logistic regression, SVM, random forests models to select indicators with importance above the median for further analysis. The selected indicators included M_Stage, LOS, THC, Pro_Alb, Adm_K, Pro_TC, Pro_TP, Adm_TP, Adm_lb, Pro_AGR.

The study employed various models, including Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM, and Linear Discriminant Analysis. To address data imbalance, 1:2 undersampling was applied. The results demonstrated that in 1:2, 1:1, and 1:3 undersampled datasets, models such as logistic regression and random forest performed exceptionally well, with Random Forest showing the best overall performance (AUC = 0.881). These models excelled in key performance metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, and precision, indicating that undersampling effectively mitigated data imbalance and enhanced the models' ability to identify both positive and negative classes.

In handling imbalanced datasets, undersampling at ratios of 1:2, 1:1, and 1:3 significantly improved the issue of data imbalance, enhancing the models' ability to identify positive classes (e.g., adverse prognosis) while maintaining high recognition rates for negative classes (e.g., no adverse prognosis).

Our key finding is that traditional machine learning algorithms:particularly Random Forest (RF) and Logistic Regression (LR):achieved robust and interpretable performance when integrating novel predictors derived from inpatient laboratory monitoring alongside established clinical features. This approach demonstrates significant potential for clinical deployment in resource-constrained hospital settings.

Machine learning models have demonstrated superior performance in various aspects of breast cancer management, including efficient screening, diagnosis, precise prognosis assessment, and personalized treatment plans. For instance, machine learning has been used to predict survival rates at different stages of breast cancer and to identify non-indications for radiotherapy using DIBH. Widely adopted models encompass traditional machine learning algorithms such as K-nearest Neighbors (KNN), random forests (RF), and support vector machines (SVM). In contemporary machine learning research, it is common practice to employ a variety of algorithms to construct different models and evaluate their performance to identify the optimal one. For example, Huang Q, Yang Y et al. developed models using different machine learning algorithms to predict high-risk symptom burden clusters in breast cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, identifying the RF algorithm as the best performer with an AUC of 0.91, while logistic regression outperformed in calibration metrics. Song X and Chu J et al. included 6,477 patients from affiliated hospitals, using eight different machine learning algorithms and varying training/testing set ratios to validate 15 clinical features significantly associated with breast cancer survival. They found that XGBoost exhibited the highest performance, with age, tumor size, lymph node status, and hormone receptor status being important prognostic predictors.

In the analysis of 1:1 undersampled data, Random Forest (RF) models demonstrated superior performance (AUC = 0.881), followed by XGBoost (AUC = 0.875) and Logistic Regression (LR, AUC = 0.859).The selection of classical machine learning algorithms (RF, LR, SVM, XGBoost, etc.) over deep learning or large language models was deliberate and grounded in the specific demands of clinical risk stratification. Our primary objectives were to develop a model that is: (1) highly interpretable to foster clinician trust and guide decision-making, (2) computationally efficient for potential integration into real-time hospital workflows, and (3) robust with the available structured electronic health record (EHR) data and sample size (N = 4,242). Deep learning models, while powerful in domains like image analysis, often function as "black boxes," requiring substantial computational resources and larger datasets to avoid overfitting:characteristics incompatible with the need for transparent, actionable risk scores at the point of care. RF and LR, enhanced by SHAP analysis, provided the optimal balance of predictive accuracy, stability across validation sets, and critically, the ability to elucidate the driving factors behind predictions.

While previous breast cancer prognostic studies have achieved optimal results, their feature selection lacked comprehensiveness. Prior research by Ganggayah and Taib considered demographic characteristics, surgical approaches, and tumor grade but omitted clinical laboratory indicators. Similarly, Zuo's analysis of recurrence risk focused solely on clinical features such as tumor size, cancer grade, and molecular subtypes.

Our study innovatively incorporates both admission laboratory tests (Adm_K, Adm_TP, Adm_lb) and follow-up indicators (Pro_Alb, Pro_TC, Pro_TP, Pro_AGR) alongside conventional clinical features. Through univariate analysis, multivariate analysis, and feature importance ranking, we identified the top 10 predictive indicators. Our findings establish that admission laboratory markers and prognostic indicators serve as significant predictors of adverse outcomes (mortality or recurrence) in breast cancer patients.

The pronounced class imbalance (406 adverse vs. 3,836 stable outcomes) presented a major challenge. Our systematic application of random undersampling (1:1, 1:2, 1:3 ratios) effectively mitigated this imbalance, substantially improving model sensitivity (identification of adverse outcomes) while preserving high specificity. Among the evaluated algorithms, RF consistently demonstrated the best overall performance, achieving peak accuracy (88.69%), sensitivity (0.733), specificity (0.952), and AUC (0.881-0.898) in the 1:2 undersampled data.LR also performed exceptionally well, particularly excelling in specificity (0.950 in 1:3) and offering inherent interpretability. This finding aligns with prior studies utilizing ML for breast cancer prognosis. For instance, Huang et al. similarly identified RF as the top performer (AUC = 0.91) for predicting high-risk symptom clusters during chemotherapy, while Song et al. found XGBoost optimal for survival prediction, highlighting tumor characteristics like size and nodal status. Our results reinforce that RF and LR are highly effective for structured clinical prognostic modeling.

SHAP analysis quantified the risk contribution of individual features, identifying metastasis (SHAP = + 6.0) as the predominant risk driver, with an impact substantially exceeding that of treatment-related variables (chemotherapy: +2.5; reconstruction surgery: +1.2). Protective factors primarily included marital status (-2.8) and the Luminal A molecular subtype (-2.1). In this model, the individualized prediction for this patient (-1.044 versus a baseline of 0.514) was positively influenced by biochemical markers (e.g., THC = + 1.12) and negatively influenced by metastatic progression. Notably, the modest protective effect associated with reconstruction surgery is more likely to reflect clinical selection bias rather than a direct biological protective mechanism. These findings not only enhance the interpretability of the model but also provide a quantitative basis for understanding the relative weight of risk factors and advancing personalized diagnosis and treatment.
Limitations and future research
Limitations

.This study has several limitations. First, the data were derived from a single institution, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings due to regional variations in healthcare resources, patient demographics, and clinical practices. Second, the study focused primarily on establishing predictive performance without investigating causal relationships between the identified indicators and adverse outcomes, thereby limiting its contribution to mechanistic understanding. Third, the temporal validation design (training set: 2005-2020; validation set: 2021-2024) may introduce confounding, as significant advances in breast cancer management:such as the widespread adoption of HER2-targeted therapies:during this period could independently influence patient outcomes and affect the interpretation of model performance across different treatment eras. Finally, this work remains a proof-of-concept study and has not yet been developed into a readily applicable clinical tool, such as a nomogram or risk score, for point-of-care use.
Future Research

To address these limitations, future research should consider the following directions: First, multi-center collaborations incorporating data from diverse geographic and healthcare settings are needed to enhance the external validity and clinical applicability of the model. Second, integrating multi-omics data (e.g., genomics, proteomics, transcriptomics) could help elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying the predictive indicators and bridge the gap between prediction and pathological insight. Third, methodologically, feature selection could be refined using regularization approaches such as Lasso regression, and robustness could be improved through multi-algorithm voting schemes; moreover, methods such as propensity score matching should be applied in validation designs to control for confounding due to temporal changes in treatment standards. Fourth, efforts should be directed toward translating the model into user-friendly clinical tools (e.g., risk calculators) and conducting implementation studies to evaluate their feasibility and utility in real-world settings. Finally, systematic comparison with established prognostic models is essential to clarify the incremental value and clinical positioning of the proposed tool.
Conclusion

This study developed and validated machine learning models to predict adverse prognosis in breast cancer patients using a cohort of 4,242 cases (3,836 stable progression, 406 adverse outcomes). Through rigorous feature selection (univariate/multivariate analysis and machine learning-based importance ranking), we identified key predictive indicators, including tumor metastasis stage (M_Stage), hospitalization duration (LOS), total healthcare costs (THC), and critical laboratory markers (Adm_K, Adm_TP, Pro_Alb, etc.). Among multiple algorithms evaluated, Random Forest (RF) demonstrated superior performance, achieving an AUC of 0.881 in 1:2 undersampled data, with balanced sensitivity (0.679) and specificity (0.952). SHAP analysis further revealed metastasis as the strongest risk predictor (SHAP = + 6.0), while marital status and Luminal A subtype exhibited protective effects.Overall, these methodological strategies:including rigorous handling of class imbalance, selection of robust algorithms, and interpretable explainability techniques:collectively contribute to a clinically applicable and transparent prognostic tool. Future validation in multi-center, prospective cohorts, along with benchmarking against existing clinical scores, will further establish its utility in real-world oncology practice.
