passages.text: Since all hCG + MPTmix doses reduced the levels of both active PGs, we examined expression of all PG synthases under each treatment condition. Despite only select synthases being known to increase following LH/hCG stimulation, phthalate-induced alterations in the expression or activity of constitutively expressed synthases or synthases not induced by LH/hCG may also impair PG-mediated ovulatory processes. Treatment with hCG increased PLA2G4A (12hr) and PTGES (all time points) expression compared to DMSO (Fig. 3A, C). However, hCG treatment also decreased PLA2G4A (6 and 36hr), PTGS1 (36hr), and PTGES2 (all time points) expression relative to DMSO (Fig. 3A, B, D). In contrast, PTGES3 expression was unaffected by hCG treatment at all tested time points (Fig. 3E). Compared to hCG controls, MPTmix exposure increased PLA2G4A expression at 6hr (500 mug/ml), while 36hr expression was both increased (10 and 100 mug/ml) and decreased (500 mug/ml) (Fig. 3A). Treatment with hCG + MPTmix increased (100 mug/ml) and decreased (500 mug/ml) 6hr PTGS1 expression compared to hCG, but only decreased expression at the 12 (500 mug/ml), 24 (100 mug/ml), and 36hr (500 mug/ml) time points (Fig. 3B). PTGES expression was decreased with MPTmix exposure relative to hCG controls at 6 (10 and 500 mug/ml), 24 (10, 100, and 500 mug/ml), and 36hr (1, 100, and 500 mug/ml) time points (Fig. 3C). Treatment with hCG + MPTmix increased 6 (100 and 500 mug/ml), 12 (1 and 500 mug/ml), and 24hr (500 mug/ml) PTGES2 expression, but decreased expression at 36hr (500 mug/ml) compared to hCG controls (Fig. 3D). PTGES3 expression was increased at 24hr (500 mug/ml) with MPTmix exposure, while 36hr expression was both increased (100 mug/ml) and decreased (500 mug/ml) relative to hCG (Fig. 3E).
Effect of MPTmix on PG metabolism

In addition to LH/hCG-driven increases in PGE2 and PGF2alpha production, PG metabolism is concurrently downregulated to maintain elevated levels of active PGs. In this study, we measured inactive PG metabolites and HPGD (PG metabolic enzyme) protein activity during the late ovulatory period (24 and 36hr) following hCG + MPTmix treatment. We also assessed the expression of HPGD and AKR (aldo-keto reductase) family members across the ovulatory window (6, 12, 24, and 36hr). AKR enzymes may modulate active PGE2 levels or activity, either by converting PG precursors (PGH2) directly into PGF2alpha (AKR1C3) or by interconverting PGE2 and PGF2alpha (AKR1C1). This is particularly significant because, as noted in Section 1, PGE2 is consistently recognized as the critical PG for ovulation. Treatment with hCG increased inactive PGE2 metabolite levels, likely reflecting higher levels of PGE2 available for metabolism, but did not alter inactive PGF2alpha metabolite levels at either time point compared to DMSO (Fig. 4A and B). In contrast, hCG + MPTmix reduced PGE2 metabolite levels (100 and 500 mug/ml) at both time points and decreased PGF2alpha metabolite levels (1 mug/ml) at 24hr, but also increased PGF2alpha metabolite levels at 24 (500 mug/ml) and 36hr (100 and 500 mug/ml) time points relative to hCG (Fig. 4A and B). As expected, hCG treatment reduced HPGD protein activity (24 and 36hr) and gene expression (12, 24, and 36hr) compared to DMSO (Fig. 4C and D). However, hCG + MPTmix increased HPGD activity at 24 (all doses) and 36hr (1 and 500 mug/ml), and increased gene expression at 6 (100 and 500 mug/ml), 12 (500 mug/ml), 24 (500 mug/ml), and 36hr (100 and 500 mug/ml) relative to hCG (Fig. 4C and D). For AKR family members, hCG treatment induced a dynamic response. AKR1C1 (which interconverts PGE2 and PGF2alpha) expression increased at 6, 12, and 24hr but decreased at 36hr, while AKR1C3 (which directly synthesizes PGF2alpha) expression was consistently reduced compared to DMSO (Fig. 4E and F). With hCG + MPTmix, AKR1C1 expression was increased at 6 (100 mug/ml), 12 (10, 100, and 500 mug/ml), 24 (10, 100, and 500 mug/ml), and 36hr (10, 100, and 500 mug/ml), despite a single dose (1 mug/ml) that was decreased at 24hr relative to hCG (Fig. 4E). Similarly, AKR1C3 expression was upregulated with hCG + MPTmix at 6 (all doses), 12 (10 and 500 mug/ml), 24 (1 and 500 mug/ml), and 36hr (10 and 100 mug/ml) compared to hCG controls (Fig. 4F).
Effect of MPTmix on PG transporters

PG transporters are also regulated by LH/hCG and modulate the influx/efflux of PGs, which act in both an autocrine and paracrine manner. To assess the impact of phthalates on PG transport to/from granulosa cells, we measured the expression of the two key transporters (ABCC4 and SLCO2A1) across the ovulatory period. Treatment with hCG increased ABCC4 (6 and 12hr) and SLCO2A1 (6, 12, and 24hr) expression, but decreased 36hr SLCO2A1 expression compared to DMSO (Fig. 5A and B). ABCC4 expression was decreased with hCG + MPTmix treatment at 6 (10 mug/ml), 24 (1 mug/ml), and 36hr (500 mug/ml) time points compared to hCG controls, whereas SLCO2A1 expression was increased at 6 (100 and 500 mug/ml), 12 (1, 10, and 100 mug/ml), and 36hr (10 and 100 mug/ml) time points (Fig. 5A and B). However, a single MPTmix dose (500 mug/ml) decreased 36hr SLCO2A1 expression relative to hCG (Fig. 5B).
Effect of MPTmix on PG receptors

PGs mediate their ovulatory effects by binding to receptors expressed on multiple cell types within the ovarian follicle, including granulosa cells. To investigate how phthalates may influence PG function, we measured the expression of the four PGE2 receptors (PTGER1-4) and the singular PGF2alpha receptor (PTGFR) across the ovulatory period. Treatment with hCG decreased PTGER1 (6, 12, and 36hr) and PTGER4 (all time points) expression compared to DMSO, but increased expression of PTGER2 (6 and 12hr), PTGER3 (6hr), and PTGFR (24 and 36hr) (Fig. 6A-E). PTGER1 expression was elevated at all time points when treated with the hCG + MPTmix 500 mug/ml dose, but was reduced at 6hr with the 10 mug/ml dose (Fig. 6A). PTGER2 expression was largely suppressed by hCG + MPTmix at 6 (10, 100, and 500 mug/ml), 12 (500 mug/ml), 24 (1 and 500 mug/ml), and 36hr (500 mug/ml) time points, though a single MPTmix dose (10 mug/ml) increased 36hr expression (Fig. 6B). For PTGER3, hCG + MPTmix 1 mug/ml decreased 6hr expression, and the 500 mug/ml dose decreased expression at 24 and 36hr relative to hCG (Fig. 6C). PTGER4 expression was also reduced by hCG + MPTmix 500 mug/ml treatment at 6 and 36hr relative to hCG (Fig. 6D). Expression of PTGFR was decreased by hCG + MPTmix treatment at 6 (100 mug/ml), 24 (100 and 500 mug/ml), and 36hr (500 mug/ml) time points, although 12hr expression was increased (500 mug/ml) when compared to hCG controls (Fig. 6E).
Effect of MPTmix on P4 steroidogenesis and PGR

Previous studies from our group using the same IVF granulosa cell model have shown that PGR signaling is required for the hCG-induced increases in PGE2 and PGF2alpha, certain PG synthases/AKRs (PTGS2, PTGES, AKR1C1), and transporters (ABCC4, SLCO2A1). Across various species, increases in P4 and PGR following LH/hCG stimulation are well-established, and disruption or loss of P4/PGR signaling during the ovulatory period results in anovulation. To investigate whether phthalates disrupt P4 steroidogenesis and PGR signaling:and thereby potentially impair downstream ovulatory PG production/function:we measured P4 levels and expression of PGR and P4 steroidogenic genes (STAR, CYP11A1, and HSD3B2) across the ovulatory period following hCG + MPTmix treatment. As expected, hCG treatment increased P4 levels (all time points) and PGR expression (6, 12, and 36hr) compared to DMSO (Fig. 7A and B). Expression of STAR, CYP11A1, and HSD3B2 was also upregulated by hCG at all time points (Fig. 7C-E). In contrast, hCG + MPTmix reduced P4 levels at 6 (100 and 500 mug/ml), 12 (100 and 500 mug/ml), 24 (500 mug/ml), and 36hr (500 mug/ml) relative to hCG, though a single MPTmix dose (10 mug/ml) increased 36hr levels (Fig. 7A). The mRNA levels of PGR were consistently decreased at all time points with the 500 mug/ml MPTmix dose compared to hCG (Fig. 7B). For steroidogenic proteins and enzymes, hCG + MPTmix 500 mug/ml treatment consistently suppressed STAR, CYP11A1, and HSD3B2 expression at 6hr. At this same time point, CYP11A1 expression was also reduced with a lower MPTmix dose (100 mug/ml), whereas STAR (1 mug/ml) and HSD3B2 (10 and 100 mug/ml) expression was increased relative to hCG (Fig. 7C-E). At 12hr, STAR (1, 10, and 500 mug/ml) and HSD3B2 (100 and 500 mug/ml) expression was reduced with hCG + MPTmix treatment relative to hCG (Fig. 7C-E). At 24hr, hCG + MPTmix treatment decreased STAR (1 and 500 mug/ml), CYP11A1 (1, 10, and 500 mug/ml), and HSD3B2 (500 mug/ml) expression compared to hCG (Fig. 7C-E). At 36hr, hCG + MPTmix treatment reduced expression of STAR (500 mug/ml), CYP11A1 (100 and 500 mug/ml), and HSD3B2 (500 mug/ml), although STAR expression was increased with a single MPTmix dose (100 mug/ml) compared to hCG control groups. (Fig. 7C-E).
Effect of MPTmix on LH/hCG-activated intracellular signaling cascades

Increased PG levels during ovulation are facilitated via complex signaling cascades. Activation of LHCGR promptly elevates cAMP and activates PKA signaling, leading to increased PGR levels. As noted in Section 1, PGR signaling directly regulates the induction of PG synthases, PG transporters, and PG levels in human granulosa cells. LH/hCG stimulation rapidly activates additional intracellular signaling pathways, including AKT/PKB and ERK1/2, with ERK1/2 proposed to drive PG production through direct induction of PTGS2 transcription. To determine whether MPTmix exposure disrupts these essential signaling cascades, we measured cAMP, PKA activity, p-AKT, and p-ERK1/2 levels shortly after treatment with hCG + MPTmix (0.5hr). As anticipated, hCG treatment rapidly increased cAMP, PKA activity, p-AKT, and p-ERK1/2 levels compared to DMSO (Fig. 8A-D). In contrast, hCG + MPTmix 500 mug/ml reduced cAMP, PKA activity, and p-ERK1/2 levels relative to hCG controls (Fig. 8A-D).
Discussion

This study provides the first evidence that exposure to an environmentally relevant phthalate mixture, formulated from urinary concentrations in women and representative of in vivo ovarian exposure, disrupts ovulatory PG function through multiple mechanisms. Fig. 9 summarizes these main findings and mechanisms. Specifically, MPTmix exposure reduces active PG levels (PGE2 and PGF2alpha) and impairs PG function by altering their synthesis, metabolism, transport, and receptor availability. We propose that these effects are mediated through upstream suppression of P4 production and PGR signaling, with higher MPTmix doses also disrupting intracellular signaling cascades that are promptly activated following LHCGR binding. Importantly, cytotoxicity is unlikely to account for the observed effects, as MTS assays assessing cell viability and metabolism revealed no statistically significant differences across all treatment groups prior to hCG stimulation, indicating no detectable differences in the number or viability of these primary human granulosa cells in response to MPTmix exposure. Therefore, any MPTmix-induced changes observed following hCG treatment are unlikely due to cell death and instead reflect disruptions downstream of LHCGR activation. Considering the indispensable roles of PGs and P4/PGR in oocyte release and subsequent CL formation, our findings highlight the potential for phthalate exposure to disrupt ovulation and adversely impact fertility in women (; 2015).

passages.text: At the level of PG synthesis, MPTmix exposure consistently decreased active PGE2 and PGF2alpha levels that coincided with reduced expression and activity of PTGS2, the rate-limiting PG synthase that has proven requisite for ovulation and fertility. Although increased expression of PLA2G4A potentially reflects a compensatory attempt to liberate more arachidonic acid available for conversion into active PGs, this response appeared ineffective. The ineffectiveness likely stems from MPTmix-induced suppression of the downstream key PG synthase (PTGS2) and the PGE2-specific synthase (PTGES), both of which are abundantly upregulated by LH/hCG stimulation. MPTmix exposure also affected additional PG-related synthases, including PTGS1 and the PGE2-specific synthases PTGES2 and PTGES3. Specifically, PTGS1 expression was further suppressed by MPTmix relative to hCG controls, whereas PTGES2 and PTGES3 were generally upregulated, potentially reflecting compensatory increases in response to PTGES suppression. Together, these findings demonstrate that phthalate exposure broadly disrupts the production of ovulatory PGs. The resulting reduction in PGE2 levels at each tested dose of the MPTmix is particularly concerning given the essential roles of PGE2 in facilitating successful oocyte release. Specifically, well-timed treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (PTGS2 inhibitors) block ovulation in women, and PGE2 receptor knockout mouse models exhibit sterility due to anovulation.

Metabolic assessments revealed additional disruption. Inactive PGE2 metabolite levels were also decreased by MPTmix exposure, despite increased expression and activity of the metabolic enzyme HPGD. This is most likely explained by diminished levels of active PGE2 available for metabolism. Conversely, inactive PGF2alpha metabolite levels were elevated, suggesting a phthalate-driven metabolic shift away from PGE2 and toward PGF2alpha production and terminal metabolism. This catabolic/metabolic shift is reinforced by MPTmix-induced upregulation of AKR1C1 and AKR1C3, members of the aldo-keto reductase (AKR) enzyme family that either interconvert PGE2 and PGF2alpha or directly synthesize PGF2alpha from the short-lived PGH2 intermediate. Notably, a study using human granulosa cells reported that AKR1C1 exhibits unidirectional isomerase activity and exclusively converts PGE2 to PGF2alpha, which further highlights the enhanced catabolic influence of the MPTmix. This redirection of PG metabolism is concerning as PGE2 is indispensable for ovulation and fertility, whereas the physiological role of PGF2alpha during oocyte release is unclear, and mice lacking PGF2alpha receptor expression ovulate normally.

Phthalates may also disrupt PG transport. At select doses, MPTmix exposure decreased expression of ABCC4, an efflux transporter that actively pumps PGs out of cells, while increasing expression of SLCO2A1, a transporter that primarily mediates PG uptake into cells. These changes, when considered alongside MPTmix-induced disruptions in PG production and the resulting reduction in active PG levels, may indicate a cellular mechanism aimed at sustaining intracellular PG signaling by limiting PG efflux and conserving newly synthesized PGs, albeit at a diminished capacity evident by decreased PGE2 synthesis detailed above.

At the receptor level, MPTmix exposure altered expression of multiple PGE2 receptors (PTGER1-4), which regulate distinct ovulatory processes depending on their location within the follicle. Under normal ovulatory conditions, PTGER1 signaling in mural granulosa cells stabilizes the follicle wall to prevent premature rupture, while PTGER2 and PTGER4 signaling at the follicle apex promotes protease expression required for COC expansion and follicle rupture. PTGER3 provides additional regulation depending on receptor isoform. In mural granulosa cells away from the apex, PTGER3 (isoform 5) increases protease inhibitors to strengthen the follicle wall; whereas PTGER3 (isoform 5) expression is low at the apex, allowing PTGER2 and PTGER4-mediated protease activity to dominate and enable rupture. Exposure to the MPTmix disrupted this balance. PTGER1 levels were consistently increased even at late ovulatory time points, which could lead to excessive follicle wall stabilization and the entrapment of oocytes:a hallmark of luteinized unruptured follicle syndrome (LUFS). Simultaneously, PTGER2 and PTGER4 levels were decreased, potentially suggesting impaired protease-driven follicle wall breakdown at the apex and a reinforcement of wall integrity where rupture should occur. In contrast, similar MPTmix doses and time points that increased PTGER1 expression decreased mRNA levels of PTGER3 isoform 5 (Fig. 6C). Collectively, these receptor-level alterations suggest that phthalate exposure disrupts the coordinated signaling required for successful follicle rupture and provides a mechanistic link to LUFS-like phenotypes. While epidemiological associations between phthalate exposure and LUFS have not yet been investigated in the literature, various studies have reported associations between elevated phthalate levels and female reproductive disorders that involve impaired follicle rupture, including anovulation, PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome), and POI (premature ovarian insufficiency).

Finally, upstream regulators of PG synthesis were markedly affected by phthalates. MPTmix treatment generally decreased P4 levels (with the exception of one dose at a single time point), and the highest MPTmix dose (500 mug/ml) consistently suppressed PGR expression across the ovulatory period. These effects were accompanied by alterations in key proteins and enzymes required for P4 steroidogenesis. Notably, the 500 mug/ml MPTmix dose also reduced the levels of cAMP, PKA activity, and p-ERK1/2, suggesting that initial LHCGR signaling may be impaired only with the highest MPTmix dose. In contrast, lower MPTmix concentrations did not appear to disrupt initial LHCGR signaling events, indicating that distinct molecular mechanisms may underline the observed effects across doses, and these warrant further investigation. One plausible mechanism involves phthalate-mediated modulation of nuclear receptor signaling. Phthalates and their metabolites have been reported to interact with multiple nuclear receptors, including estrogen and androgen receptors, as well as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) subtypes, potentially influencing transcriptional networks that regulate steroidogenesis and reproductive function in endocrine tissues. Activation or antagonism of these receptors could contribute to reduced P4 biosynthesis and altered expression of enzymes and receptors within the PG synthesis and signaling pathways. However, direct ligand-receptor interactions in the human ovary remain uncharacterized, and available evidence suggests that such effects on estrogen receptors, androgen receptors, and PPARs are likely receptor- and context-dependent. In addition to transcriptional regulation, phthalates have been shown to disrupt intracellular signaling pathways independent of classical nuclear receptor mechanisms . Consistent with previous findings demonstrating that parent phthalates impair PGR signaling through the cAMP-PKA pathway, our findings from the present study extend this mechanism to include disruption of ERK1/2 signaling by phthalate metabolites. Given that both cAMP-PKA-PGR and EGFR-ERK1/2 pathways regulate transcription of key PG synthases such as PTGS2, these impairments likely compound the observed deficits in PG synthesis and function following exposure to phthalates. To further define the contribution of EGFR-dependent pathways, future studies in our laboratory will assess EGFR and its EGF-like peptide ligands to determine how MPTmix exposure alters additional ovulatory signaling mechanisms. These future studies will utilize the cumulus cells that undergo expansion in response to EGFR signaling and are also collected during the IVF retrieval process. In addition to impaired intracellular signaling, phthalate-induced ovulatory dysfunction may also arise indirectly through mechanisms such as oxidative stress or mitochondrial dysfunction, both of which have been implicated in phthalate-induced toxicity of reproductive tissues. Ultimately, the observed decreases in P4 and PGR are particularly concerning given the indispensable role of P4/PGR signaling in ovulation, with PGR deficiency leading to ovulatory failure, LUFS, and infertility across species. Collectively, these findings support a multifaceted model in which phthalates disrupt ovulatory function through coordinated effects on intracellular signaling, steroidogenesis, and PG pathways.

passages.text: Alongside the observed decreases in PG synthesis (PTGS1, PTGS2, PTGES) and increases in catabolism/metabolism (AKR1C1, AKR1C3, HPGD), additional MPTmix-induced alterations were identified that conflict with the typical temporal gene expression profile during the ovulatory period. In this study, hCG treatment generally upregulated PTGS2, PTGES, AKR1C1, ABCC4, SLCO2A1, PTGER2, PTGER3, PTGFR, PGR, STAR, CYP11A1, and HSD3B2 expression, while downregulating PLA2G4A, PTGS1, PTGES2, HPGD, AKR1C3, PTGER1, and PTGER4 expression. These patterns are consistent with the well-documented temporal regulation of PG and P4/PGR production and action during ovulation. However, treatment with hCG + MPTmix broadly suppressed upregulation of hCG-induced genes. Notable exceptions included AKR1C1 and SLCO2A1, where MPTmix further increased these hCG-stimulated genes. This aligns with a shift toward PGF2alpha production and a potential compensatory attempt to increase intracellular PG levels following phthalate exposure. Conversely, for genes typically downregulated by hCG, MPTmix exposure produced expression patterns more similar to DMSO vehicle controls than hCG-treated cells, although this pattern was less consistent than the suppression observed among hCG-induced genes. Overall, these changes indicate a disruption of the normal ovulatory environment by favoring production of PGF2alpha over PGE2 (via increased AKR1C3), promoting excessive PG inactivation (via increased HPGD mRNA and activity), and enhancing follicle wall stabilization (via increased PTGER1 and decreased PTGER2/4). Furthermore, the molecular profile induced by phthalate exposure closely parallels the non-ovulatory (DMSO-vehicle) phenotype. This disruption extends beyond gene expression to protein activity, as seen with the key PG synthase (PTGS2) and metabolic enzyme (HPGD). In both cases, the expected hCG-induced increase in PTGS2 and decrease in HPGD were negated by MPTmix exposure, producing transcript and protein activity levels similar to those of the non-ovulatory, DMSO vehicle control groups.

The present findings reveal that exposure to a mixture of phthalate metabolites, designed to mimic human ovarian exposure, alters ovulatory PG production and PG-related pathways through changes in synthesis, metabolism, transport, and receptor expression. These effects occur alongside disrupted P4/PGR signaling and, at the highest MPTmix dose, impairment of upstream intracellular signaling pathways. Although the overall pattern of responses in this study was largely directionally consistent across doses, some non-monotonic dose responses were observed depending on the endpoint and time point measured (Figs. 3A, 3B, 3D, 3E, 4B, 4E, 5B, 6A, 6B, 6E, 7A, 7C, and 7E). Non-monotonic dose-response relationships are a well-recognized feature of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and have been attributed to several molecular mechanisms, including opposing actions mediated by multiple receptors with differing affinities, receptor desensitization, engagement of negative feedback mechanisms at higher doses, and dose-dependent modulation of chemical metabolism. In the context of the present study, the directionally coherent responses and the non-monotonic responses suggest that disruption of ovulatory pathways occurs across a range of phthalate exposures. Taken together, these findings identify potential mechanisms through which environmentally relevant phthalate exposure may impact ovulatory function and fertility in women. While this study identifies phthalate-associated alterations in PG production and signaling under hCG-stimulated conditions, future studies employing pharmacologic or genetic manipulation of these pathways will be essential to elucidate causal mechanisms of toxicity.

passages.text: Major strengths of this study include the use of primary human ovarian granulosa cells with a mixture-based exposure paradigm composed of bioactive phthalate metabolites, designed to more closely reflect true human ovarian exposure. Whereas many prior studies rely on rodent models or parent phthalate compounds, our primary human granulosa cell model is innovative in its ability to recapitulate key ovulatory signaling and PG-dependent outcomes observed in vivo. Moreover, the use of a phthalate metabolite-containing mixture derived from urinary concentrations measured in women enhances both environmental and translational relevance, given that the parent phthalate compounds ubiquitous in consumer products are rapidly metabolized following absorption. Importantly, this metabolite-based exposure paradigm addresses a central limitation of previous toxicological studies, including our earlier work, by modeling the chemical forms most relevant to human ovarian exposure. Specifically, it is the bioactive metabolites, not the parent compounds, that are measured in women's ovarian follicular fluid, and the 1 mug/ml dose used in the present study contains levels of individual phthalate metabolites that are within the range measured in women's ovaries. Under these more relevant exposure conditions, this study introduces new mechanistic insight, implicating additional LH/hCG signaling cascades and altered PG enzymatic protein activity, alongside disruptions in cAMP-PKA pathways, P4 steroidogenesis, PGR signaling, and ovulatory PG production and function in human granulosa cells. These findings are the first to demonstrate that a mixture of bioactive phthalate metabolites act directly on human ovarian cells to impair essential ovulatory signaling networks. By employing an environmentally and biologically relevant metabolite mixture, this study overcomes limitations inherent to exposures involving individual or parent phthalate compounds and advances the mechanistic framework for understanding phthalate-induced ovulatory dysfunction in women. Furthermore, by identifying previously uncharacterized alterations in LHCGR signaling and PG-related enzyme activity, these results expand our understanding of how relevant phthalate exposures disrupt multiple biochemical pathways critical for ovulation. Together, this work establishes a physiologically relevant paradigm for evaluating ovarian toxicity and advances mechanistic understanding of how environmental exposure to phthalates may contribute to impaired ovulatory function and reduced fertility in women.

A limitation of the present study includes the inability to isolate specific mural granulosa cell subpopulations from follicular aspirates (apex vs non-apex regions), which restricts our ability to fully characterize the effect of phthalates on PG receptors. As mentioned above, the PG receptors function in a spatially dependent manner within the follicle to stabilize or promote rupture at the apex during ovulation. Although the use of primary human granulosa cells represents a major strength, our in vitro culture system focuses on a single ovarian cell type and does not capture the contribution of other components of the ovulatory follicle, including cumulus cells, theca cells, the ovarian stroma, or the neuroendocrine axis:all of which may respond to phthalate exposure in an intact human. Accordingly, this model cannot directly assess the systemic effects of phthalates. However, due to ethical constraints, experimental studies evaluating systemic phthalate exposure in humans are, understandably, limited to epidemiological investigations. Importantly, these epidemiological studies have consistently linked elevated phthalate exposure with adverse ovarian- and ovulation-related outcomes, including decreased pregnancy rates, reduced fecundity, poorer IVF outcomes (fewer oocytes retrieved and lower live birth rates), altered sex steroid hormone levels, and disrupted menstrual cycle length. Such associations underscore the critical need for direct mechanistic studies, and the present findings offer toxicological evidence and potential cellular mechanisms by which phthalates may contribute to the ovarian and ovulatory dysfunction reported in human populations. Another potential limitation relates to the source of granulosa cells, which were collected from 62 patients undergoing IVF. Of these patients, 52% had no documented infertility diagnosis specific to ovarian function and 44% had no reported infertility diagnosis at all (Supplementary Table 1). We are actively expanding this cohort to evaluate whether non-reproductive pathologies or infertility diagnoses are associated with adverse outcomes in this model. Notably, we did not observe major differences in the hCG response among patient samples in the current dataset, regardless of fertility status or potential pathologies linked to altered PG and P4/PGR-mediated signaling. In parallel, phthalate concentrations are being quantified in follicular fluid aspirates collected at oocyte retrieval to determine whether elevated exposure correlates with infertility diagnoses and/or poor IVF outcomes. These analyses will further allow us to test whether baseline phthalate exposure reduces granulosa cell responsiveness to hCG and/or predisposes cells to heightened phthalate toxicity in our in vitro models. It is also important to note that urinary phthalate metabolite levels do not consistently or robustly correlate with follicular fluid concentrations, suggesting that urinary measurements may only partially capture ovarian-relevant exposures. To address this limitation, future studies will also leverage follicular fluid phthalate measurements to guide both exposure concentrations and potentially metabolite mixture composition in our experimental models to better approximate in vivo follicular conditions.

passages.text: Conclusion

In this study, we examined the effects of an environmentally relevant mixture of phthalate metabolites, derived from urinary levels in women, on P4/PGR signaling and downstream PG production and function in primary human granulosa cells. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that phthalate exposure disrupts intracellular signaling pathways involved in P4 steroidogenesis and PGR signaling, and also impairs PG production. Moreover, phthalates altered PG metabolic enzymes, transporters, and receptors, further compromising PG function. P4/PGR and PGs mediate ovulatory processes such as follicle wall breakdown, tissue remodeling, COC expansion and stability, oocyte maturation, and angiogenesis, and phthalate mixture-induced defects in these specific ovulatory events are being explored in our ongoing studies using human and mouse models. Collectively, these results advance mechanistic understanding of how common, unavoidable environmental exposures impair women's reproductive health, which can potentially inform more effective infertility treatments and improve the overall approach to women's healthcare.

Schematic of ovulatory P4/PGR (A) and PG (B) pathways. In granulosa cells, LH/hCG binding to its receptor (LHCGR) upregulates proteins and enzymes required for progesterone (P4) steroidogenesis [purple] and activates intracellular signaling [red] that leads to increased progesterone receptor (PGR) levels (A). In humans, elevated P4/PGR signaling promotes transcription of key prostaglandin (PG) synthases and transporters. The resulting increase in PGE2 and PGF2alpha [pink] drives follicular events essential for ovulation (B). PG synthases [orange] and reductases [yellow] produce PGs, while metabolic enzymes (HPGD) are downregulated to maintain elevated levels of active PGs during ovulation. PG influx/efflux are regulated by transporters [green], and PGs act through their receptors [blue] to promote oocyte release. Bold orange text indicates the primary synthases driving ovulatory PG production, while non-bold orange text denotes synthases that play a lesser role in this process. Created in BioRender. Land, K. MPTmix-induced effects on ovulatory PG production. Human granulosa cells obtained from in vitro fertilization patients were cultured with DMSO (vehicle control) or phthalate metabolite mixture (MPTmix; 1-500 mug/ml) for 48hr prior to hCG stimulation. After 48hr, cells were treated +- hCG and +- MPTmix. Media and cells were collected at multiple time points following hCG treatment to assess PGE2 (A) and PGF2alpha (B) levels, PTGS2 protein activity (C), and PTGS2 mRNA levels (D) using ELISAs, qPCR, or protein activity assays. Data are presented as a percent change or percent fold change relative to hCG controls at each time point. Graphs represent mean +- SEM, and asterisks represent statistical significance compared to hCG controls (n = 7-19 patients/group; p <= 0.05).

After 48hr, cells were treated +- hCG and +- MPTmix. Cells were collected 0.5hr following hCG treatment to assess levels of cAMP (A), PKA activity (B), p-AKT (C), and p-ERK1/2 (D) via ELISAs. Data are presented as percent change relative to hCG controls. Graphs represent mean +- SEM, and asterisks represent statistical significance compared to hCG controls (n = 7-10 patients/group; p <= 0.05).

Proposed model of MPTmix-induced impairments in ovulatory P4/PGR (A) and PG (B) function in human granulosa cells. Exposure to the MPTmix suppressed LH/hCG-induced upregulation of P4 and its steroidogenic genes [purple] (A). Further, MPTmix exposure reduced intracellular signaling molecules [red], which likely led to decreased PGR mRNA levels (A). These impairments in P4/PGR signaling likely contributed to the observed reductions in PG synthase expression [orange] and the resulting decreases in active PGE2 and PGF2alpha levels [pink] (B). MPTmix exposure also increased expression of genes involved in PG catabolism/metabolism [yellow] and altered expression of PG transporters [green] and receptors [blue], providing additional mechanistic insight into how phthalates may disrupt PG production and function (B). Bold orange text indicates the primary synthases driving ovulatory PG production, while non-bold orange text denotes synthases that play a lesser role in this process. Solid red and green arrows indicate that MPTmix exposure exclusively decreased or increased, respectively, gene expression, protein activity, or levels compared to hCG ovulatory control groups. Hollow red and green arrows indicate that MPTmix exposure mostly decreased or increased these measures, but with some minor exceptions relative to the hCG ovulatory controls. Created in BioRender. passages.text: Tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 2(TET2)-dependent epigenetic regulation in the pathogenesis of polycystic ovary syndrome

Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a complex endocrine disorder and a major cause of female infertility. While epigenetic dysregulation, notably DNA methylation, has been recognized as a key driver of PCOS pathogenesis, the specific involvement of active demethylation mediated by Ten-Eleven Translocation (TET) enzymes in the onset of the disease is currently poorly understood. In order to explore the role of TET2-mediated 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) modifications and the underlying molecular drivers of PCOS, genome-wide 5hmC profiling was utilized to analyze granulosa cells from both PCOS patients and normal controls. Higher global 5hmC levels and TET2 expression were found in the granulosa cells of PCOS patients. Through integrated analysis, significant alterations in 5hmC at specific genomic loci were revealed, which were enriched in pathways related to MAPK signaling, gap junction communication, and oocyte meiosis. Furthermore, USP45 was identified as a downstream target of TET2 via ChIP-seq analysis. Functional experiments demonstrated that TET2 drives the overactivation of autophagic flux under hyperandrogenic conditions by stabilizing PRKAA1 via USP45-mediated deubiquitination. Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of TET2 effectively rescued these autophagic abnormalities. TET2-mediated 5hmC modification is revealed by this study as a key driver of PCOS pathogenesis; these insights offer a novel epigenetic framework for the development of PCOS therapies.
Graphical abstract

The underlying mechanisms of TET2-mediated 5hmC epigenetic regulation in PCOS progression. Genome-wide 5hmC profiling in PCOS patient granulosa cells revealed increased global 5hmC levels and elevated TET2 expression. Integrated analysis showed significant 5hmC alterations at specific genomic loci, enriching pathways like MAPK signaling and oocyte meiosis. Crucially, we identified USP45 as a novel TET2 target, demonstrating that TET2 promotes hyperandrogenism-induced autophagy in granulosa cells via USP45-mediated PRKAA1 deubiquitination. These findings provide the first evidence for a significant role of TET2-mediated 5hmC epigenetic regulation in PCOS, linking aberrant epigenetics to impaired ovarian function through excessive autophagy.

Introduction

Polycystic ovary syndrome is an endocrine and metabolic disorder characterized by polycystic ovarian morphology, menstrual irregularities, and anovulation. The estimated global prevalence of PCOS among women of reproductive age ranges from approximately 5% to 15%, with significant variations observed across different ethnic groups and geographic regions. In recent years, the incidence of PCOS has been continuously increasing. However, the etiology of PCOS remains not fully elucidated. Its onset is likely driven by a multifactorial interplay between genetic predisposition and external triggers, including endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), chronic systemic inflammation, environmental pollutants, and other emerging factors. PCOS impairs folliculogenesis, resulting in ovulatory dysfunction characterized by irregular or absent ovulation. These reproductive aberrations significantly compromise fertility, positioning PCOS as a primary cause of anovulatory infertility in women of reproductive age. Consequently, further elucidation of the pathophysiological mechanisms of PCOS and the development of targeted therapeutic interventions are imperative.

The primary ovarian features in PCOS include an increased number of small antral follicles and disrupted follicular development, often characterized by arrested growth at the pre-antral or early antral stage. Research indicates a significantly elevated antral follicle count in the ovaries of women with PCOS (generally defined as 12 or more follicles with diameters of 2-9 mm), with a large proportion of these follicles remaining at an early developmental stage. Due to granulosa cell dysfunction, these follicles fail to complete the final stages of maturation, resulting in a significantly increased rate of follicular atresia. Additionally, follicular development in PCOS patients often arrests at the pre-antral stage, preventing proper transition to the antral follicle stage. Hyperandrogenemia further contributes to this developmental arrest by inhibiting aromatase (CYP19A1) activity in granulosa cells, leading to decreased estrogen production. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms that drive abnormal follicular development is crucial for the effective treatment of PCOS. Autophagy is a physiological process through which cells degrade damaged proteins or excess components via the lysosomal pathway, playing a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis. Autophagy serves as a vital quality-control mechanism that maintains proteostasis by eliminating dysfunctional mitochondria and protein aggregates. However, when pathologically sustained, excessive autophagic flux can compromise cellular integrity and overwhelm compensatory pathways. Consequently, non-selective organelle degradation occurs, leading to the attrition of cellular structure and viability. Moreover, excessive autophagy may lead to substantial intracellular ATP consumption, resulting in energy depletion and subsequently impairing normal cellular metabolic functions. The emerging understanding from recent studies emphasizes the critical role of autophagy as a potential key player in both the onset and the progression of PCOS. This recognition is significant as it suggests that modulating autophagic pathways could represent a novel avenue for therapeutic intervention in managing and potentially preventing this complex disorder. The dysregulation of the autophagic pathway within PCOS granulosa cells triggers excessive cellular self-digestion, contributing to impaired folliculogenesis and premature follicle loss. Thus, effectively regulating autophagy levels within granulosa cells could be a valuable novel therapeutic approach and a key theoretical foundation for PCOS intervention and treatment.

Recent studies have unequivocally demonstrated the involvement of a range of epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are dysregulated in women with PCOS and contribute to its key features. Among these epigenetic modifications, 5hmC has emerged as a pivotal DNA modification integral to the facilitation of gene transcription, the modulation of chromatin structural dynamics, and its dynamic regulation during cellular differentiation. The formation of 5hmC is primarily catalyzed by the TET family of dioxygenases, comprising TET1, TET2, and TET3, each exhibiting distinct expression profiles across different tissue types. Advancements in high-throughput sequencing technologies have facilitated the identification of 5hmC as a key regulatory epigenetic mark in both physiological and pathological contexts. Accumulating evidence suggests that granulosa cells from PCOS patients exhibit elevated levels of 5hmC, accompanied by increased expression of TET enzymes. Animal model studies further indicate that TET1 expression is downregulated in aging mice, and its overexpression promotes granulosa cell proliferation while inhibiting apoptosis. However, the functional contributions of TET enzymes and their resultant epigenetic targets in PCOS granulosa cells remain largely undefined, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive investigation.

This research investigates the mechanistic involvement of 5hmC in the etiology and clinical advancement of PCOS. Through the integration of APOBEC-assisted 5hmC profiling with the Illumina Infinium HumanMethylation 850 K array, a significant elevation of 5hmC was identified at multiple genomic locations in PCOS ovarian granulosa cells. Genome-wide target gene analysis via TET2 ChIP-seq was conducted to decipher its regulatory functions. Furthermore, the effects of TET2 on the proliferation and autophagy of KGN cells were systematically evaluated. Based on these integrated findings, the pivotal involvement of 5hmC modification in PCOS pathogenesis is highlighted, and TET2 is proposed as a potential therapeutic avenue, suggesting that a novel approach for PCOS intervention could be offered by targeting its activity.

Based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 24 participants were recruited, including 12 healthy controls and 12 patients diagnosed with PCOS. The baseline characteristics of both groups are shown in Table 1. There were no significant differences in age and basal follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels between the two groups. However, PCOS patients exhibited significantly higher Luteinizing Hormone (LH) levels (P < 0.05). In addition, BMI, levels of LH/FSH ratio, testosterone (T), and anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) were significantly elevated in the PCOS group compared to controls (P < 0.05). Granulosa cells were collected from both groups, and total genomic DNA was extracted using a DNA extraction kit. DNA concentrations were adjusted to 100 ng/muL according to the kit's instructions. The relative 5hmC modification levels were measured using an ELISA-based assay. ELISA results revealed that the total 5hmC levels in granulosa cells were increased in the PCOS group compared to non-PCOS controls (Fig. 1A). Furthermore, immunofluorescence staining for 5hmC demonstrated enhanced relative fluorescence intensity in granulosa cells from PCOS patients, consistent with the ELISA findings (Fig. 1B). To further investigate the distribution of differentially modified 5hmC sites in granulosa cells, we employed the Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip to profile DNA from both groups, analyzing over 850,000 CpG sites to detect differences in 5hmC modification between PCOS patients and controls. The results revealed distinct enrichment patterns of 5hmC-modified loci between the two groups. Density plots of beta-values indicated a global increase in 5hmC levels in the PCOS group compared to controls (Fig. 1C). More precisely, 5hmC enrichment was found to be elevated in the granulosa cell DNA of the PCOS group, particularly at proximal promoter elements (TSS1500) and the 5'UTR (Fig. 1D). In total, 71 hyper-hydroxymethylated probes (DMPs) and 76 hypo-hydroxymethylated probes (DMPs) were identified between the PCOS and control groups (Fig. 1E). We also analyzed the distribution of transcription factor binding sites in relation to their target genes. Hydroxymethylation trend plots around +- 5 kb of transcription start sites (TSS) revealed significant differences in 5hmC enrichment between the two groups, as confirmed by statistical analysis (Fig. 1F). These findings demonstrate that ovarian granulosa cells from PCOS patients exhibit elevated levels of 5hmC modification compared to healthy controls.

To elucidate the molecular changes in PCOS ovarian granulosa cells, KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was conducted on genes harboring differentially modified 5hmC sites. Results indicated that hyper-hydroxymethylated genes in the PCOS group were predominantly enriched in the MAPK signaling, gap junction, and oocyte meiosis pathways (Fig. 2A). Conversely, hypo-hydroxymethylated genes were primarily associated with Wnt and ErbB signaling pathways (Fig. 2B). Gene Ontology (GO) analysis further indicated that the differentially modified genes were mainly involved in metabolism-related pathways (Fig. 2C). As polycystic ovary syndrome is a disease triggered by gene-environment interactions, we examined the methylation status of known PCOS susceptibility loci. We compared the genes annotated from DMPs with PCOS susceptibility genes listed in the GWAS Catalog database (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/). This analysis identified four genes:ASIC2, CCDC91, CHEK2, and FTO:corresponding to probes cg24044290, cg08568970, cg04661358, and cg10331105, respectively (Fig. 2D). We designed primers for the four probe regions and validated the 5hmC modification levels using hydroxymethylated DNA immunoprecipitation followed by quantitative PCR (hMeDIP-qPCR) in granulosa cells from an independent validation cohort of 16 individuals. The results showed significant differences in 5hmC modification levels at the ASIC2 and CCDC91 loci between PCOS and control groups, while CHEK2 and FTO did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 2E). Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed for each of the four candidate loci, and ROC curves were plotted. Individually, these loci exhibited limited predictive power for PCOS (Supplementary Fig. 1A). However, when combined, the four loci demonstrated high predictive accuracy for PCOS diagnosis, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.953 (Fig. 2F).

Since genomic 5hmC levels are mediated by the TET family, we first screened the expression of TET1-3 in PCOS granulosa cells to elucidate the specific enzymatic contributor to the observed epigenetic changes. Western blotting showed that TET1 and TET2:but not TET3:were upregulated in PCOS-derived granulosa cells, with TET2 displaying the most significant elevation (Fig. 3A and B). TET2 lacks the CXXC domain of TET1/3, requiring transcription factor interaction for recruitment. This specificity makes targeting TET2 a safer, more precise alternative to toxic, broad-spectrum epigenetic inhibition. Consequently, TET2 was prioritized as the primary target for our investigation. To further investigate the potential genomic targets of TET2 in ovarian granulosa cells, we conducted ChIP-seq analysis. First, we assessed the specificity of the TET2 antibody used in immunoprecipitation. The IP results confirmed that the antibody had good specificity and met the requirements for subsequent ChIP-seq experiments (Fig. 3C). Analysis of the sequencing data revealed that TET2 binding sites were predominantly enriched in promoter regions (Fig. 3D). Examination of the distribution of TET2 binding around transcription start sites (TSS) indicated a clear enrichment in the TET2_IP group at TSS regions, whereas the TET2_Input control group exhibited much weaker signals. This supports the specific binding of TET2 to TSS regions (Fig. 3E). Motif analysis identified CTAGATCAAATA as the most significantly enriched DNA motif at TET2 binding sites (Fig. 3F). Additionally, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses of TET2-bound genes revealed that they were primarily enriched in the mTOR signaling pathway and regulation of biological processes (Supplementary Fig. 2A, 2B). We also highlighted the top five genes showing the most significant TET2 binding enrichment, illustrating potential direct transcriptional targets of TET2 (Fig. 3G).

Previous studies have reported that TET2 can promote autophagy through various pathways. However, whether TET2 regulates autophagy in ovarian granulosa cells requires further experimental validation. To investigate this, we established a TET2-overexpressing human granulosa cell model by transfecting KGN cells with an overexpression plasmid. The efficiency of TET2 overexpression was confirmed by qPCR and Western blot analysis, demonstrating a significant increase in both TET2 mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 4A and B). To assess the impact of TET2 on cell proliferation, we performed 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation assays, which revealed a significant inhibition of granulosa cell proliferation upon TET2 overexpression (Fig. 4C). While hyperandrogenism is known to induce autophagy in PCOS, its role in regulating TET2 remains controversial, as studies in prostate cancer suggest an inhibitory effect. To reconcile this inconsistency, we examined the dose-dependent effects of DHEA on TET2 in granulosa cells. Surprisingly, Western blot and q-PCR analysis revealed that TET2 expression remained unchanged across all tested concentrations of DHEA (Fig. 4D and E). Then we analyzed autophagy-related protein expression via Western blot to evaluate the impact of TET2 on autophagy. The results showed that TET2 overexpression enhanced DHEA-induced autophagic flux, whereas treatment with a TET2 inhibitor markedly suppressed autophagy (Fig. 4F). Furthermore, we transfected KGN cells with a GFP-RFP-LC3 dual-labeled plasmid using liposome-mediated transfection to visualize autophagosome formation. The results indicated that TET2 significantly promoted androgen-induced autophagosome formation, while the TET2 inhibitor exerted a suppressive effect (Fig. 4G). We designed three sets of siRNAs targeting TET2 and identified siRNA-2 as exhibiting the most potent knockdown efficiency at the mRNA level (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Subsequently, the protein expression of TET2 following knockdown was assessed via Western blot, which confirmed a significant reduction in TET2 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 1C). Utilizing this TET2-siRNA, we observed that TET2 silencing suppressed the activation of autophagic flux induced by DHEA, suggesting that TET2 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for improving ovarian function in PCOS, particularly in those with hyperandrogenism (Fig. 4H).

By intersecting the differentially 5hmC-modified genes in PCOS granulosa cells with TET2 ChIP-seq target genes, we identified USP45 as a potential downstream target of TET2 within the ovarian follicular microenvironment (Fig. 5A). Analysis of the USP45 promoter region identified multiple TET2 binding motifs (Fig. 5B). Based on sequencing results, we designed primers for two USP45 promoter sites and performed hMeDIP-qPCR to assess 5hmC levels. Results showed that TET2 overexpression significantly elevated 5hmC modification at both sites (Fig. 5C and D). In addition, we designed MSP primers for the USP45 promoter region and performed methylation detection on the promoter sites following bisulfite conversion of DNA from granulosa cells in both PCOS and control groups. The results showed that the methylation level of USP45 in the control group was significantly higher than that in the PCOS group (Fig. 5E). Furthermore, a comparison of the 5hmC modification levels at the USP45 promoter in granulosa cells revealed a significant increase in the PCOS group compared to the control group (Fig. 5F). Comparing the mRNA levels of USP45 in granulosa cells between the two groups revealed that USP45 mRNA expression was significantly increased in the PCOS group (Fig. 5G). Collectively, these findings suggest that TET2 may participate in the progression of PCOS by regulating USP45.As a deubiquitinating enzyme, USP45 selectively removes ubiquitin from target proteins to prevent proteasomal degradation and maintain protein homeostasis. To identify the downstream targets of USP45, we searched relevant databases and identified PRKAA1 as a potential candidate. To further validate this interaction, we established USP45 knockdown and overexpression models (Fig. 6A and B, Supplementary Fig. 1D). Western blot analysis revealed that the expression pattern of PRKAA1 was largely consistent with that of USP45 (Fig. 6C). Overexpression of TET2 led to a significant increase in USP45 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Fig. 6D and E). However, overexpression of TET2 had no significant effect on mitochondrial membrane potential or ROS levels in granulosa cells (Supplementary Fig. 1E, 1F). Western blot analysis revealed that TET2 overexpression reduced overall cellular ubiquitination levels and upregulated PRKAA1, a downstream target of USP45, suggesting that TET2 may promote PRKAA1 deubiquitination through USP45 and thereby enhance granulosa cell autophagy (Fig. 6F). Furthermore, the effects of TET2 overexpression and USP45 knockdown on downstream proteins were analyzed. It was observed that mTOR activation is inhibited by TET2, thereby promoting the occurrence of pathological autophagy. Conversely, upon the knockdown of USP45, the inhibitory effect of PRKAA1 on mTOR was attenuated, resulting in increased mTOR phosphorylation and a partial suppression of autophagic flux (Fig. 6G). It is further suggested by our study that cellular autophagy may be promoted by TET2 via the USP45/PRKAA1 axis, leading to further impairment of ovarian function.
Discussion

PCOS is a common reproductive disorder marked by impaired folliculogenesis and ovulatory dysfunction. Given its complex pathogenesis, the role of epigenetic modifications has become a focal point of research. In this study, we sought to elucidate the functional significance and underlying mechanisms of 5hmC in PCOS progression. By employing APOBEC-mediated deamination-based 5hmC profiling in conjunction with the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC (850 K) BeadChip, we characterized the 5hmC landscape in ovarian granulosa cells. Additionally, integrated with functional in vitro assays, our findings further elucidate the critical importance of epigenetic modifications in driving PCOS pathogenesis.

Current research has predominantly focused on DNA methylation, leaving the potential role of DNA 5hmC largely unexplored. Early research indicated that there is no significant difference in global DNA methylation levels in peripheral blood between PCOS. Due to the scarcity and limited accessibility of ovarian tissue from patients with PCOS, only a few studies have reported the DNA methylation landscape of human ovarian tissue. Compared to controls, PCOS patients exhibit significantly higher methylation levels at CpG shores (regions 1-2 kb from CpG islands) and promoters with high CpG content outside of core promoter regions, while showing lower methylation levels within gene bodies. Additionally, 342 genes were identified as having specific methylation changes, and these genes are functionally enriched in categories such as protein binding, hormone activity, and transcription factor activity. Some studies have also shown that the overall DNA methylation level in ovarian granulosa cells of PCOS patients is reduced, with the first intron being the primary genomic region exhibiting hypomethylation in PCOS. Targeted analysis of DNA methylation at genomic loci:including key genes:in granulosa cells has identified hypomethylation of promoters such as YAP1, LHCGR, NCOR1, and HDAC3, which are associated with ovarian pathology; this hypomethylation may be linked to granulosa cell proliferation, LH receptor overexpression, and dysregulation of hormonal signaling. Another study employing high-throughput next-generation sulfite sequencing identified substantial alterations in DNA methylation, characterized by hypomethylation at 977 CpG sites affecting 2063 genes and hypermethylation at 2509 CpG sites affecting 1777 genes. Pathway analysis indicated that these differentially methylated genes are linked to ovarian morphology, function, and hormonal regulation.

Our study found that the overall 5hmC modification level of DNA in ovarian granulosa cells from PCOS patients is increased, with differential modification sites located at TSS1500 and 5'UTR regions. The TSS1500 is primarily the promoter region of genes, where transcription factors bind, and it is a key site for DNA methylation modifications. We performed enrichment analysis of differentially modified genes with GWAS genes and found an overlap with four genes: ASIC2, CCDC91, CHEK2, and FTO. CHEK2 is a key serine/threonine protein kinase that can promote DNA repair or initiation by activating the downstream ATM pathway. A recent large-scale GWAS study also reported an association between CHEK2 and genetic variations in PCOS. ASIC2 primarily encodes a subunit of acid-sensing ion channels, which mediate membrane depolarization and intracellular signal transduction through the influx of sodium and calcium ions. It may be associated with insulin resistance in PCOS. CCDC91 (Coiled-Coil Domain Containing 91) is a gene encoding a protein with a coiled-coil domain, primarily involved in intracellular transport and metabolic regulation. To date, no studies have reported a direct association between CCDC91 and PCOS. However, considering that granulosa cells in PCOS patients exhibit abnormally increased autophagic activity, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic disturbances, abnormalities in CCDC91-mediated Golgi-to-lysosome transport may impair lysosomal maturation or the degradation efficiency of autophagosomes, thereby exacerbating metabolic dysregulation in PCOS, FTO is an RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase that catalyzes the removal of methyl groups from m6A sites on mRNA and lncRNA, thereby influencing RNA stability, translational efficiency, and degradation. Recent studies have reported a strong association between FTO and PCOS. In our study, we constructed a predictive model for polycystic ovary syndrome using four probes, which demonstrated strong predictive value (AUC = 0.952). As the cohort was restricted to Han Chinese individuals from a single center, the role of TET2 might vary across different ethnic groups due to population-specific epigenetic landscapes. Additionally, given the modest sample size, future multi-ethnic and multi-center studies are essential to validate the clinical applicability of our findings.

To further investigate the role of TET enzymes in granulosa cells, we analyzed the expression profiles of the TET enzyme family in PCOS and found that TET2 exhibited the most significant difference between the two groups. TET2, a dioxygenase, regulates gene expression by oxidizing 5mCin DNA to generate 5hmC. In contrast to the CXXC domain-containing TET1/3, TET2 recruitment to promoters is mediated indirectly via interactions with transcription factors. This distinct regulatory mechanism bypasses the off-target effects typical of direct enzymatic inhibition. Consequently, disrupting the specific recruitment of TET2 by transcription factors offers a more refined and safer strategy for targeted therapeutic intervention. In ovarian granulosa cells of aged mice, the conversion of 5mC to 5hmC is reduced, accompanied by decreased expression of TET2. By generating TET1 and TET2 double-knockout mice, it was found that the knockout resulted in decreased levels of 5hmC and increased expression of 5mC, along with aberrant methylation observed in multiple imprinted genes. Moreover, female knockout mice exhibited reduced ovarian size and impaired fertility, suggesting that TET2 plays a critical role in ovarian function.

Recent studies have highlighted the role of TET2 in promoting autophagy through various pathways, such as suppressing BCL2 expression or inhibiting mTORC1 signaling via mRNA oxidation. Autophagy is a fundamental catabolic process essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis; however, its dysregulation is increasingly recognized as a hallmark of PCOS. In PCOS, granulosa cells frequently exhibit aberrant autophagic activation, which leads to mitochondrial dysfunction, increased apoptosis, and impaired follicular development. High androgen levels further exacerbate this process, contributing to insulin resistance and endocrine imbalances. While it is known that Metformin can alleviate PCOS symptoms by modulating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR-mediated autophagy pathway, the precise epigenetic mechanisms driving autophagic dysfunction remain poorly understood. In this study, we employed genome-wide TET2 ChIP-seq and functional assays to investigate its impact on GC proliferation and autophagy. Our findings reveal that TET2 facilitates the 5hmC modification of the USP45 promoter, thereby enhancing its expression. USP45, a deubiquitinating enzyme belonging to the ubiquitin-specific protease family, can specifically remove ubiquitin molecules from ubiquitinated proteins by recognizing and binding to them, thereby reversing their ubiquitination. USP45 maintains intracellular protein homeostasis by regulating the stability and activation of target proteins. In serous ovarian cancer cells, USP45 has been found to promote cell proliferation by deubiquitinating the SNAIL protein, thereby preventing its degradation. We queried the BioGRID database and identified PRKAA1 as a potential downstream target of USP45. Upon activation, PRKAA1 can inhibit the activity of mTORC1, thereby relieving its suppression of the ULK1 complex. This primarily promotes the initiation of autophagy and the early stages of autophagosome formation, rather than directly inducing the expression of autophagy-related genes such as LC3 and ATG7, which are often regulated by other cellular stresses and transcription factors. The activation of ULK1 subsequently accelerates the autophagic flux process. Our study found that TET2 can promote the 5hmC modification of the USP45 promoter, thereby enhancing its expression. USP45 regulates the ubiquitination of the downstream target PRKAA1, inhibiting its degradation and promoting the sustained activation of the autophagy pathway. This suggests that epigenetic modifications may exacerbate androgen-induced autophagic responses.
Conclusion

This study provides evidence for a potential role of 5hmC modifications in PCOS pathogenesis. We observed widespread 5hmC modifications and increased TET1/2 expression in granulosa cells of PCOS patients. Importantly, we found that elevated TET2 expression triggers autophagy, a process implicated in PCOS-related follicular developmental disorders. Our findings further demonstrated that TET2-mediated 5hmC modification of USP45 promotes autophagy. Specifically, USP45 targets PRKAA1 to inhibit mTOR phosphorylation, resulting in an excessive autophagic flux that contributes to the pathological autophagic process in PCOS. These findings suggest that aberrant 5hmC modifications, potentially regulated by TET2, contribute to PCOS and identify TET2 as a potential target for future therapeutic strategies.
Materials and methods
Patient recruitment

A total of 40 women participated in this study, who underwent in vitro fertilization (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)treatment after receiving an ovulation induction protocol. A GnRH antagonist protocol was employed for ovulation induction in all patients. In this study, participants had no history of diseases such as severe endometriosis, thyroid dysfunction disease or severe comorbidities (including insulin-dependent diabetes, non-insulin-dependent diabetes or gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, pulmonary, liver or kidney diseases). The Rotterdam criteria was used to diagnose PCOS. The study excluded individuals with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumors, Cushing's syndrome, thyroid disease, or hyperprolactinemia. Healthy controls, characterized by regular menstrual cycles, normal steroid hormone levels, and normal ovarian morphology (antral follicle count, AFC < 12), were women undergoing in vitro fertilization for tubal factor and/or male factor infertility. All participants (patients and controls) had a washout period of at least 3 months without hormone therapy before study inclusion.

passages.text: Granulosa cell collection

Ovarian granulosa cells were collected from patients diagnosed with PCOS and control patients at the Reproductive Medicine Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine. All participants underwent a standard GnRH antagonist stimulation protocol, followed by ovulation induction using human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a GnRH agonist, or a dual trigger.
5hmC immunofluorescence staining

Following granulosa cell collection, the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and washed three times with PBS. After permeabilization with Triton X-100, the cells were again washed three times with PBS. Samples were then blocked with an immunofluorescence blocking solution for 1 h, followed by incubation with a specific 5hmC antibody (1:500, Active Motif) overnight. After three washes with PBS, fluorescently labeled rabbit secondary antibodies were applied. Following another three PBS washes, an antifade mounting medium was added, and fluorescence imaging was performed.
Hydroxymethylation microarray analysis

Granulosa cells were collected and stored at -80  C. To minimize inter-array variability, all samples were processed simultaneously. Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA) according to the manufacturer's instructions.A total of 500 ng to 1 mug of genomic DNA was sheared to approximately 300 bp fragments using a Covaris S220 ultrasonicator. For glucosylation, 1 mug of fragmented gDNA was incubated at 37  C for 1 h with uridine diphosphate glucose (UDP-glucose) and T4 beta-glucosyltransferase (T4-betaGT, NEB, #M0357S). The reaction products were then denatured at 85  C for 10 min using formamide and rapidly cooled on ice. The denatured DNA was subjected to deamination by incubation with the APOBEC enzyme (NEB, #E7120S) from the Next Enzymatic Methyl-seq Kit at 37  C for 3 h. The resulting DNA was then analyzed using a DNA methylation microarray, such as the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip (850 K array), following the standard protocol provided by the manufacturer.
Differential DNA differential methylation position analysis

For non-paired samples, the champ DMP function in the ChAMP package can be used for differential methylation analysis of DMPs. For the p-values obtained from the analysis, the Benjamini & Hochberg method can be applied for multiple hypothesis testing to reduce false positives.
Cell culture

KGN cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM/F12 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37  C with 5% CO2.
RNA interference

Small interfering RNA (siRNA) was employed to knockdown TET2 and USP45 in KGN cells. The specific siRNA sequences were designed and synthesized by Genomeditech (Shanghai, China); detailed sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Cells were transfected with the siRNA using HiPerFect Transfection Reagent (QIAGEN, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions, followed by a 24-h incubation.
Plasmid transfection

TET2 overexpression plasmids were purchased from BIOWORLD (Nanjing, China), and USP45 overexpression plasmids were obtained from Genomeditech (Shanghai, China). Cells were transfected with the respective plasmids using Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol, followed by a 24-h incubation.
Western blot

Cells were collected and lysed using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, China) supplemented with protease inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined using the BCA assay. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes at 400 mA for 40 min. The membranes were blocked at room temperature for 30 min using a rapid blocking solution. After three washes with TBST, membranes were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4  C. Following primary antibody incubation, membranes were washed three times with TBST and incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using chemiluminescent substrate and imaged. The primary and secondary antibodies used were: TET1(Affinity Biosciences, China, 1:1000), TET2(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), TET3(Signal antibody, China, 1:1000), beta-Tubulin(Proteintech, China, 1:5000), ATG7(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), Beclin(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), LC I/II(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), P62/SQSTM1(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), USP45(Affinity Biosciences, China, 1:1000), PRKAA1(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), mTOR(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), p-mTOR(Proteintech, China, 1:1000), UB(Affinity Biosciences, China, 1:1000).
Agarose gel electrophoresis

Agarose gel electrophoresis was performed to analyze PCR products. A 1% pre-cast agarose gel (Beyotime, China) was placed in the electrophoresis chamber and covered with TEA buffer. For each sample, 5 muL of PCR product were mixed with 1 muL of 6 x loading buffer via gentle vortexing. The resulting mixtures were then carefully loaded into the gel wells using a micropipette, taking care not to damage the gel. Electrophoresis was carried out at a constant voltage of 100 V for 45 min. Following electrophoresis, DNA bands were visualized under UV illumination and digitally captured.
Hydroxymethylated DNA immunoprecipitation-qPCR (hMeDIP-qPCR)

This experiment was conducted using the Hydroxymethylated DNA Immunoprecipitation (hMeDIP) Kit from Active Motif (Catalog No. 55010, USA), following the manufacturer's instructions. Genomic DNA obtained using the kit method was divided into two groups: control and TET2-overexpression, with 500 ng of DNA used per sample. For each group, one sample was designated as the immunoprecipitation (IP) group and the other as the IgG negative control.Each reaction tube was prepared by adding 10 muL of Buffer C, 1 muL of PIC solution, 4 muL of 5-hmC antibody (for IP group) or rabbit IgG antibody (for IgG negative control), and sterile water to bring the total volume to 100 muL. Samples were thoroughly mixed in 8-strip PCR tubes and incubated overnight at 4  C on a rotator. Subsequently, 25 muL of Protein G magnetic beads were added to each tube, followed by 2 h of incubation at 4  C with rotation. Beads were collected using a magnetic stand, and the supernatant was carefully removed. The beads were washed three times with 200 muL of pre-chilled Buffer C by gentle inversion, followed by three additional washes with 200 muL of pre-chilled Buffer D. After washing, 50 muL of Elution Buffer AM2 was added to each tube, mixed thoroughly, and incubated at 4  C for 15 min with rotation. Tubes were briefly centrifuged, and beads were magnetically separated. The supernatant was carefully transferred to a new 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube and mixed with 50 muL of Neutralization Buffer. For DNA purification, 2 muL of proteinase K (0.5 mg/mL) was added to each tube, followed by incubation at 50  C for 30 min and then at 80  C for 10 min. The purified DNA was used for subsequent RT-qPCR analysis. Input DNA was diluted to concentrations of 10, 1, 0.1, and 0.01 ng/muL for generating a standard curve, using the appropriate primer sequences. A standard curve was generated by plotting the log10(Input DNA concentration) on the x-axis and corresponding CT values on the y-axis. A standard equation was derived from the curve, and CT values from experimental samples were used to calculate the log-transformed DNA concentration, which was then converted to actual concentration. Fold enrichment was calculated as: Fold enrichment = Amount of enriched sample DNA (ng) / Amount of enriched IgG DNA (ng).
DNA bisulfite conversion

DNA bisulfite conversion was performed using the BeyoMag  DNA Bisulfite Conversion Kit (Beyotime, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, the conversion reagent was prepared by dissolving the conversion powder in Protection Solution. A total of 2 ug of genomic DNA was mixed with 130 uL of the conversion solution. The mixture underwent thermal cycling in a PCR system, consisting of initial denaturation at 95  C followed by multiple cycles of denaturation at 95  C and conversion at 70  C to achieve chemical modification. Subsequently, the converted DNA was incubated with BeyoMag magnetic beads for 5-15 min for binding. After an initial wash, desulfonation was carried out using a freshly prepared desulfonation solution at room temperature for exactly 20 min. Following two additional washes and air-drying of the beads, the purified DNA was recovered in 20 ul of Elution Buffer. The converted DNA samples were stored at -20  C or -80  C for subsequent analysis.
Mitochondrial membrane potential measurement

Mitochondrial health in KGN cells was assessed by measuring membrane potential changes with JC-1 staining (Beyotime, China). Briefly, cells were treated with 10 mum JC-1 for 20 min at 37  C in the dark, followed by two rinses with DPBS. Images were captured using a fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan). The probe functions as a dual-emission sensor where red fluorescence (aggregates) indicates polarized mitochondria and green fluorescence (monomers) denotes depolarization. Fluorescence quantification was executed through ImageJ analysis. To determine relative differences in mitochondrial polarization, the ratio of red to green fluorescence intensity was calculated for each group.
ROS staining analysis

The production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in granulosa cells was monitored using H2DCFDA (Sigma, USA). After incubating the cells with the probe (5uM) in a dark environment at 37  C for 30 min, they were collected via 0.05% trypsin-EDTA digestion. The resulting cell suspension was immediately analyzed using a flow cytometer to quantify fluorescence intensity.
Statistical analysis

Continuous experimental data are presented as mean +- standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 7.00. Comparisons between two groups were conducted using Student's t-tests (independent or paired, as appropriate). Comparisons between three or more groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by a post hoc test if the ANOVA yielded a significant result. Data normality was assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. For normally distributed data, Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) test was used for post hoc multiple comparisons following a significant ANOVA. For non-normally distributed data, the Kruskal-Wallis test was conducted for comparisons across multiple groups, followed by Dunn's post hoc test for pairwise comparisons. Correlations between categorical variables were evaluated using Pearson's chi-square test. A P-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.
