Where A is the measured absorbance at the selected wavelength, epsilon the molar extinction coefficient, and l the optical path length. Where applicable, spectral overlap between payload and antibody absorbance was taken into account.
DAR was calculated as the ratio between the molar concentration of payload and antibody:

In parallel experiments, DAR estimation was performed by Western blot. To that end, clinically approved ADCs with known DAR values were used as internal reference standards (belantamab mafodotin, T-DM1 and T-DXd). Cetuximab conjugated to the different payloads (MMAF, DM1 and DXd) was analyzed in parallel with the corresponding reference ADCs, all run on the same SDS-PAGE gel. For each ADC, three different protein loads (50, 100 and 500 ng) were analyzed to ensure signal proportionality within the linear dynamic range of detection. Payload-specific signals (detected using anti-payload antibodies) were quantified by densitometry and normalized to total protein per lane using stain-free imaging. DAR values for the cetuximab-based ADCs were calculated by comparing the normalized payload signal to that of the corresponding reference ADC and multiplying by the known DAR of the reference, using the formula: DARCetuximab = (PayloadCetuximab signal/ PayloadReference signal) x DARReference. Final DAR values were reported as the average of the three loading conditions, of at least two independent experiments.
Cell culture and proliferation assays

OVCAR8, SKOV3, OVCAR3, PEO4, and PEO6 cells were cultured in DMEM containing high glucose (4500 mg/L), while A2780 and IGROV1 cells were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium. Both media included antibiotics (100 U/mL penicillin, 100 mug/mL streptomycin) and were supplemented with 10% FBS. Cells were maintained in a humidified atmosphere at 37 C with 5% CO2. The cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA), and their authenticity was verified by STR analyses.

Cell proliferation was assessed using cell counting. Cells were plated in 6-well plates at a density of 20,000 to 100,000 cells, depending on the cell line. Cells were then incubated overnight at 37 C in culture media and the following day fresh media containing different drug treatments added. Cells were counted 5 days after treatment using a Z1 Coulter Particle Counter (Beckman Coulter, Pasadena, CA, USA).
Protein extraction and western blot

Cells were cultured in 100 mm dishes and treated 24 hours after seeding. At the indicated times, monolayers were washed with cold PBS and lysed in 140 mM NaCl, 50 mM Ethylene-diaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 10% glycerol, 1% Nonidet P-40, 20 mM Tris (pH 7.0), 1 muM pepstatin, 1 mug/ml aprotinin, 1 mug/ml leupeptin, 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), 25 mM beta-glycerophosphate, 50 mM sodium fluoride, and 1 mM sodium orthovanadate. Samples were then centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4 C to obtain the clarified extracts. Protein concentration was measured using the BCA assay (ThermoFisher, Madrid, Spain). In general, 50 micrograms of protein from each sample were loaded in SDS-PAGE gels, which contained 2,2,2-trichloroethanol (50 mul/10 ml of final gel solution). Stain free gel images were taken using the ChemiDoc Detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories). For western blotting, gels were transferred to Immobilon-P membranes, which were then blocked for 1 h with Tris-buffered saline with Tween (TBST) (100 mM Tris [pH 7.5], 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% Tween 20) containing 1% BSA and 0.05% sodium azide. Membranes were incubated with the corresponding primary antibody (2-16 hours), washed three times, 7 minutes each, with TBST and then incubated with HRP-conjugated anti-mouse or anti-rabbit secondary antibodies for 30 minutes. Chemiluminescent detection was performed using the ChemiDoc apparatus, and band quantitation analyzed with Image Lab  Software Version 6.0.1 (Bio-Rad Laboratories). Tubulin or actin were used as loading controls.
Quantitative RT-PCR

RNA from ovarian cancer cell lines was extracted using the Ambion PureLink RNA MiniKit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and cDNA was synthesized with the M-MLV reverse transcriptase kit (Invitrogen). Quantitative RT-PCR was performed in 96-well optical plates. Samples were prepared by adding 6.35 microL of Sybr Green (ThermoFisher), containing 0.2 microL of each forward and reverse primers (resuspended in water at a concentration of 10 microM), and 10 ng of each cDNA sample. The final reaction volume was adjusted to 12.5 microL with RNase-Free Water. For negative controls, water was added instead of cDNA. The plate was centrifuged at 3,700 rpm for 3 minutes to remove any air bubbles. RT-PCR was carried out on a Quant Studio 1 System (ThermoFisher). All samples were analyzed in duplicates and normalized to the endogenous control GAPDH. mRNA levels were calculated based on the RQ values and are represented as the mean +- SD of duplicates from a representative experiment repeated twice. The primers used for amplification of the EGFR gene and the endogenous control GAPDH were as follows: EGFR forward 5'-AGGTGAAAACAGCTGCAAGG-3'; EGFR reverse 5'-CCAGAAGGTTGCACTTGTCC-3'; GAPDH forward 5'-GAGTCAACGGATTTGGTCGT-3'; GAPDH reverse 5'-GATCTCGCTCCTGGAAGATG-3'.
Immunofluorescence assays

OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cell lines were seeded on glass coverslips in 35 mm dishes at a density of 100,000 cells per dish. Twenty-four hours post-plating, the cells were treated with 10 nM cetuximab-vc-MMAF. The immunofluorescence protocol has been described. Samples were visualized using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany) and then analyzed using Leica LAS X software. Quantitation of colocalization in the immunofluorescence experiments between the cetuximab-vc-MMAF and the different endocytic vesicles was performed using ImageJ software (Coloc2 plugin). For each image, automatic thresholding was applied to minimize background noise, and the Manders' coefficients (M1 and M2) were calculated as measures of the degree of overlap between fluorescent signals. The results were expressed as the percentage of colocalization. For each vesicle type and time point, 10 randomly selected fields were analyzed, and the mean +- SD of the colocalization coefficients was calculated and represented.
Flow cytometry experiments

For the detection of cell surface EGFR by flow cytometry, cetuximab was directly labelled with the fluorescent dye DyLight 488. Cetuximab was prepared at a concentration of 2.5 mg/mL in 0.05 M sodium borate buffer (pH 8.5), in a final volume of 200 microL. The antibody was then added to one vial (1 mg) of the DyLight Amine-Reactive Dyes Kit (ThermoFisher) and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. The excess dye was removed using Dye Removal Columns (ThermoFisher).

Ovarian cancer cell lines were plated in 60 mm plates and, upon reaching 70% confluence, were trypsinized, and then trypsin removed by a short centrifugation. Cells were resuspended in PBS+1% BSA and labeled for 15 minutes in the dark, using 10 nM cetuximab-DyLight 488. Fluorescence acquisition was performed using an Accuri C6 flow cytometer (BD-biosciences). A minimum of 50,000 events were analyzed for each condition. Results are presented as graphs of a representative experiment repeated at least three times. Quantification of these assays is presented as the mean +- SD of all experiments performed. Cell cycle and apoptosis evaluation by flow cytometry were carried out as described.
Fluorometric detection of caspase activity

OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cell lines were treated for different times (24 h and 48 h) with 10 nM cetuximab-vc-MMAF and lysed according to the protein extraction protocol described above under "Protein extraction" section. Fifty microg of extract were incubated in the caspase reaction buffer (25 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% CHAPS, 10% sucrose, and 10 mM DTT) along with the fluorescent detection substrate Ac-DEVD-AFC (BD Biosystems), at a concentration of 5 microM. Lysates were incubated at 37 C for 1 h, and the fluorescent signal measured at 400/505 nm using a Synergy4 multiwell plate reader (BioTek Instruments, Winooski, VT, USA).
In vivo experiments

Animal experiments were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines and protocol approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Salamanca (Salamanca, Spain, approval code: CBE-2019-325). Female BALB/C nu/nu athymic mice, aged six weeks and weighing 18-20 g (Charles River Laboratories, Wilmington, MA, USA), were kept in pathogen-free facilities at the University of Salamanca's Animal Care Facility (Salamanca, Spain). Mice were injected one week after the quarantine period with 1 x 106 OVCAR8 cells or 2 x 106 SKOV3 cells, resuspended in a 1:1 mixture of DMEM and Matrigel (ThermoFisher). Tumor cells were injected into the caudal region of the dorsal flank. Once tumors reached a volume of 100-150 mm3, mice were randomized into two groups (six animals per group). One group received the vehicle (PBS), and the other group was treated with cetuximab-vc-MMAF. Treatments were administered by intraperitoneal injection once per week. To assess tolerability, SKOV3-bearing mice received weekly escalating doses, consisting of 3 mg/kg in weeks 1 and 2; 5 mg/kg in week 3; and 10 mg/kg in week 4. Mice bearing OVCAR8 tumors received a fixed weekly dose of 5 mg/kg throughout the treatment period. Mice were euthanized with isoflurane once tumor volume reached 1500 mm3. Tumor size and body weight were monitored three times per week. Tumor volume was calculated using the formula: V = (L/2) x (W/2)2 x (4/3) x pi where V represents tumor volume (mm3), L is tumor length (mm), and W is tumor width (mm).

Blood samples were collected via maxillary vein puncture on days 1, 2, 5, 9, 14, and 19 post-treatment. Samples were collected in EDTA tubes to prevent coagulation and centrifuged for 10 minutes at 3000 rpm at 4 C to obtain plasma. At the study endpoint, tumors and selected organs were harvested and either stored at -80 C for biochemical or fixed for immunohistochemical analyses.
Sandwich ELISA analysis

Analysis of cetuximab-vc-MMAF in plasma and tumor samples was performed using ELISA or western. To distinguish between total antibody levels (human IgG detection) and MMAF-associated antibody species, two complementary immunoassays were employed. Total human IgG (representing the cetuximab antibody backbone) was quantified using a commercial Human IgG ELISA Kit (ThermoFisher). Plasma samples obtained from mice were diluted 1:400 in PBS, and 100 microL of each sample was analyzed according to the manufacturer's instructions. MMAF bound to the antibody was detected using a custom sandwich ELISA. Plates were coated with 50 muL per well of anti-human IgG Fc-specific antibody (10 mug/mL) and incubated overnight. After incubation, the antibody solution was discarded and wells were blocked with PBS containing 3% BSA for at least one hour. Then the blocking solution was discarded, and 50 microl of 1:100 diluted plasma was added and incubated for at least 2 hours. Plates were then washed four times with PBS, and the primary anti-MMAF antibody was applied at a 1:1000 dilution. After four washes with 300 microL of PBS each, the secondary antibody for MMAF detection (anti-mouse HRP, 1:1000) was incubated for 1 h. After washing again four times with 300 microL of PBS, the ELISA was developed by adding 50 microL of TMB substrate for 15 minutes, and the reaction was stopped with 50 microL of 1 M ortho-phosphoric acid. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm, with wavelength correction at 570 nm, using a Tecan microplate reader (Tecan, Mannedorf, Switzerland). To generate the standard curve, we used a commercial antibody conjugated to MMAF (Belantamab Mafodotin, MedChem Express), allowing detection within a concentration range of 1.3-100 ng/ml. All samples were analyzed in duplicate, and results are presented as the mean +- SD of a representative experiment, with a minimum of two independent experiments.
Immunohistochemical and biochemical analyses of tumor samples

Immunohistochemical analyses were performed as described. The antibodies were used at a 1:100 dilution. The results were evaluated by expert pathologists from the Comparative Molecular Pathology Service of our center. For quantitation, positive cells were counted in 10 randomly selected fields (40x magnification) using ImageJ 1.44p software. Three independent samples from each condition were analyzed for each antibody. For biochemical analyses, tumors preserved at -80 C were lysed using a gentleMACS  Octo Dissociator (Miltenyi Biotec), and the extracts were clarified for subsequent analysis by western blot or ELISA.
Statistical analyses

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). For Western blot analyses of patient samples, data were represented as box plots showing the median and the interquartile range (IQR) for each group. In the in vivo experiments, t-tests were used to analyze differences in tumor volume between control and treated groups, yielding an overall p-value for the experiment. Similarly, t-tests were used to determine significant differences in the western blot and IHC experiments derived from the in vivo studies. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
EGFR expression in ovarian cancer

Fig 1 dummy alt text

To explore the possibility that the EGFR may represent a target of antibody-drug conjugates in ovarian cancer, the expression of the protein was assessed by western blotting in a set of 58 samples from tumors of diverse histological origin, including high grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC, n = 32), low grade serous ovarian carcinoma (LGSOC, n = 8), borderline tumors (n = 11), and endometrioid ovarian tumors (n = 7). As shown in Fig. 1A, EGFR expression was found in all four analyzed subtypes. Quantitative analysis (Fig. 1B) relativizing to the stain free gels (Supplementary figure 1), showed that the amount of EGFR was variable among the different samples. Of note, normal ovarian tissues also expressed the EGFR. The expression of the EGFR was also analyzed in seven ovarian cancer cell lines representative of HGSOC (OVCAR3, OVCAR8, PEO4 and PEO6), LGSOC (SKOV3), and endometrioid ovarian cancer (IGROV1 and A2780). Western blotting (Fig. 1C) and qPCR (Fig. 1D) showed variable expression of the EGFR in the cell lines analyzed.

To represent an ADC target, the domain of the protein recognized by the ADC should be exposed to the extracellular space. To analyze the surface expression of the EGFR in the ovarian cancer cell lines, cytometric analyses were carried out using cetuximab labelled with DyLight 488. Cetuximab is a clinically-approved humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to the ectodomain of the EGFR. Preliminary experiments showed that the coupling of DyLight 488 to cetuximab did not alter its ability to interact with the EGFR (data not shown). All the cell lines bound cetuximab-DyLight 488 (Fig. 1E). Quantitative analysis showed correlation between the amount of cell surface EGFR (Fig. 1F) and the total levels of the receptor, suggesting that cells expressing high amounts of the EGFR will also expose the receptor at the cell surface. Taken together, the quantitative analyses of the expression of the EGFR in the different cell lines indicated that OVCAR8 and SKOV3 expressed higher amounts than IGROV1 or OVCAR3 cells, which in turn expressed higher amounts than PEO4 and PEO6. The cell line with the lowest EGFR expression was A2780.
Biological effect of ADCs targeting the EGFR

Construction and effectiveness of different cetuximab-based ADCs. A. Schematic representation of the ADCs structure composed by a cetuximab backbone conjugated to different payloads. Green chains indicate non-cleavable linkers; blue lines with scissors indicate cleavable linkers. B. Western analyses of the conjugation of cetuximab to different payloads. One-hundred ng of each antibody were loaded in a stain-free SDS-PAGE gel. After image capture (top), the gel was transferred to PVDF membranes, that were then cut to be incubated with the indicated anti-payload antibodies (bottom) to confirm antibody-payload conjugation. C. Dose-response proliferation assays with the four cetuximab-based ADCs in the seven ovarian cancer cell lines. Cells were plated and treated with the indicated doses of the four different ADCs (1 pM to 10 nM), and cell counting was performed 5 days later. Results, relativized to the untreated controls, are represented as the mean +- SD of triplicates of a representative experiment that was repeated at least twice.
Fig 2 dummy alt text

The expression of the EGFR in patient samples confirmed that this membrane receptor could serve as a docking site for ADCs in ovarian cancer. Moreover, the expression of EGFR in human cell lines allowed their use to explore the potential antiproliferative action of EGFR targeting with ADCs. Taking these circumstances into consideration, and also the availability of cetuximab, we decided to use that antibody as a backbone for the construction of ADCs containing different cytotoxic payloads (schematically represented in Fig. 2A). Three cytotoxics were used, namely DM1, deruxtecan (DXd) and monomethyl auristatin F (MMAF), because of their already demonstrated clinical value. In the case of MMAF, two versions were prepared, one including a cleavable valine-citrulline (vc) linker and the other of a non-cleavable MC-alkyl-hydrazine linker (Supplementary figure 2). Gel electrophoresis followed by stain-free analysis showed an increase in the molecular weight of the heavy and light chains of the ADCs prepared, when compared to the nude antibody used for the coupling (Fig. 2B, stain free gel). The gel containing the different coupled antibodies as well as uncoupled cetuximab, was then transferred to a PVDF membrane that was sliced to be incubated with antibodies that recognized the different payloads. These studies showed that the anti-payload antibodies recognized the coupled cytotoxic, failing to interact with the nude antibody backbone. DXd and MMAF were coupled to the heavy and light chains of cetuximab, while DM1 preferentially coupled to the heavy Ig chain (Fig. 2B). The average drug-antibody ratio (DAR) of the cetuximab-based ADCs was determined by UV-visible spectrophotometry (Supplementary figure 3A). The prepared ADCs exhibited average DAR values within the range expected for ADCs generated using their respective conjugation chemistries. DAR values were also estimated using a Western blot-based approach. In these experiments, clinically approved ADCs with known DARs were included as internal reference standards on the same gels. Specifically, belantamab mafodotin, trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) were run in parallel with the cetuximab-based ADCs and blots probed with payload-specific antibodies. As shown in supplementary Figures 3B-D, the relative signal intensities of the cetuximab-based ADCs closely matched those of the corresponding reference ADCs, allowing estimation of average DAR values based on direct comparison under identical experimental conditions. Stain-free gel imaging demonstrated comparable antibody integrity across all ADC preparations.

The effect of the different cetuximab-based ADCs was then evaluated in the seven ovarian cancer cell lines. Dose-response studies were performed by cell counting with the four cetuximab-based ADCs, and results obtained in those cell lines plotted (Fig. 2C). MMAF-coupled cetuximab ADCs exerted a strong antiproliferative effect on most cell lines, except in the case of A2780 and PEO4. In the latter two cell lines, the poor effect (see also supplementary figure 4) could be related to the low level of EGFR expression as compared to that present in the other ovarian cancer cell lines. Cetuximab-DM1 had a minimal antiproliferative effect on any of the cell lines. Similarly, cetuximab-DXd was found to be less potent and efficient than the MMAF-coupled cetuximab ADCs. Together, these experiments indicated that MMAF-coupled cetuximab was more potent than DM1- or DXd-coupled cetuximab-based ADCs. Because of that, we developed further studies using MMAF-coupled cetuximab.

Fig 3 dummy alt text

To explore whether attachment of the payload favored the action of the ADC, experiments were designed to measure the antiproliferative activity of the payload (MMAF) or the nude antibody (cetuximab) alone, comparing their effectiveness to that of the ADCs (cetuximab-vc-MMAF, cetuximab-mc-MMAF). As shown in Fig. 3A, the different cell lines responded similarly to free MMAF, which reached a maximal effect at concentrations between 0.5-1 muM. The antiproliferative effect of cetuximab-vc-MMAF and cetuximab-mc-MMAF was more potent, reaching a maximal effect at concentrations of 500 pM, except in the case of A2780, who was largely resistant to the ADCs. The nude antibody, at concentrations up to 10 nM, did not have a major effect on cell proliferation (Fig. 3B).
Internalization of cetuximab-vc-MMAF

For time 0 h, cells were incubated on ice for 30 minutes to visualize membrane staining. Nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 in all cases. Scale bar: 10 mum. B. Cells were treated as above, and colocalization (yellow) with markers for early endosomes (EEA1), late endosomes (RAB7), and lysosomes (LAMP1) analysed at the indicated times. Scale bar: 5 mum. C. Quantitation of colocalization was performed using ImageJ and expressed as a percentage. Data are presented as the mean +- SD of 10 fields per time point, for each vesicle type.
Fig 4 dummy alt text

The mechanisms of the antiproliferative action of MMAF-coupled cetuximab-based ADCs in ovarian cancer cells was then explored. Since internalization of ADC-target complexes represents an initial critical step in the mechanism of action of ADCs, the internalization of cetuximab-vc-MMAF over time was then explored. To that end, OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells were treated with a saturating dose of the antibody (10 nM) for different times. Immunofluorescent studies showed that at early incubation times, the ADC presented cell membrane staining (Fig. 4A and supplementary figure 5A). Extending the incubation times showed that in addition to the cell surface staining pattern, accumulation of the ADC was also present, following a dotted pattern. That dotted pattern progressively increased at times of 3 hours and beyond, reaching larger dots after 24 hours of incubation with cetuximab-vc-MMAF.

To analyze the intracellular trafficking of cetuximab-vc-MMAF, colocalization experiments with the EGFR as well as with markers of intracellular endocytic compartments were performed in OVCAR8 (Fig.s 4B and C) and SKOV3 (Supplementary figure 6). The ADC colocalized with the EGFR, as indicated by co-staining experiments using an anti-endodomain anti-EGFR antibody (Supplementary figure 5B and C). Moreover, treatment with the ADC provoked a time-dependent decrease in the total amount of the EGFR in both cell lines (Supplementary figure 5D). Cetuximab-vc-MMAF colocalized with EEA1, a marker of early endosomes, at the first time point analyzed (15 minutes) indicating that endocytosis of the ADC was fast. Colocalization of cetuximab-vc-MMAF with EEA1 peaked at one hour, decreasing thereafter (Fig. 4C). In the case of RAB7, a marker of late endosomes and lysosomes, colocalization started to be observed after one hour of treatment with the ADC, and progressively increased up to 24 hours. Similar kinetics of colocalization to those with RAB7 were observed in the case of the lysosomal marker LAMP1 (Fig. 4C and supplementary figure 6).

To explore the mechanism underlying the antiproliferative activity of cetuximab-vc-MMAF in ovarian cancer, we first evaluated its impact on cell morphology and cell cycle dynamics. Phase contrast microscopy of OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells showed that the ADC provoked rounding of cells (Fig. 5A). Flow cytometric analyses of DNA content in OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells showed that the ADC induced accumulation of cells in the G2/M phase compared to untreated controls, accompanied by a reduction of cells in the G0/G1 cell cycle phases (Fig. 5B and C).

Biochemically, treatment of OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells with cetuximab-vc-MMAF led to increased levels of phosphorylated histone H3 (pHH3), a canonical marker of mitotic chromatin condensation, and phospho-BUBR1, a spindle assembly checkpoint kinase (Fig. 5D). Cyclin B1, which partners with CDK1 to drive mitosis, was upregulated, especially in SKOV3 cells. These biochemical signatures suggested that cetuximab-vc-MMAF impaired mitotic progression. Moreover, increased phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (pRb Ser780) was observed, further reflecting sustained CDK activity during mitosis, and suggesting cell cycle deregulation and incomplete mitotic exit.

Since MMAF acts by disrupting tubulin polymerization, a critical step for mitotic spindle assembly during mitosis, the effect of cetuximab-vc-MMAF on mitotic spindles was explored. Staining of mitotic cells with beta-tubulin and DAPI revealed that ADC-treated OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells developed aberrant mitotic figures, including multipolar and disorganized spindle structures (Fig. 5E and F). These abnormalities suggest that cetuximab-vc-MMAF disrupts proper spindle formation, which could interfere with accurate chromosome segregation and delay cell cycle progression.

Live cells are shown in the lower left quadrant (Annexin V-/PI-), while the other three quadrants represent different stages of non-viable cells. B. Graphical representation of non-viable cells for each condition. Data are plotted as mean +- SD of three independent experiments. C. Western blot analysis of apoptosis-related proteins at the indicated time points following treatment with 10 nM cetuximab-vc-MMAF. Actin was used as a loading control, and molecular weight markers are shown at the right. D. Analysis of caspase-3 activity in cells treated with cetuximab-vc-MMAF (10 nM) for the indicated times. Data represent mean +- SD of fluorescence intensity resulting from substrate cleavage (Ac-DEVD-AFC) by activated caspase-3 in two independent experiments.

Prolonged mitotic arrest can trigger mitotic catastrophe, a cell death process associated with defective mitosis. To determine whether cetuximab-vc-MMAF induces cell death following mitotic arrest, markers of apoptosis were examined. Flow cytometry analyses using Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide staining demonstrated a time-dependent increase in non-viable cells upon ADC treatment (Fig.s 6A and B). In both OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cell lines, the percentage of dead cells increased progressively at 24 and 48 hours post-treatment (Fig.s 6A and B).

To explore the potential involvement of DNA damage as part of the cascade of events triggered by the ADC, we analyzed apoptotic and DNA damage markers by western blot. Treatment with cetuximab-vc-MMAF resulted in a time-dependent decrease in PARP and an increase in cleaved caspase-3 in both cell lines (Fig. 6C). Enzymatic activity studies confirmed the activation of Caspase-3 by the ADC (Fig. 6D). Notably, increased levels of phosphorylated H2AX (gammaH2AX), a sensitive marker of DNA double-strand breaks, were also observed after 24 and 48 hours of ADC exposure.
In vivo action of cetuximab-vc-MMAF

The overall duration of each experiment is indicated. Cetuximab-vc-MMAF was administrated once weekly by intraperitoneal injection (indicated by the syringe icon). SKOV3-bearing mice were treated using a weekly dose escalation (3 mg/kg during weeks 1 and 2, followed by 5 mg/kg in week 3 and 10 mg/kg in week 4), while OVCAR8 injected mice received a constant weekly dose of 5 mg/kg throughout the experiment. Blood sampling time points from the submandibular vein are indicated by a blood drop symbol. At the end of each experiment, tumors (generated from OVCAR8 and SKOV3), and organs (from SKOV3-injected animals) were collected for analysis. B-C. Mean tumor volume (mm3) for SKOV3 (B) and OVCAR8 (C) xenografts in vehicle-treated (PBS) and cetuximab-vc-MMAF-treated groups. Global p-values < 0.05 are considered significant. d-E. Body weight monitoring for SKOV3 (D) and OVCAR8 (E) xenografts. F-G. Kaplan-Meier survival curves for SKOV3 (F) and OVCAR8 (G) xenografts comparing vehicle and cetuximab-vc-MMAF treated groups. In the OVCAR8 experiment, all animals were euthanized at the experimental endpoint according to study design. H-I. Tumor growth change (%) for SKOV3 (H) and OVCAR8 (I), calculated for each tumor using the formula: TGC = ((Vf - Vi)/Vi) x 100, where Vi is the tumor volume at treatment initiation (Day 0) and Vf the final tumor volume at experiment endpoint. Values below zero indicate tumor regression.
Fig 7 dummy alt text

To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of cetuximab-vc-MMAF in vivo, OVCAR8 and SKOV3 cells were xenografted into immunodeficient female mice. Treatment with the ADC was initiated once tumors reached 150 mm3 (OVCAR8) or 200 mm3 (SKOV3), following the schedule outlined in Fig. 7A. In addition to measurements of tumor growth, blood samples were taken at the indicated days for pharmacokinetic analyses of ADC blood concentrations. As also indicated in Fig. 7A, the experiment using SKOV3 cells terminated 26 days after the first ADC injection, due to the fast-growing kinetics of tumors in untreated animals. In the case of animals injected with OVCAR8 cells, and due to the slower growth rate of the tumors, the experiment was extended for 107 days after the first injection of the ADC. At the termination of the experiments, several organs and the tumors (if present) were collected for the analysis of ADC accumulation in these tissues. In addition, several markers of cell cycle progression/apoptosis were analyzed in tumors, both biochemically and/or immunohistochemically.

Administration of cetuximab-vc-MMAF to mice bearing tumors derived from the injection of SKOV3 (Fig. 7B) or OVCAR8 (Fig. 7C) cells, resulted in a pronounced inhibition of tumor growth compared to the vehicle (PBS)-treated groups. Tumor volume in mice treated with the conjugate remained significantly lower throughout the study period, with P values of 0.0081 or < 0.0001 in SKOV3 and OVCAR8 tumors, compared to their respective control arms. Treatment with the ADC did not significantly affect the weight of the mice (Fig.s 7D and E) suggesting that the dose of the ADC used did not exert major toxicity. Kaplan-Meier analyses revealed prolonged survival in mice receiving the conjugate compared to control groups (Fig.s 7F and G). Individualized analysis of the tumors in mice treated with the ADC showed that some of the tumors reduced their size with respect to the values at treatment initiation (Fig.s 7H and I). Together, these results indicated that cetuximab-vc-MMAF exerted antitumor activity in vivo, effectively suppressing tumor growth, and improving overall survival in the two ovarian cancer xenograft models tested.

To analyze the pharmacokinetics of cetuximab-vc-MMAF, plasma concentrations of both human IgG (cetuximab) and MMAF coupled to cetuximab were monitored by ELISA, in animals xenografted with SKOV3 (Fig. 8A) or OVCAR8 (Fig. 8B) cells. Of note, samples from untreated animals did not give any signal in these experiments (data not shown), as neither did the first serum time point analyzed, which was taken one day before treatment initiation (Fig.s 8A and B). Injection of cetuximab-vc-MMAF caused an increase in the plasma levels of human IgG, which represents a readout of the cetuximab backbone, peaking at one day after the initial dose of the ADC (Fig.s 8A and B, left graphics). The plasma concentration of the ADC decreased thereafter until a second dose was administered, nine days after the initial one. Of note, the plasma levels achieved were substantially higher than the dose of 10 nM (indicated in the figure), that caused maximal antiproliferative effect in vitro. Similar pharmacokinetic curves were obtained when analyzing the levels of MMAF coupled to cetuximab (Fig.s 8A and B, right panels).

ELISA analyses demonstrated accumulation of both human IgG and MMAF within tumor tissues of mice treated with cetuximab-vc-MMAF, with no detectable levels in non-treated mice (Fig. 8C). Such accumulation was further assessed by western of tumors from untreated as well as cetuximab-vc-MMAF treated mice, using the anti-MMAF antibody (Fig. 8D). Immunohistochemical studies detected cetuximab-vc-MMAF within parenchymatous tumoral cells as well as in the interstices between them (Fig. 8E). The latter pattern was compatible with membrane reinforcement, characteristic of staining of membrane proteins. In addition, in animals treated with the ADC, staining was also present in the tumor-associated vasculature, with clear distinction from control treatments (Fig. 8E). Accumulation of cetuximab-vc-MMAF in other organs (lung, liver, kidney, brain, spleen, and heart) remained low, with respect to accumulation in the tumoral tissues of treated mice (Fig.s 8F and G and supplementary figure 7). Collectively, these findings indicate that cetuximab-vc-MMAF exhibits selective tumor targeting, prolonged systemic and intratumoral exposure, and minimal off-target distribution.

Additional studies were performed to explore biochemical changes related to the action of cetuximab-vc-MMAF in vivo. Western blotting (Fig.s 9A and B) as well as immunohistochemical (Fig. 9C) studies showed that treatment with the ADC caused a decrease in the amount of the proliferation marker Ki67. In addition, an increase in the mitotic marker pHH3 was detected both in the western blotting and the immunohistochemical studies (Fig.s 9A-C). The immunohistochemical analyses also revealed that the ADC augmented the amount of cleaved caspase 3 and gammaH2AX (Fig. 9C). EGFR expression decreased in the tumor samples treated with the ADC (Fig.s 9A and B).
Discussion

The present study demonstrates the preclinical activity of cetuximab-based antibody-drug conjugates in EGFR-expressing ovarian cancer models. Our data show that cetuximab conjugated to the microtubule-disrupting agent MMAF exerted potent antitumor effects both in vitro and in vivo. These results support the potential use of cetuximab, a clinically approved anti-EGFR antibody, as a targeted delivery vehicle for cytotoxic agents in ovarian cancer.

passages.text: EGFR overexpression is frequently observed in epithelial ovarian carcinomas and is associated with poor prognosis, chemoresistance, and enhanced tumor aggressiveness. Despite this, EGFR-targeted therapies such as cetuximab and tyrosine kinase inhibitors have shown limited clinical benefit in ovarian cancer, likely due to low EGFR dependency in many tumors. However, the exploitation of EGFR as a target for ADCs does not solely rely on functional EGFR inhibition but rather on its ability to mediate efficient internalization of the payload-conjugated antibody. This paradigm shift opens new therapeutic avenues in tumors where EGFR is expressed but not necessarily oncogenic. Our data demonstrate that the expression of EGFR in ovarian cancer cells is sufficient to enable internalization and payload delivery, as evidenced by the potent cytotoxicity of cetuximab-MMAF in EGFR-expressing models. In fact, the internalization studies using cetuximab-vc-MMAF further confirm that EGFR effectively mediates intracellular trafficking of the ADCs in ovarian cancer cells. These findings reinforce the notion that EGFR is not only a valid surface target but also an efficient conduit for payload delivery, even in tumors that may not be driven by EGFR signaling.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: One of the key observations from our study is the differential activity of the four cetuximab-based ADCs tested. Cetuximab-MMAF consistently showed greater potency than cetuximab-DM1 or cetuximab-DXd across a panel of ovarian cancer cell lines. This is consistent with reports showing that MMAF exhibits more efficient killing in certain cell types, by virtue of its ability to persist intracellularly and induce mitotic catastrophe. Although MMAE is a clinically established auristatin ADC payload, similar to MMAF, with membrane permeability and a documented bystander effect, MMAF was intentionally selected in this study to ensure that cytotoxic activity was strictly dependent on EGFR-mediated internalization and intracellular processing, allowing a more controlled assessment of target-specific delivery. In contrast, DM1, a maytansinoid payload used in the FDA-approved ADC trastuzumab-emtansine (T-DM1), and DXd, used in trastuzumab-deruxtecan, appear to be less potent in the in vitro ovarian cancer models tested, suggesting that the choice of payload significantly impacts ADC efficacy in this tumor type. Although membrane-permeable payloads such as deruxtecan can potentially enhance antitumor activity in vivo, cetuximab-DXd displayed minimal cytotoxicity in several ovarian cancer cell models in vitro, despite adequate EGFR expression. Consequently, the in vivo studies were prioritized for ADCs that demonstrated strong preclinical efficacy in vitro. Further investigations will be required to determine whether cetuximab-deruxtecan shows therapeutic activity in vivo. Moreover, in OVCAR3 and OVCAR8 cells, the cleavable form of cetuximab-MMAF was more potent than the uncleavable form, suggesting that linker chemistry represents another factor that influences ADC potency.

passages.text: Importantly, our study demonstrates that cetuximab-based ADCs retain selectivity for EGFR-expressing cells. This was evidenced by the minimal cytotoxic effect of either ADC in EGFR-low models, such as A2780, and by the correlation between surface EGFR levels and sensitivity. These results suggest that EGFR expression could serve as a predictive biomarker for ADC activity in ovarian cancer. The possibility of using existing clinical diagnostics to identify patients with EGFR-positive tumors enhances the translational potential of these findings.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: The in vivo efficacy studies in OVCAR8 and SKOV3 xenografts provide compelling evidence of the therapeutic potential of cetuximab-vc-MMAF. This ADC significantly reduced tumor growth, without causing significant weight loss or apparent toxicity in mice. The pharmacokinetic studies showed that the serum levels of the ADC remained substantially above the dose (10 nM) that exerted maximal in vitro antiproliferative effect. Therefore, under the experimental conditions established, the ADC should be available at maximal effective concentrations to act on tumoral cells at least for three weeks. Moreover, both ELISA and western studies confirmed accumulation of the ADC in tumors, while its presence in normal tissues was marginal. This is relevant as it indicates that the ADC has preference for homing to the tissues with high antigen expression. However, it is relevant to mention that cetuximab does not interact with the murine version of the EGFR, impeding accurate assessment of on-target, off-tumor effects of the ADC. That represents a limitation of the present study. Immunohistochemical and biochemical studies of tumor samples offered results compatible with the in vitro mechanistic studies. The ADC provoked a profound decrease in the amount of the proliferation marker Ki67, and augmented the levels of pHH3. These data are in line with the antiproliferative effects of the ADC. In addition, cetuximab-vc-MMAF caused an increase in gammaH2AX and cleaved caspase 3, indicating that the compound was able to promote DNA damage and cell death also in vivo. These results validate the antitumor activity observed in vitro and highlight the translational relevance of cetuximab-vc-MMAF.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: It is worth noting that although cetuximab has been previously tested in ovarian cancer as a single agent or in combination with chemotherapy, its clinical efficacy has been modest. Our findings suggest that the therapeutic utility of cetuximab could be significantly enhanced by converting it into an ADC. This approach takes advantage of the well-characterized pharmacokinetics and safety profile of cetuximab, while expanding its antitumor activity beyond EGFR blockade. Furthermore, the clinical experience with cetuximab could facilitate the clinical development of cetuximab-based ADCs by leveraging existing regulatory and manufacturing pathways. The feasibility of EGFR-targeted ADCs is further supported by ongoing clinical development in other tumor types, as well as by the approval in Japan of an anti-EGFR ADC. Nevertheless, clinical translation of EGFR-targeted ADCs has proven challenging. Several EGFR-directed ADCs have entered clinical development, with depatuxizumab mafodotin (ABT-414) representing the most advanced example to date. Although this EGFR-directed MMAF-based ADC showed encouraging preclinical activity, clinical studies revealed limited efficacy at tolerated doses together with dose-limiting ocular toxicity. In ovarian cancer, the clinical approval of the folate receptor alpha-directed ADC mirvetuximab soravtansine, carrying the maytansinoid DM4, provides a relevant benchmark for the therapeutic potential of microtubule-disrupting ADCs in this disease. In this framework, our results demonstrate that EGFR can function as an efficient delivery route in ovarian cancer models and that ADC design, including the use of MMAF with sustained intracellular persistence and mitotic arrest activity, may help overcome limitations observed with earlier EGFR-ADC approaches.

An important strength of our study is the use of both in vitro and in vivo models to evaluate ADC efficacy. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, while our in vivo experiments demonstrate significant antitumor activity, they were performed in immunodeficient mice, which do not recapitulate the immune microenvironment of human ovarian tumors. Given that cetuximab has known immune effector functions via FcgammaR binding, future studies in immunocompetent or humanized models may be necessary to assess the contribution of antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) to the overall efficacy of the ADCs. Second, although we focused on surface EGFR levels as a biomarker of sensitivity, additional factors such as internalization rate, trafficking efficiency, lysosomal function, and expression of drug efflux pumps could modulate ADC response. These parameters warrant further investigation to refine patient selection strategies. Finally, as mentioned above, while cetuximab-vc-MMAF did not show overt off-target cytotoxic activity, it is worth mentioning that cetuximab does not recognize the murine version of the EGFR, therefore preventing evaluation of on-target effects of the ADC in normal tissues. This represents a limitation of the present study, as it is the lack of evaluation of cetuximab-deruxtecan in an in vivo setting.
Conclusion

In this study, we developed and characterized cetuximab-based antibody-drug conjugates directed against EGFR, which exhibited strong and selective antitumor effects in ovarian cancer models. These ADCs effectively inhibited cell proliferation and induced mitotic arrest and apoptosis both in vitro and in vivo. Our findings provide compelling preclinical evidence supporting the development of EGFR-targeted ADCs as a promising therapeutic strategy for patients with EGFR-expressing ovarian tumors.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants for the collection and use of their biological specimens. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board Ethics Committee on Human Research at the University Hospital of Salamanca (PI 2019 04 297).

Throughout the study, tumor volumes were carefully monitored, and this limit was not exceeded in any experimental animal.

passages.text: Longitudinal multi-omics profiling of spinal muscular atrophy

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by SMN1 gene variants, leading to the degeneration of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord. It is a disabling disease with varying severity. Nusinersen, the first approved in France, has dramatically transformed SMA management. However, the significant variability in patient response and disease progression highlights a critical need for objective, measurable indicators. This study aims to identify biomarkers in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma associated with the clinical status of treatment-naive patients and their disease progression during therapy. We performed targeted metabolomics and proteomics analyses on plasma and CSF samples from SMA patients before and after six months of treatment, along with controls. The differential analysis was carried out to discover the SMA biomarkers. We found that levels of acylcarnitines, biogenic amines, and neurology-related proteins were mainly elevated, while glycerophospholipids primarily decreased in SMA plasma samples compared to controls. The biomarkers showed good performance in distinguishing SMA from controls with plasma AUCs >0.9. NEFH and creatinine were among the most prominent biomarkers for SMA diagnosis. Besides, 26 neurology-related proteins were found to be altered in patient CSF compared to controls. Furthermore, 11 potential proteins were identified to distinguish patients with 2 copies of SMN2 from those with 3 or 4 copies using plasma. By unveiling specific biomarkers, this study offers valuable insights for accurate disease diagnosis and monitoring treatment effectiveness. This enables personalized SMA management and accelerates the development of targeted therapies.

Introduction

Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene, which encodes the SMN protein (survival motor neuron protein). This disease is characterized by progressive degeneration of the motor neurons, resulting in generalized muscular weakness and secondary moderate to severe impairment, with an incidence of 1:8400 births in Europe and 1:11,000 births in the USA. Clinically, SMA exhibits a broad spectrum of severity and age of onset. The current classification differentiates five subtypes based on the age of onset, severity and maximal motor milestone reached: type 0 is the most severe, with death shortly after birth; type 1 is non-sitters, type 2 are sitters, type 3 are walkers and type 4 is adult onset. Cognitive functions are usually preserved, even if in the most severely affected patients neurodegeneration could reach not only the anterior horn cells but also be widespread in the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, brainstem, and cerebellum. At the molecular level, homozygous deletions or loss-of-function variants in SMN1 are the leading SMA-determining cause. The severity of the disease is modulated by the copy number of a nearly identical paralog gene, SMN2. Both genes are located on chromosome 5q13. The difference between SMN1 and SMN2 lies in a few nucleotides, including one critical substitution in exon 7 of SMN2 that leads to alternative splicing and exclusion of exon 7 in about 90 % of transcripts. This results in the production of an unstable SMN protein. Of note, SMN2 is present in at least one copy, but the number of copies varies among individuals. Usually, the SMN2 copy number is inversely correlated with SMA severity, but other factors, such as hypoxia and PLS3 expression, could influence the phenotype.

Over recent years, novel therapies have been developed to treat SMA. Nusinersen (Spinraza), a synthetic antisense oligonucleotide, binds to intron 7 of the SMN2 pre-mRNA and promotes the production of a fully functional SMN protein. It is administered intrathecally with a loading dose in the first two months (day 1, 15, 29, 64) and maintenance doses every fourth months. The earlier the drug is given, the higher the success rate. Other therapies are Onasemnogene Abeparvovec (Zolgensma ), a one-time SMN1 gene replacement therapy given intravenously or intrathecally, and Risdiplam (Evrisdy ), an orally administered small molecule that modulates SMN2 splicing. The current innovative therapies can significantly alter the disease course. To facilitate presymptomatic diagnosis and improve outcomes, newborn screening programs for SMA have been implemented in several countries, including the USA, Germany, Belgium, and Australia. France is expected to launch its program in September 2025. Although SMN2 copy number is the most significant known genetic modifier, the correlation between genotype and phenotype is incomplete. Effective SMA management has markedly improved over the years through advances in understanding genotypes, phenotypes and severity which help in stratifying patients and in therapeutic decisions. Ongoing research would enable more personalized and more objective treatment plans.

Comprehensive omics approaches offer a powerful biological lens to understand disease mechanisms and treatment response. For instance, the SMN protein in blood or CSF has been used extensively as a biomarker for SMA. Treatments aim to raise their levels, with increases indicating target engagement and monitoring treatment response. However, their overlap across clinical subtypes limits their utility as severity markers. Variability in disease severity, especially in milder or late-onset cases, makes decisions complex. Reliable biomarkers that predict severity and monitor response are essential. In this study, we focused on metabolomic and proteomic profiling of plasma and CSF samples from SMA patients before and after six months of Nusinersen treatment at two French centers. In this study, we performed metabolomic and proteomic profiling of plasma and CSF samples from SMA patients both longitudinally (before and after six months of Nusinersen treatment) and cross-sectionally (compared to control individuals). Our objectives were to identify biomarkers correlating with disease severity and monitoring treatment response. These findings could improve disease monitoring and support appropriate and timely treatment for SMA patients.
Materials and Methods
Patients and samples

Patients with a molecularly confirmed SMA diagnosis who underwent treatment with Nusinersen in two French centers were included. Plasma and CSF samples were collected during the regular visits for treatment (before treatment, day 15, day 30, day 64, day 184, every four months). Different scales to evaluate motor function (Motor Function Measurement, HINE, HFMSE, CHOP intend), respiratory function (vital capacity), and digestive and orthopedic statuses were used to evaluate the severity of the disease and efficacy of treatment. Fifty-three plasma samples SMA patients were selected for the study before treatment (baseline) and were compared to 71 age and sex matched plasma samples from controls (from two French centers: Caen University Hospital and Toulouse University Hospital). Twenty-three plasma samples at day 184 after treatment initiation were selected. Twenty-eight CSF samples before treatment and 22 CSF samples at day 184 after treatment initiation were analyzed. Age and sex matched CSF controls from 49 participants (Caen University Hospital and Toulouse University Hospital) have been used. All procedures were performed under the ethical standards of the institutional and/or national research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. To identify the biomarkers for SMA management, the comparisons between SMA and control groups were performed (i) SMA samples with different phenotype characteristics at baseline before Nusinersen treatment and control samples and (ii) SMA samples at baseline before Nusinersen treatment and samples at day 184 after treatment.
Targeted metabolomics
Reagents

All reagents, internal and calibration standards, quality controls, test mix, and a patented 96-well filter plate required for the AbsoluteIDQ p180 analysis are included in the kit or provided by Biocrates Life Science AG (Innsbruck, Austria). All metabolites were identified and quantified using isotopically labeled internal standards and multiple reaction monitoring as optimized and provided by Biocrates Life Sciences AG (Innsbruck, Austria).
Metabolite quantitation

Sample preparation was carried out according to the manufacturer's protocol. Briefly, 10 muL of plasma was transferred to the upper 96-well plate and dried under a nitrogen stream. After that, 50 muL of a 5 % PITC solution was added to derivatize amino acids and biogenic amines. After incubation, the spots were dried again before the metabolites were extracted using 5 mM ammonium acetate in methanol (300 muL) into the lower 96-well plate for analysis after further dilution using the MS running solvent A. Quantification was carried out using isotopically labeled internal standards and a calibration curve. The AbsoluteIDQ  p180 kit is a fully internal standards for quantitation. Amino acids and biogenic amines are determined in automated assay based on phenylisothiocyanate derivatization of the target analytes in bodily fluids using liquid chromatography-tandem mass-spectrometry LC-MS mode, acylcarnitines, phospholipids, sphingomyelins, and the sum of hexoses are analyzed in flow injection analysis. The analyses were performed following the instructions of the kit manufacturer using LC instrument Shimadzu UFLC System (Shimadzu, Prominence, Kyoto, Japan) coupled to the 4000 Qtrap mass spectrometer (Sciex, Framingham, MA, USA) with an electrospray ion source. Data acquisition and processing were performed using the Analyst 1.6.3 software (Sciex, Framingham, MA, USA).
Targeted proteomics profiling

An amount of 1 muL of plasma and CSF samples were subjected to targeted proteomics by applying the multiplex proximity extension assay (PEA) technology (Olink Target 96) using Olink  Signature Q100. Protein measurement was conducted using the Olink Target 96 Neurology assay version v.3911 (Olink, Uppssala, Sweden), which includes 92 oligonucleotide-labeled antibody probe pairs targeting proteins related to neurobiological processes and neurological diseases. These proteins are associated with neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation, which are central to SMA pathology. Additionally, this panel includes promising markers of SMA, such as neurofilament light chain (NEFL). Once bound to the targets, new DNA amplicons, identified by barcodes corresponding to their respective antigens, were established. Measurement of the amplicons was conducted using the Fluidigm BioMark HD real-time PCR technique. The counts of known barcode sequences were converted into normalized protein expression (NPX) units, a relative protein quantification unit on a log2 scale. For the Olink data were processed using Olink's standard pipeline, which includes extension control, inter-plate control, and normalization to produce NPX values on a log2 scale. To monitor assay performance control samples were included on each plate, and inter-plate variation was assessed using the internal controls provided by Olink. Data was acquired with Olink Signature B100, and processed using NPX  Signature software (v.1.9.0). NEFH in plasma and CSF was quantified using electrochemiluminescence assays (Meso Scale Discovery [MSD], Rockville, MD, USA). Data will be acquired using a SECTOR S 6000 plate reader (Meso Scale Diagnostics, Rockville, MD, USA). NEFH levels were then log-2 transformed and combined with NPX data for subsequent analysis.
Phospholipase A2 activity assessment

Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) activity was measured in plasma and CSF based on the method from Fonteh et al. using Invitrogen EnzChek  Phospholipase A2 Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). To summarize, a Lipid Mix was created using 30 muL 10 mM dioleoylphosphatidylcholine, 30 muL 10 mM dioleoylphosphatidylglycerol, and 30 muL 1 mM PLA2 substrate. The substrate-liposome mix were generated by slowly adding 50 muL of Lipid Mix to 5 mL 1X PLA2 reaction buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl at pH 8.9, 100 mM NaCl, and 1 mM CaCl2) in a 20 mL beaker containing a small magnetic stir bar. The available diluted CSF and plasma samples were placed in 96-well plates, and PLA2 activity was activated by adding 50 mul of the substrate-liposome mix. Fluorescence was measured (excitation at 360 nm and emission at 460 nm), and the specific activity [relative fluorescent units (RFU)/mug protein/min] for each sample was calculated.
Data visualization

All data analyses and visualizations were performed using R version 4.3.0. Significantly altered analytes were visualized as a volcano plot using the EnhancedVolcano R package (version 1.20.0). Upset plots were created to assess the commonality of the significant molecules between different comparisons. The UpSetR package (version 1.4.0) was used to generate the upset plots. Heatmaps were conducted using the ComplexHeatmap R package (version 2.18.0) to visualize the level of molecules. The ggplot2 R package (version 3.January 5, 9000) was utilized to create violin plots.
Data analysis

All data matrices are provided in supplementary tables. The data matrix was log2-transformed. Missing values were imputed using the nearest neighbor averaging algorithm using the KNNimp(.) function in the multiUS package version 1.2.3. The limma package was used for differential analysis, with sex and age considered by adding them as covariates. A mixed-effect model adjusting sex and age and treating sampleID as a random factor was performed for the comparison between samples collected after 184 days and at baseline using OlinkAnalyze package version 3.8.2 and lmerTest package version 3.1-3. Enrichment analysis was conducted on significant proteins using the Enrichr package version 3.2. Spearman correlation analysis was performed using the correlation package version 0.8.4. False discovery rates (FDR) were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg-Yekutieli method. Significantly altered molecules were determined with a cut-off of FDR 0.05. The diagnostic performance of significant molecules revealed from the comparison between the sample at baseline and the control was subsequently assessed. The potential biomarkers were evaluated based on the AUC through the classical univariate receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses in the MetaboAnalystR package version 4.0.0. The multivariate analyses consisting of three machine learning models of partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), support vector machines (SVM), and random forest (RF) were implemented using the caret (version 6.0-94) package. The predictive models were validated by nested cross-validation. The process involved an outer loop for performance estimation and an inner loop for hyperparameter tuning. The dataset was partitioned into 5 stratified folds. For each iteration of the outer loop, a single fold was reserved as the test set to evaluate the final model's performance, while the remaining folds served as the training data for the inner loop, with a second level of 5-fold cross-validation performed to optimize model hyperparameters.

Fig. 2

For plasma samples, the statistical analysis identified 22 proteins and 55 metabolites (19 glycerophospholipids, 18 acylcarnitines, 13 amino acids and 5 biogenic amines) that were differentially altered in SMA (Baseline) compared to controls, while 28 proteins and 69 metabolites (35 acylcarnitines, 17 glycerophospholipids, 9 biogenic amines, 5 amino acids, and 3 sphingomyelins) were found in SMA (J184) compared to controls (Fig. 2a).

In terms of disease severity, the comparison between SMA (Mild) and SMA (Severe) with controls yielded 20 and 110 features, respectively. Moreover, 76 (15 proteins and 61 metabolites) and 56 (12 proteins and 44 metabolites) molecules were disturbed in SMN2 (Copy2) and SMN2 (Copy3/4) compared to controls. Among 19 prominent proteins with log(FC) > 1.5, 16 proteins (including WWWP2, EIF4B, PMVK, and NAA10) were up-regulated consistently from SMA (Baseline) to SMA (J184) compared to controls (Fig. 2b). Of note, PMVK expression level increased more than 4 times in SMA (Baseline) and more than 12 times in SMA (J184) compared to controls. Meanwhile, NEFH and NEFL expression were increased in SMA (Baseline), then decreased in SMA (J184) compared to controls. Conversely, PTS was down-regulated in SMA compared to control groups. Regarding metabolome, creatinine and c4-OH-Pro levels were lower, while acylcarnitines (compressing C18:1-OH, C18, C6:1, and C5:1), phosphatidylcholines (PCs) (PC aa C26:0, and PC aa C24:0), and ether-linked phosphatidylcholines [PC(O-)] PC ae C30:2 were higher in SMA than in control groups (Fig. 2c and d). Volcano plots resulting from differential analysis using plasma samples between SMA patients and controls are exhibited in Supplementary Figs. S1-S3. The top five significant analytes in each comparison are visualized in Supplementary Fig. S4.

Regarding CSF samples, 25 proteins were perturbed in SMA (J184) compared to controls (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. S5). In terms of clinical severity, PRTFDC1 was altered in SMA (Severe) versus controls, as well as in SMA (Copy2) and SMA (Copy3/4) compared to controls. Among them, ADGRB3, NXPH1, and CD302 were down-regulated consistently in SMA compared to control groups. PRTFDC1 was up-regulated in SMA compared to the control groups. The upset plot shows the intersection of significant omics features altered in the SMA groups compared to controls in the plasma analysis (Fig. 3). Significant molecules were highly overlapped between comparisons, revealing potential biomarkers for SMA groups with different phenotypes. PMVK, PRTFDC1, and AKT1S1 were shared among comparisons between SMA groups with different phenotypes versus controls. Significant proteins were then investigated to elucidate the underlying biological processes, revealing several altered pathways (Table 1). The complete list of significant molecules and their related statistics is presented in Supplementary Tables S4 and S5.
Diagnosis biomarker

Univariate ROC curve analysis using plasma samples from SMA patients at baseline and controls yielded AUCs >0.6 of 12 proteins (Supplementary Table S6). Of note, PMVK, EIF4B and PRTFDC1 exhibited AUCs >=0.8. For plasma metabolomics, there were 11 significant metabolites with AUCs >0.6. Among them, 6 metabolites had AUCs from 0.70 to 0.78, and C18:2 had an AUC of 0.83 (Supplementary Table S7). Creatinine had a good diagnostic ability with AUC = 0.94.

Diagnosis biomarker validation. a) Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves from classification models using significant neurology-related proteins from plasma samples. b) The mean importance score of significant neurology-related proteins in plasma samples classification models. c) ROC curves from classification models using significant metabolites from plasma samples. d) The mean importance score of significant metabolites in plasma samples classification models. PLS-DA: partial least squares discriminant analysis; SVM: support vector machines; RF: random forest; ROC: receiver operating characteristic curve.
Fig. 4

The biomarkers, both proteins and metabolites, showed good performance (almost AUCs >0.9) in classifying the plasma samples from SMA with control groups (Fig. 4). Three models, including RF, SVM, and PLS-DA, demonstrated AUCs of 0.96 +- 0.03, 0.84 +- 0.04, and 0.95 +- 0.02 using protein markers (Fig. 4a). NEFH, IFI30, and PMVK had the most important roles in the classifications (Fig. 4b). And AUCs of 0.97 +- 0.02, 0.93 +- 0.04, and 0.91 +- 0.04 using metabolite marker applied RF, SVM, and PLS-DA algorithms with the prominent contribution of creatinine and cis-4-Hydroxyproline (C4 OH Pro) (Fig. 4c and d).
The alteration of correlation with NEFH and NEFL across time
Alterations of significant correlations between NEFH and other molecules in the baseline SMA group. a) Plasma samples. b) Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples. CSF: cerebrospinal fluid.
Fig. 5

Since NEFH and NEFL were reported to be potential biomarkers for SMA, the correlations between NEFH and NEFL with other molecules in baseline SMA samples were investigated. The significant correlations are shown in Supplementary Table S8-10. Remarkably, NEFH was significantly up-regulated in SMA (Baseline) compared to controls. Therefore, we focused on the alterations of these significant correlations of NEFH in SMA (Baseline) compared to SMA (J184) and controls. This protein was positively correlated with 6 proteins (NEFL, ISLR2, KIRREL2, TNFRSF13C, FGFR2, and CDH15) in plasma baseline samples (Fig. 5a). The correlations increased in the baseline compared to controls and decreased in the samples after 184 days of treatment. For CSF samples, significant correlations were observed between NEFH with 3 proteins (NEFL, ISLR2, and SFRP1) at baseline (Fig. 5b). Interestingly, NEFH was correlated with NEFL and ISLR2 regardless of sample type, whether plasma or CSF. In the same vein, the positive correlations between NEFH and NEFL, ISLR2, and SFRP1 were augmented in baseline compared to controls and declined after 184 days of treatment.
Potential protein biomarker for stratification of patients with different SMN2 copy numbers

Classification of patients with different SMN2 copy numbers. a) Receiver operating characteristic curve curves from classification models using selected neurology-related proteins from plasma samples. b) The mean importance score of selected neurology-related proteins in plasma samples classification models. c) Violin plots of the top 5 potential neurology-related proteins. PLS-DA: partial least squares discriminant analysis; SVM: support vector machines; RF: random forest; ROC: Receiver operating characteristic curve.
Fig. 6

In our cohort, machine learning approaches using all analytes showed that plasma proteome had a differentiated capacity, while plasma metabolome and CSF profiles failed to classify SMA (Copy2) with SMA (Copy3/4) groups. Among the top 20 important proteins, 11 overlapped proteins from RF, SVM, and PLS-DA models were selected to be validated subsequently. Fig. 6a exhibited acceptable performance with AUCs of 0.86 +- 0.02, 0.73 +- 0.06, and 0.76 +- 0.08 using SVM, PLS-DA, and RF algorithms. NEFL, ISLR2, KIRREL2, CDH15, and FGFR2 contributed the most to the classification of patients with different SMN2 copy numbers (Fig. 6b). All these 5 proteins were upregulated in SMA (Copy2) compared to SMA (Copy3/4) groups (Fig. 6c).
Phospholipase A2 activity as a potential biomarker for response to treatment
Phospholipase A activity in the plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
Fig. 7

In SMA plasma samples, PC species levels are mainly elevated, whereas lysoPC levels are generally reduced compared to controls (Table S4). Phospholipase A2 catalyzes the deacylation of PC into LysoPC. Consequently, our findings may indicate diminished phospholipase A2 activity in SMA patients. To verify this, we evaluated phospholipase A2 activity. As a result, PLA2 activity in CSF significantly declined in SMA samples at baseline and after 6 months of treatment compared to controls (Fig. 7). However, no significant changes in PLA2 activity were observed in plasma samples, although there was an increasing trend over time.
Discussion

SMA disease is a neuromuscular disorder characterized by clinical heterogeneity. Currently, there is a pressing need to identify reliable biomarkers for patient stratification and disease monitoring. The emergence of new targeted and innovative therapies highlights the importance of developing tools for early diagnosis and treatment assessment. These specific biomarkers could streamline patient stratification. We performed targeted metabolomic and proteomic analyses on an SMA cohort before and after Nusinersen treatment, comparing them to control individuals. The study revealed significant metabolic and proteomic remodeling in untreated SMA patients. We observed differential changes in these profiles when comparing SMA patients to controls, as well as among SMA individuals with varying clinical severities and copy numbers.

Several prominent proteins were revealed for SMA diagnostic. Neurofilaments, phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNEFH) and NEFL, are released during axonal degeneration. Their levels increase in CSF and plasma/serum of patients with motor neuronopathy and are associated with disease activity. In this work, plasma NEFH was significantly upregulated in SMA patients at baseline compared to controls and then decreased after 184 days of Nusinersen treatment. This aligns with previous studies showing higher levels at baseline in SMA versus non-SMA and a rapid decline at 2 months of treatment, which was more pronounced at 10 months and varied according to clinical severity. NEFH is a neuronal cytoskeleton protein released into circulation after axonal damage, indicating neuronal degeneration, and its high levels are found in neurodegenerative diseases.

The molecular alterations observed in this study likely reflect a combination of primary effects of SMN deficiency and secondary downstream consequences of motor neuron degeneration, muscle wasting, and systemic metabolic adaptation. Changes in neurofilaments and axon-related proteins detected in both plasma and CSF and partially reversed after Nusinersen treatment support a direct link to SMN-dependent neuronal pathology. In contrast, alterations in metabolites such as creatinine, acylcarnitines, and phospholipids are more consistent with secondary effects related to denervation, reduced muscle mass, and altered energy metabolism.

Moreover, NEFH was positively correlated in plasma and CSF with NEFL and ISLR2 (Immunoglobulin superfamily containing leucine-rich repeat protein 2). The correlation between neurofilament heavy and light chains has been described, and both are considered potential biomarkers. NEFL shows a strong correlation with disease severity, being higher in patients with 2 SMN2 copies compared to those with 3 and 4 copies. It is also significantly elevated in patients at baseline versus controls, aligning with reported works. Moreover, younger patients showed a greater reduction in NEFL levels compared to older patients, therefore predicting motor improvement following treatment with Nusinersen. Besides, ISLR2 is a protein involved in axon guidance in brain development, thought to positively regulate axon extension and help reorganize the cytoskeleton of developing neurons. The strong correlation between ISLR2 and neurofilaments in plasma and CSF may be due to their roles in axon development and stability. We observed a significant negative correlation between NEFH and four other plasma proteins (KIRREL2, TNFRSF13C, FGFR2, and CDH15) with severity, as their levels were higher in patients with 2 SMN2 copies compared to those with 3 or 4 copies. Our predictive models identified another potential plasma diagnostic biomarker, IFI30, or Lysosomal Thiol Reductase, which helps unfold proteins for lysosomal breakdown and signals. IFI30 was decreased in patients at baseline compared to controls. One study suggested it might predict treatment response, as Nusinersen responders showed less decrease in CSF levels of IFI30 (along with ARSB, ENTPD2, and NEFL) than non-responders. Moreover, high expression of PMVK (Phosphomevalonate kinase) was observed in the plasma of SMA patients at baseline compared to controls, and after treatment compared to before treatment, making it a prominent potential biomarker. PMVK is an ATP-dependent, peroxisomal enzyme that converts mevalonate-5-phosphate into mevalonate-5-pyrophosphate in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway and the isoprenoid synthesis pathway. Intronic variants in the PMVK gene have been associated with the wearing-off phenomenon in Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disease. Besides, we determined several novel CSF potential biomarkers such as ADGRB3 (Adhesion G protein-coupled receptor B3), PRTFDC1 (Phosphoribosyltransferase domain-containing protein 1), CEACAM3 (a member of the family of carcinoembryonic antigen-related cell adhesion molecules), PFDN2 (Prefoldin subunit 2), CD302 (C-type lectin domain family 13 member A), NXPH1 (Neurexophilin-1) that downregulated in SMA patients after 6 months of treatment. External validation of the novel potential biomarkers is warranted in future work using an independent cohort.

passages.text: Further potential response markers were described in the literature were response to treatment was found correlated to an increase in OL1A2 and GRIA4 proteins, reduction in SEMA6A in CSF of SMA type III while in SMA type I an increase in Apolipoproteins (APOA1, APOE) and Transthyretin (TTR). Moreover, an increase in PARK7 (DJ-1) with decrease in Cathepsin D (CTSD) were found in CSF of responders.

Metabolome investigations were also SMA informative and provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms of the disease. Of note, plasma creatinine was found to be a remarkable biomarker for SMA diagnosis. Serum creatinine has been related to muscle deterioration, but its variability is broad. The increase in creatinine with decreasing creatine kinase during Nusinersen treatment suggests reduced muscle wasting and better energy metabolism. However, further prospective studies are necessary. Metabolic abnormalities (alteration of fatty acid metabolism, glucose tolerance impairment, and mitochondrial defects) were reported in SMA animals and patients, and there is a possible impact of SMN deficiency on metabolic abnormalities.
